loop:0.t: The R L Loop. Learning by doing: try something, see what happens, adjust.

loop:1.t:
Meet Pip, a little mouse in a little maze.Watch the cheese appear in the top corner. And right next to it, a sleeping cat.
Pip has no map and no instructions.Whatever it learns, it learns by trying things. That's reinforcement learning.

loop:2.t:
First, the one making choices. Pip, circled in teal. That's the agent.
Then the gold box. Everything else is the environment.Walls, rocks, cheese, cat, and the rules.
Pip controls its own moves, nothing more. It can't push a rock or wake the cat.

loop:3.t:
Watch the numbers fill the cells.Since nothing else ever moves, the situation is just where Pip stands.That's the state. Pip starts in cell sixteen.
Here, Pip always knows its cell. A robot with a camera might only see part of the room, and that's harder.

loop:4.t:
Four arrows, four moves. Up, right, down, left. That's the whole menu.
Now watch Pip try down.Bump. A wall. It stays put.Left bumps too.
The environment decides what each move really does.

loop:5.t:
Look at the number in each cell.Mostly zeros. The cheese pays plus one, the cat minus one.
Either one ends the walk.
Pip doesn't know these numbers in advance. All it wants is more reward.

loop:6.t:
Here's the whole cycle in one picture.The agent sends an action across.The environment sends back two things, the next state and a reward.
Then round it goes again. Watch the dot circle.That's the R L loop. Every method in this course runs on it.

loop:7.t:
Time ticks along this axis, zero, one, two, three.
Watch the letters line up. A state, an action, then a reward.Notice the reward carries the next tick's number. The answer always comes one tick later.
Teal for states, gold for actions, rose for rewards.

loop:8.t:
Pip knows nothing yet, so it rolls a four sided die.The die says right.
Watch Pip slide from cell sixteen to seventeen.Reward zero.That's one full turn of the loop, written in symbols on the card.

loop:9.t:
Pip walks a couple of steps, then rolls down.Bump. There's a wall below.
Pip stays in cell eighteen, and the reward is zero.
A wasted move still uses up a time step. The teal dots are Pip's footprints.

loop:10.t:
Round and round it goes. Watch Pip wander.Bumping, stepping back and forth, walking into a rock.
Each line of the log is one turn of the loop.And every single reward is zero.
Thirteen moves, and nothing to show for it.

loop:11.t:
Watch the last move. Pip steps up onto the cheese.Plus one!
Cheese and cat are terminal. Reaching one ends the walk.That whole walk is called an episode.
Then Pip is put back at the start, and a new episode begins.

loop:12.t:
Now let random Pip walk again and again.Each bar below is one episode. Taller means more steps.
Teal bars found the cheese. Rose bars found the cat.Out of these first ten, only three reach the cheese.

loop:13.t:
A hundred episodes, and only twenty six reached the cheese.
Why so few? Watch the rose arrows.The cat can be entered from four cells.The cheese, from only two.
And blind wandering is slow, about sixty three steps per episode.

loop:14.t:
Here's episode one again, move by move.Every reward is zero, until the very last.
So which moves earned the cheese? Nobody says.
That's the big difference from supervised learning.There, every example comes with the right answer. Here, only a score, and often a late one.

loop:15.t:
So what does Pip want? The most reward in total, over a whole episode.The next reward alone says almost nothing.
Twenty six cheeses, seventy four cats.The random policy averages minus point four eight per episode.
A policy is just a rule for picking moves. Later reels find much better ones.

loop:16.t:
Now you're the agent.Tap an arrow on the pad.
Each tap is one turn, and the log records it.
Try bumping into a rock. Then go find the cheese.

loop:17.t:
The same loop runs much bigger problems.D Q N watched screen pixels and played Atari for points.AlphaGo was rewarded only at the end, win or lose.
Chat models too. A whole reply can be one action, scored once.Only the sizes change.

loop:18.t:
So that's the loop.The agent acts, the environment answers with a reward and the next state, again and again until the episode ends.
Nobody tells Pip the right move. It just wants the most reward in total. And adding rewards up hides a catch, coming next.

returns:0.t: Rewards  and  Returns. Why the agent cares about the total, not just the next snack.

returns:1.t:
Back in Pip's maze. Watch Pip replay its first random walk.
Each step drops one reward into the row below.Zero, zero, zero, and only at the very end, plus one.
So how good was that walk, as a whole?

returns:2.t:
Watch the rewards fly into the jar.Thirteen zeros add nothing. Then the cheese adds one.
That total is the return. It scores a whole stretch of the walk, not one single step.

returns:3.t:
Here's the return written down. People use the letter G.It adds every reward after time t, all the way to the end.
Notice it starts one tick later, because each reward arrives just after its move.For episode one, the return from the start is one.

returns:4.t:
Why not judge a move by its own reward?Look at the four moves from the start.Every one pays zero next.
The next reward can't tell them apart.What differs comes later, and that's what the return counts.

returns:5.t:
Three random walks, all ending at the cheese.Watch how differently they wander.
Ten steps, fourteen steps, and a hundred and forty seven.Yet every return is exactly one.
With these rewards, a long detour costs nothing. Pip has no reason to hurry.

returns:6.t:
A common fix is a step cost.Watch the cells. Every ordinary step now costs a tenth.Bumps too.
The cheese and the cat stay the same, and both still end the walk.
Why a tenth? Just a small choice. Its size will matter.

returns:7.t:
Recount with the step cost.The gold path is the shortest way to the cheese, seven steps.
It now scores point four.The long hundred and forty seven step walk sinks to minus thirteen point six.
Now the total prefers short walks.

returns:8.t:
Here are all hundred random walks.Further right means longer. Higher means a better return.
Teal dots ended at the cheese, rose dots at the cat.They sit on two sloping lines. On each line, shorter is better.

returns:9.t:
Returns can start from any step. Look at the shortest walk.Next to the cheese, only the plus one is left. Its return is one.
One step back, pay the step cost first. Point nine.
Each return is the next reward, plus the return after it.All the way back to point four at the start.

returns:10.t:
From the very same start, random Pip's returns are all over the place.The best scored point three. The worst, about minus thirty.
So the return is a random number. Here it averages minus six point seven.
Average it over many walks from a cell, and you get what a later reel calls a value.

returns:11.t:
But the size of the cost matters.Make it one and a half per step.Compare the gold walk to the cheese with the rose walk into the cat.
The cheese walk scores minus eight. The cat walk, minus seven.The cat wins!
The agent chases the return you wrote down, not the one you meant.

returns:12.t:
This happens with real agents.
In a boat racing game, points came from hitting targets.Watch the boat circle the lagoon, where targets keep coming back.
It crashes, catches fire, never finishes, and still scores more than winning would.The reward said points, not winning.

returns:13.t:
Pip's walks always end. Many tasks don't.Up top, the episode stops, and the sum is one.
Below, a task that just keeps going, plus one every step.Watch the sum grow, and grow, forever.
Two agents with infinite returns can't be compared. The next reel fixes that.

returns:14.t:
Your turn. Drag the step cost.Three walks, three bars.The shortest cheese walk, episode one, and the quick dash into the cat.
At zero, the cheese walks tie.Push the cost up and watch the cat walk climb, until above one it's the best plan.

returns:15.t:
All of R L rests on one bet, the reward hypothesis.
Any goal can be written as getting the largest expected return.Expected just means averaged over all the luck along the way.
It's an assumption, not a theorem. But with careful rewards, it has carried R L a long way.

returns:16.t:
So, a reward scores one step.The return adds up every reward from a step until the end, and that's what an agent tries to make big.
And how you set the rewards decides what good means. Pick them carefully.

discount:0.t: The Discount Factor gamma. A reward tomorrow is worth a bit less than a reward today.

discount:1.t:
Remember this one? The hundred and forty seven step walk.With plain rewards, it scored the same as a ten step walk.
A step cost fixed that, but too big a cost made the cat look best.
And endless tasks have sums that never stop growing. Discounting helps with both.

discount:2.t:
A quick question. A hundred rupees today, or a hundred in a year?Most people grab it today.
You can use it sooner, and the future is uncertain.
So a reward far away should count a little less. R L builds that in with one number.

discount:3.t:
That number is gamma, the discount factor, between zero and one.Watch the bars shrink as the delay grows.
With gamma at point nine, each step of delay multiplies by point nine again.Ten steps out, a reward counts only about a third.

discount:4.t:
So here's the new return.The first reward counts fully. The next is times gamma. The one after, times gamma twice.
Set gamma to one, and you're back to the plain sum.
Below one, every reward still counts, just less the later it comes.

discount:5.t:
Back to the maze, with no step cost and gamma at point nine.Watch Pip take the shortest walk.Each cell shows how much its reward is shrunk.
The cheese is six steps after the first reward, so it counts point five three.

discount:6.t:
Now the same three random walks.Ten steps scores point three nine. Fourteen steps, point two five.The long one, practically nothing.
And notice. A discounted cheese is always above zero, a discounted cat always below.So the cat can never be the best plan.

discount:7.t:
Count backward along the shortest walk again.Next to the cheese, the return is one.Each step back multiplies by point nine, down to point five three at the start.
The rule is the next reward plus gamma times the next return. It's the seed of the Bellman equation.

discount:8.t:
Why multiply by gamma? Here's one honest reason.
Suppose every step has a one in ten chance the walk just stops.The crosses mark walks cut short in each cell.
Out of ten thousand tries, Pip reached the cheese about fifty three percent of the time.That's point nine to the sixth.

discount:9.t:
So gamma acts like a survival chance.Nine in ten that the world goes on, at every step.A reward six steps away has to survive six of those.
Averaged over the luck, that's exactly the discounted return.In practice, though, the designer just picks gamma.

discount:10.t:
Reason two. Remember the task paying plus one forever?Watch the gold line with gamma at point nine.
Six and a half after ten steps. Nearly ten after fifty.It creeps toward the red line, but never passes ten.
One over one minus gamma. Every return is finite now.

discount:11.t:
That same one over one minus gamma tells how far ahead an agent looks.Gold is gamma point nine, about ten steps.Teal is point nine nine, about a hundred.
It's not a hard wall. At that distance, a reward still counts about a third.

discount:12.t:
Gamma can even change which plan is best.A crumb, worth point three, sits just two steps up.The cheese is seven steps away.
With gamma at one half, the crumb wins.With point nine, the cheese wins.
They swap near point seven nine.

discount:13.t:
Your turn. Drag gamma, and Pip walks the best plan for that setting.
The two bars show what each plan is worth.Below about point seven nine, the crumb wins. Above it, Pip is patient enough for the cheese.

discount:14.t:
So why not always use gamma near one?Each row shows random Pip's hundred returns, at three gammas.
At one half, they squash near zero. Steady, but short sighted.At point nine nine, they spread almost from minus one to plus one.
Patience costs you noise.

discount:15.t:
Discounting is old. Economists use interest rates the same way.
In R L, the designer picks gamma. The Atari player D Q N used point nine nine.Games that always end, like Go, can use one.
And people? We care far more about today versus tomorrow than day one hundred versus day one hundred and one.

discount:16.t:
So, gamma shrinks each later reward a little more.The future is uncertain, and sums stay finite even when tasks never end.
Small gamma is impatient. Gamma near one is patient, but noisier.

mdp:0.t: Markov Decision Process. The board game that almost every R L problem is written as.

mdp:1.t:
Watch the maze draw itself, cheese, then cat.Pip notes its cell, picks a move, and gets a reward.
State, action, reward. Then round again.
This reel writes the maze's rules down so precisely that a computer could run them. That rulebook is called an M D P.

mdp:2.t:
First ingredient, the states. Watch the cell numbers appear.Take away the two rocks, and eighteen cells are left.
Two are circled in rose, the cheese and the cat.Land on either and the walk ends. They're terminal.
That leaves sixteen cells where Pip still has to choose.

mdp:3.t:
Second ingredient, the actions.Up, right, down, left. The same four in every cell.
Now watch Pip try left at the wall.Bump. It stays put, and that still counts as a step.

mdp:4.t:
Third ingredient, the rewards.Plus one for landing on the cheese, minus one for the cat.And zero everywhere else.
In general, a reward could depend on the cell, the move, and where Pip lands. Here, only the landing cell matters.

mdp:5.t:
Now a twist. Someone mopped the floor.Watch Pip try to go up.
Eight times in ten, it goes up.Otherwise it slides sideways, one in ten each way. Never backwards.
The same action can now lead to different cells. The world has become random.

mdp:6.t:
Pip stands at the start and tries right, again and again.It might move right, slide up, or slide into the wall and stay.
Watch the bars count where each try ended.After ten tries, nine went right and one slid up.

mdp:7.t:
Now keep going, to a thousand tries.Watch the bars settle.Seven hundred and ninety five went right. About a hundred each way otherwise.
Each single try is a surprise. But the chances behind them are fixed, eight in ten and one in ten.

mdp:8.t:
These chances get a name, transition probabilities.The chance of landing in each next cell, given where Pip is and what it tries.
From the start, trying right, they're point eight, point one, and point one.They always add up to one.

mdp:9.t:
Here's the whole rulebook.States, actions, transition chances, rewards, and gamma, the discount, at point nine.
That list is an M D P.
But Pip never reads it. It learns by trying.Working out the best plan from the rulebook itself is called planning.

mdp:10.t:
Here's the key assumption.Watch two paths reach the same cell. A gold detour, and a teal path straight up.
Either way, trying right gives the same chances.The past adds nothing, once you know the cell.
That's the Markov property.

mdp:11.t:
Can we check that in data?Pip arrives at this cell from below, or from above.
Each row of the table counts where it landed after trying right.The rows nearly match. Same eight in ten, whatever the past.
When the rules are hidden, this is how you'd test it.

mdp:12.t:
Now a rule that breaks it.The cat wakes after Pip's tenth step.
On the left, step four, the cat sleeps. Safe.On the right, step twelve, same cell. Pounce!
Same cell, different futures. Not Markov.The fix is to count the steps in the state too.

mdp:13.t:
So why does Markov matter so much?
Because Pip can file everything it learns per cell. Just sixteen of them.
If the past mattered, it would need a page for every path.After ten steps, that's over two hundred thousand paths.

mdp:14.t:
Look at this cell.In two thousand random walks, Pip stood here about sixteen thousand times.Most arrivals came by a brand new path.
Filed by path, each page would hold one lonely visit. Filed by cell, they all share one page. Markov makes that pooling fair.

mdp:15.t:
Your turn. Pip memorised a route as a fixed list. Up three, right four.Drag the slip chance, and the list runs a thousand times.
At point two, only two hundred and twenty nine runs reach the cheese.A list can't react to slips. A rule for every cell can. That's a policy, coming next.

mdp:16.t:
The name honours Andrey Markov, who studied chains of random events over a century ago.Richard Bellman put decisions into them in the nineteen fifties.
Robots, board games, and more are often written as MDPs.And when one snapshot isn't enough, people widen the state. The Atari player looked at the last four frames, so it could see motion.

mdp:17.t:
So, an M D P writes a world down. States, actions, chances, rewards, and gamma.Outcomes can be random, but the chances are fixed.
And because of Markov, Pip can learn cell by cell, not path by path.

policy:0.t: Policies. The agent’s rulebook: in this situation, do that.

policy:1.t:
Remember Pip's memorised list? Seven moves, on a wet floor.Watch this run.
On move two, Pip slides off the route.The list doesn't care. It still says up, then right, straight into rocks.
A list only works if nothing goes wrong.

policy:2.t:
So instead, Pip writes a rule card.Watch the arrows appear, one in every cell.
That's a policy, written pi. Wherever Pip stands, the card says what to do.
Why is the cell enough? Because the maze is Markov. This card is policy A.

policy:3.t:
Watch policy A on the wet floor.On move two, Pip slides right instead of going up.
No problem. The new cell has its own arrow, pointing back to the route.Cheese in nine steps instead of seven.
A policy never assumes where Pip will be. It only asks, where am I now?

policy:4.t:
How many rule cards are there?Watch random cards flash by.
Four choices in each of sixteen cells. That's about four point three billion cards.
Most are silly. Trying them all is hopeless. Finding a good one without that is what the rest of R L is about.

policy:5.t:
Here's a second card, policy B.It's a copy of A, with one arrow changed. Look at the rose box, just left of the cat.
A points up. B points down, into a rock.
Pip only lands there by slipping. So is B really worse? Pip has to walk to find out.

policy:6.t:
How do we score a walk? By its return, with gamma at point nine.Watch the steps count along policy A's route.
Seven steps to the cheese scores point five three.A cat scores the same, but negative.

policy:7.t:
Pip walks once with each card.To be fair, both walks use the same dice. The same slips at the same moments.
Watch them go side by side.Both reach the cheese in nine steps. Point four three each.
A tie. It tells us nothing.

policy:8.t:
Walk two. Watch the top row.Pip slips down into the changed cell.
On the left, A points up, and Pip climbs back to the cheese.On the right, B points into the rock. Bump, then a slip into the cat.
Once there, B always ends on the cat.

policy:9.t:
Now five thousand walks each.Watch the average return. The lines jump early, then flatten.
A settles near point three three. B, near point two nine.Luck is only about five thousandths here, so the gap is real.
Average return, measured from every cell, is a policy's value. That's next.

policy:10.t:
So far, each cell held one fixed move. That's deterministic.Now watch this cell hold chances instead.Left, point eight five. Each other move, point oh five.
That's a stochastic policy.Careful, two kinds of chance now. The floor's slips are the world's. These dice are Pip's choice.

policy:11.t:
Why would Pip roll dice on purpose?A learner has to explore, to try moves it wouldn't normally make.And against an opponent, being predictable gets punished. Think rock, paper, scissors.
But a fixed maze has no opponent. The best policy there needs no dice.

policy:12.t:
Drag epsilon. With that chance, Pip ignores its arrow and moves at random.Watch for the orange dice.
The number on top is the average return.At zero, it's point three three one.Turn it all the way up, and it drops to about zero.

policy:13.t:
Your turn. Tap a cell to turn its arrow.Pip walks your card five thousand times, with the same dice.
Policy A scores point three three one. Can you beat it?Barely. The very best card is only a hair better. Or try breaking A. Which cells matter?

policy:14.t:
Policies are everywhere.A thermostat runs a tiny one. Too cold, heat on.A robot maps its sensors to motor commands.
AlphaGo's policy network gave a chance to every legal move.It learned from millions of human moves, then by playing itself.

policy:15.t:
So, a policy is a rule from state to action.An arrow in every cell, so it keeps working after any slip.
To compare policies, run each many times and average the returns.One walk is luck. That average, from every cell, is a policy's value. That's next.

values:0.t: Value Functions. How good is it to be here? How good is this move?

values:1.t:
Back in Pip's maze. Watch it draw itself.Cheese pays plus one, the cat minus one, and either ends the walk.
Gamma is point nine again.And the floor is dry, so the only randomness left is Pip's own.

values:2.t:
Pip uses policy A, the arrows from the last reel.But one move in five is random. The question marks show that.
So the arrow wins eighty five times in a hundred.Bumps still count as a step.

values:3.t:
How good is it to start in this corner? Let's just try.
Watch walk one. Up, along the top, and onto the cheese.Seven steps.
The plus one gets shrunk six times by point nine, so the return is point five three.

values:4.t:
Now three more walks from the same corner.Walk two gets distracted twice, and scores point three nine.
Walk three slips onto the cat. Minus point four eight.Walk four goes straight.
Same cell, same policy, different returns.

values:5.t:
Let's chart them.Each dot is one walk. Gold reached the cheese, rose hit the cat.
The dark line is the average so far.After four walks, it's point two four.

values:6.t:
Pip keeps walking. Watch the average line.Early on, it jumps around.
But each new walk moves it less and less.After a thousand walks, it settles at point four.
That settled number is what we were after.

values:7.t:
That settled average has a name. It's the value of the cell.The value of the start is about point four.
In probability terms, it's the expected return. What the average closes in on.

values:8.t:
Now do that from every cell.Watch the notebook fill in, one cell at a time.A thousand walks each. Brighter gold means higher value.
The cheese and cat stay blank. Standing there, the walk is already over.

values:9.t:
Beside the cheese, the value is point eight seven, not one.Why? One move in twenty there goes down, onto the cat.
Now compare two cells, both three steps away.The top row is worth more than the one beside the cat.From there, one random step right is a disaster.

values:10.t:
Meet the Wanderer. No arrows at all, every move random.
Watch its first walk. Back and forth, back and forth.It does find the cheese, but only on step thirty five.
By then, the plus one has shrunk to point oh three.

values:11.t:
Here's the Wanderer's notebook filling in.Every single value is negative.
Why? Count the ways in. Rose arrows lead onto the cat from four cells.Gold arrows reach the cheese from only two.
A random walker usually meets the cat first.

values:12.t:
The two notebooks, side by side.Look at the start. Point four under the arrows.Below zero under the Wanderer.
So a value only means something for a given policy.And the arrows win in every cell.

values:13.t:
The notebook says how good a cell is. But Pip has to choose moves.Look at the four arrows beside the cheese.
The action value, called Q, scores a move.Take that move first, then follow the policy, and average the returns.

values:14.t:
Watch the four moves get their scores.Right is the cheese, so its Q is one.Down is the cat, minus one.The best move has the biggest Q.
Mix them by the policy's chances, and you get back the notebook value, point eight seven.

values:15.t:
So why bother with values?The value of a cell lets you compare cells, and compare policies.
Q tells you which move is best next.And if a move beats the habit's value, switching to it only helps.
Much of R L builds on that.

values:16.t:
The catch? Measuring by walking is slow.This notebook took about seventy six thousand steps. The Wanderer's, about six hundred thousand.
Yet look at neighbouring cells.Point eight seven, then point seven six one step back.They're clearly linked. The next reel turns that link into a shortcut.

values:17.t:
Your turn. Drag the slider to change how random Pip is.Watch the notebook change.
Then tap any cell, and Pip walks once from there.Compare that one walk with the notebook. One walk is luck.

values:18.t:
AlphaGo had a value network.Show it a Go position, and it guessed the expected result.
Chess programs score positions in a similar spirit.And many modern learners train a value estimate called a critic.

values:19.t:
So, a cell's value is the expected return from there, following the policy.Change the policy, and the values change.
Q scores a move. Take it first, then follow the policy. And the biggest Q is the best move.

bellman:0.t: The Bellman Equation. Value of here equals reward now plus discounted value of next.

bellman:1.t:
Here's Pip's notebook from the last reel.A thousand walks from every cell.
That took about seventy six thousand steps of walking.
But look at the neighbours. Their numbers seem related.Could a cell's value be worked out from them?

bellman:2.t:
Watch one walk from the start.Cheese on step seven. Return, point five three.
Now cut it after the first step.The rest is its own walk, from the cell above, worth point five nine.
The whole walk is just the first reward, plus point nine times the rest.

bellman:3.t:
That split works for every walk, so it works on average too.The rest is a fresh walk from wherever Pip lands.
Walks that went up first averaged point four five afterwards, close to that cell's value.
So, value here is the average of the reward plus point nine times the value where Pip lands. That's the Bellman equation.

bellman:4.t:
So what exactly gets averaged? Two kinds of chance.
Pip's own. Which move it picks, mostly the arrow.
And the floor's. Where each move lands.Today's floor is dry, so each move reaches one known cell.

bellman:5.t:
Take the cell beside the cheese.Watch the four moves appear, with their chances.Right, eighty five in a hundred. Each other move, five.
Right lands on the cheese, and down on the cat. Both end the walk.Up bumps the wall. Left goes one cell back.

bellman:6.t:
Now plug in real numbers.Each move scores its reward, plus point nine times the value where it lands.
Weight them by how often each move happens.Point eight seven.And the notebook says point eight seven. The rule holds.

bellman:7.t:
Try the start cell.Up lands on point four six, right on point four five.The two bumps keep Pip where it is.
The rule gives point four one. The walks gave point four.Close, but not equal. Even a thousand walks leave a little noise.

bellman:8.t:
Now turn the rule around.Start with a blank notebook, every number zero.
Apply the rule to every cell, using the current numbers.That pass is a sweep. Repeat until nothing changes.
And Pip never takes a single step.

bellman:9.t:
Here's sweep one. Watch which cells change.Only the cells touching the cheese or the cat.
Beside the cheese, it jumps to point eight.Beside the cat, a small minus, a five percent risk.
Everything else still sees only zeros.

bellman:10.t:
Now watch the sweeps run.Each one carries the good news one cell further from the cheese.
The start stays near zero for a while.Then, at sweep seven, it jumps. The cheese is seven steps away.

bellman:11.t:
This chart tracks the start cell, sweep by sweep.Watch it climb toward the dashed line.
By sweep sixteen, nothing moves by more than a thousandth.
Why does it settle? Each sweep shrinks every error by at least point nine.

bellman:12.t:
Walks on the left, sweeps on the right.They agree within about a hundredth, and the sweeps have no noise.
The walks took seventy six thousand steps.The sweeps, about a thousand small sums.

bellman:13.t:
The catch? Sweeps need the maze's rules.For every move, where Pip can land, how likely, and what it pays.
That's a model. The walks needed none of it.
Often there's no model. Later reels keep the rule but learn from experience instead.

bellman:14.t:
Now ask for the best Pip could possibly do.
Instead of averaging over moves, take the biggest.That's the Bellman optimality equation.
Watch the sweeps. They settle after seven.The result, V star, is the best policy's value in every cell.

bellman:15.t:
In each cell, the best move has the biggest score.Watch the arrows. They lead straight to the cheese.Between the rocks, there's a tie, so either move is best.
The start is now worth point five three, against point four for Pip's habit.

bellman:16.t:
Your turn. Drag the slider to run more sweeps.Watch the news spread out from the cheese and the cat.
Then tap any cell, and the card shows the rule at work there.

bellman:17.t:
Richard Bellman called this dynamic programming, back in the nineteen fifties.
Planners with a model sweep it.Without one, T D learning nudges values toward the reward plus gamma times the next value.
And Q-learning, and the Atari player D Q N, aim at the best next move's value.

bellman:18.t:
So, a walk's return is its first reward plus gamma times the rest.Average that, and you get the Bellman equation.
Sweep it until nothing changes, and you get values without walking. Put a max inside, and you get the best possible values.

explore:0.t: Exploration versus Exploitation. Order your favourite dish, or try something new?

explore:1.t:
Meet Pip, out for dinner.On the left, its favourite café, The Usual. Always good.
On the right, a New Place just opened.It might be wonderful. It might be awful.
Pip can only eat in one place tonight. Which one?

explore:2.t:
Heading back to The Usual is exploiting. Using what already works.Trying the New Place is exploring. Taking a chance, to learn something.
Exploring might cost a good dinner tonight.But it might find a better café for every night after.

explore:3.t:
It depends on what's ahead.If Pip leaves town tomorrow, there's just one dinner left. Play it safe.
But if Pip just moved here, look at all those dinners ahead.A great find pays off again and again.
Exploring is an investment. You pay now, and collect later.

explore:4.t:
To study this, Pip visits an arcade with four cheese machines.Watch Pip pull machine C's lever.A crumb drops. That's worth one. Nothing is worth zero.
Each machine has its own hidden chance.Pip gets a thousand pulls, and wants as many crumbs as possible.

explore:5.t:
Let's peek inside the machines. Pip can't see this.Each one has its own secret crumb chance.
C is the best, seventy times in a hundred.Pip has to find that out by pulling.

explore:6.t:
First, Pip tries each machine once.A drops a crumb. B, C and D give nothing.
Now Pip follows a simple rule. Always pull the best so far.That's A. This rule is called greedy.

explore:7.t:
Watch the next thousand pulls, sped up.A, A, A, and A again.
Pip pulled A nine hundred and ninety seven times. Three hundred and eight crumbs.And C, the best machine, got just its one unlucky try.
One bad pull decided the whole evening.

explore:8.t:
Same visit, same luck. But now Pip always explores.Every pull goes to a random machine.
Watch the bars below. Pip's averages creep toward the secret chances.It learns a lot. But it collects only three hundred and ninety eight crumbs.
Three pulls in four go to machines worse than C.

explore:9.t:
To compare the two, imagine someone who knew the secrets.They'd pull C every time.
Every other pull gives up a little. Watch the costs appear.A pull of B gives up point one five of a crumb.A pull of D gives up the most.

explore:10.t:
Add those costs over the evening, and you get regret.The exploiter's bar comes in near four hundred.The explorer's, near two eighty.
Regret counts chances, not luck. It judges the choices, not the dice.

explore:11.t:
One visit isn't enough. Let's average over two thousand visits.Here's the chart.
Across, the pulls of the evening. Up, total regret so far.Lower is better. A flat line has stopped losing.

explore:12.t:
Watch the gold line. Always explore. Straight and steep.Now red, always exploit. Much lower on average.
But red never flattens.In about a third of visits, greedy got stuck on a worse machine.

explore:13.t:
Now a mixed Pip. One pull in ten goes random, the rest to the best so far.Watch the teal line.It ends at forty two, below both.
Random pulls rescue an unlucky start, so C gets its chance.But it keeps paying for them forever. Smarter ways come next.

explore:14.t:
Your turn. Tap a machine to pull its lever.You get twenty pulls.
Pull the ones you believe in, but don't forget the ones you haven't tested enough.At the end, the secrets and your regret appear.

explore:15.t:
You meet this every day.A music app slips new songs between your favourites.A website tests a new design on a few visitors.
Some medical trials send more patients to the treatment doing better.Each one is the arcade in disguise.

explore:16.t:
So, exploit what you know, or explore to learn more.Never exploring can lock you onto a worse option after one unlucky try.
Always exploring wastes your pulls. Regret measures the price of not knowing, and the next reels keep it small.

bandits:0.t: Multi-Armed Bandits. R L with one room and a row of slot machines.

bandits:1.t:
Old slot machines had one lever, an arm, and slowly took your money.People called them one armed bandits.
Pip's arcade has four, so it's a multi armed bandit.Each lever pays by its own hidden rule.
It's the simplest puzzle in R L, and one of the most useful.

bandits:2.t:
Let's name the pieces.Each machine is an arm. Picking which one to pull is the action.A crumb is worth one, nothing is worth zero.
Each arm has a hidden chance, and that chance is its true average.Pip never gets to see it.

bandits:3.t:
On the left, the maze. Every move changes where Pip stands.
On the right, the arcade. After any pull, the same four machines are waiting.
So there's no state to track.Every turn asks just one thing. Which arm?

bandits:4.t:
Pip can't see B's chance, but it can estimate it.Watch five pulls of B.Crumb, nothing, crumb, nothing, crumb.
Three crumbs in five pulls. The estimate is point six.The true chance is point five five. Close, but not exact.

bandits:5.t:
Pip doesn't need to keep a list of rewards.
Each pull nudges one number. Old estimate, plus the surprise, divided by the pull count.
Watch B's five pulls again, line by line.Each line lands exactly on the average so far.

bandits:6.t:
The surprise is how far the reward landed from what Pip expected.Dividing by n sets how big the step is.
Watch the dots shrink. The first pull moves the estimate all the way.The tenth, only a tenth of the way.
That way, every pull counts equally.

bandits:7.t:
Now a full visit. Pip plays greedy.It tries each machine once, then always pulls the highest estimate.
The bars below are Pip's estimates.After four pulls, B and C each have one crumb from one pull. A tie.

bandits:8.t:
Watch the tie breakers.B gets nothing. Then C gets nothing.C tries again, and misses again.
Then B drops a crumb, and pulls ahead for good.C is never pulled again. Two misses in a row, from a seventy percent machine. About one time in eleven.

bandits:9.t:
After a thousand pulls, B got nearly all of them.Its estimate settled near its true chance.
Now watch C's line on the chart.It's stuck at point three three, from three pulls long ago.Its true chance is point seven.

bandits:10.t:
Why can't greedy recover?
An estimate only changes when its arm is pulled.B started too high, so greedy kept pulling it, and it came back down.
But A, C and D look too low, so greedy never checks them again.Greedy fixes over optimism, never pessimism.

bandits:11.t:
Your turn. A simple fix is to try every machine a few times first.Drag to choose how many tries.
Watch the bars. Too few, and a good machine still freezes out.Too many, and Pip wastes pulls on bad machines.
The best number depends on things Pip doesn't know in advance.

bandits:12.t:
The first paper on this, in nineteen thirty three, asked how to choose between two treatments.Robbins framed the general problem in nineteen fifty two.
Today bandits choose headlines, ads, and page designs.Each click is a reward, each option an arm.

bandits:13.t:
So, a bandit has arms with hidden rewards, and no states.Estimate each arm by its average, updated as you go.
Pure greedy can freeze out a good arm after one unlucky start. The next reels explore more cleverly.

epsgreedy:0.t: epsilon-Greedy. Mostly do the best thing, occasionally roll the dice.

epsgreedy:1.t:
Back at the arcade, with the secret chances showing. Pip can't see them.Greedy Pip had another bad visit.
A paid first, so A got nine hundred and ninety seven pulls.C, the best, was tried once.
Its regret, three hundred and ninety nine point five.

epsgreedy:2.t:
The fix is almost silly. Before each pull, Pip spins a wheel.A small slice says random. Pull any machine.The rest says best so far.
The size of that slice is epsilon. This rule is epsilon greedy.

epsgreedy:3.t:
With epsilon at point one, nine pulls in ten go to the favourite.And a random pull can land on the favourite too.
So the favourite gets ninety two and a half percent.But every other machine still gets a few pulls, however bad it looks.

epsgreedy:4.t:
Same visit, same crumbs. But now Pip spins first.The first four pulls try each machine once. Only A pays.
Then the wheel in the corner mostly says best so far. And that's A.

epsgreedy:5.t:
Now watch the wheel.Random! It picks A itself.Random again. B, nothing. Then B, a crumb.
In between, greedy pulls keep going to A.C and D still show zero.

epsgreedy:6.t:
Pull thirty two. Random, and this time it picks C.A crumb!
C's average jumps to point five, above A.From now on, best so far means C.
One lucky spin undid one unlucky first try.

epsgreedy:7.t:
After a thousand pulls, C got nine hundred and one of them.Its average settled right next to its true chance.
Regret, about thirty four, against nearly four hundred for greedy.
Every estimate keeps getting fresh pulls. That's the whole point of epsilon.

epsgreedy:8.t:
Now average over two thousand visits.Red is greedy. Teal is epsilon greedy.Teal ends lower, at forty two.
In most of greedy's stuck visits, epsilon greedy found C.And it rarely lost the visits greedy got right.

epsgreedy:9.t:
But look at the teal line near the end. It never goes flat.Even when Pip is sure C is best, one pull in ten is still random.
And most of those hit worse machines.
Epsilon explores forever.

epsgreedy:10.t:
And it explores blindly.Look at the random pulls in this visit.D, the worst, got sixteen. B, the close runner up, thirty one.
On average the wheel splits them evenly, hopeless or promising. Smarter explorers come in the next reels.

epsgreedy:11.t:
Your turn. Drag epsilon.Each line is one setting, averaged over two thousand visits.
At zero, Pip is plain greedy.Too much, and pulls get wasted.Here, the lowest line is point oh five.

epsgreedy:12.t:
Early on, exploring is cheap and useful. Later, it's mostly waste.So let epsilon shrink.
Here epsilon is ten divided by the pulls so far.Watch the new brown line. It ends at twenty six point six, well below fixed epsilon.

epsgreedy:13.t:
But shrink it too fast, and Pip is greedy again.With one divided by pulls, a visit gets only about six random pulls.
C won the visit only three times in four.
So epsilon needs tuning.

epsgreedy:14.t:
Epsilon greedy is everywhere, because it's one line of code.Pip used it in the T D reel, one random move in five.
The Atari player D Q N started fully random.Watch its epsilon drop to point one over a million frames, then stay there.

epsgreedy:15.t:
So, with chance epsilon, pull a random arm. Otherwise, the best so far.An unlucky start can always be undone.
It's simple and often good enough. But it explores blindly, and epsilon needs tuning.

ucb:0.t: Upper Confidence Bound. Be optimistic about what you haven’t tried much.

ucb:1.t:
Pip's back at the cheese arcade.Four machines, each with its own hidden chance of a crumb.
C is the best. Pip doesn't know that.
Greedy gets stuck. Epsilon greedy unsticks it with random pulls. This reel finds a smarter way to explore.

ucb:2.t:
Look at the numbers under each machine.That's how often epsilon greedy pulls each one.D, the worst, still gets its share of dice rolls.
And the dice never stop. Pull ten or pull ten thousand, Pip keeps paying.

ucb:3.t:
Picture two machines.X gave nothing in its only pull. Y gave six crumbs in forty.Both look poor.
But one pull says almost nothing. X could still be great.Forty pulls pin Y down.
A smart explorer spends its tries where it's unsure.

ucb:4.t:
How much does an average wobble?Each dot is B's average after three pulls, in one visit.They're all over the place.
Now after thirty pulls. Much tighter around the true chance.Roughly, four times the pulls halves the wobble.

ucb:5.t:
U C B gives each machine a hopeful score.The bar is the estimate. The gold cap is a bonus.
The bonus is big for machines Pip barely knows.Then Pip pulls the highest total.
That's optimism in the face of uncertainty.

ucb:6.t:
Think of the bonus as stretching each estimate to the top of its plausible range.A has few pulls, so a wide band. D has many, a narrow one.
That top is an upper confidence bound. Hence the name, U C B.
Pull a worse machine enough, and its top drops below C's. Then it's rarely checked.

ucb:7.t:
Here's the bonus formula.It shrinks as a machine gets pulled. Watch the bars drop as n grows.
And it grows with the total pulls, t, but very slowly.So an ignored machine's bonus creeps up. Always another look, but rarely.

ucb:8.t:
Let's follow one visit. First, one pull of each machine.Only B gives a crumb.
Now watch the scores. Every bonus is the same, one point six seven.B's estimate puts it on top.
A score above one is fine. It's hopeful, not a chance.

ucb:9.t:
A few pulls later, look at C.Pulled only once, it has the biggest bonus, so it wins.
Pip pulls C. Nothing, again.Plain greedy, same visit, never went back to C at all.

ucb:10.t:
Watch the pulls roll by.Every pull elsewhere raises C's bonus a little.On pull twenty, C is on top again.
This time the crumbs come.The gold caps shrink, and C's bar rises toward seventy percent.

ucb:11.t:
After a thousand pulls, look at the counts.C got six hundred and seventy one. D, just twenty nine.
Now look at the tops. All four sit near one height.D is far below, so it keeps a tall cap and few pulls.B is close to C, so it needs many checks.

ucb:12.t:
So, is U C B better than epsilon greedy?Remember regret. Every pull of a worse machine adds what it gave up.
The chart shows total regret, averaged over two thousand visits.Here's epsilon greedy, the teal line. Forty two after a thousand pulls.

ucb:13.t:
Now U C B one, in gold.Surprise. It ends higher than epsilon greedy!
Its big early bonuses keep it checking B, which is close to C.
But notice. U C B's line keeps bending. Its checks get rarer.

ucb:14.t:
So play longer. Ten thousand pulls.Watch U C B one overtake, near pull two thousand eight hundred.
It finishes far lower, a hundred and forty one against two hundred and ninety four.
The card shows why. Epsilon greedy keeps pulling the hopeless D. U C B almost stops.

ucb:15.t:
To be fair, compare it with the tuned tricks from earlier reels.Shrinking epsilon, and trying each machine ten times first.Both beat U C B one here.
So what does U C B buy? No schedule to pick, and a guarantee that holds in any arcade.

ucb:16.t:
Your turn. Drag c, the bonus scale.At zero there's no bonus. That's plain greedy.
Too big, and Pip keeps rechecking machines it already knows.Here, a quarter works best. But that's tuned to this arcade.

ucb:17.t:
The fine print.
U C B one guarantees that each doubling of the pulls adds about the same regret.But only if the chances never change.
What if C got worse?Its thin cap would make Pip slow to notice.

ucb:18.t:
Optimism goes back to the nineteen eighties. U C B one, to two thousand and two.
Watch this little game tree. Each branch is like an arm.Estimate plus bonus. Explore the highest.
That's UCT. It powered strong Go programs, and AlphaGo's search used a related rule.

ucb:19.t:
So, U C B scores each machine as its estimate plus a bonus for uncertainty.The bonus shrinks with pulls, and creeps up while a machine is ignored.
Checks go where they still might matter, so regret keeps flattening.

thompson:0.t: Thompson Sampling. Act on a random guess drawn from your beliefs.

thompson:1.t:
Back at the cheese arcade.Four machines, each with a hidden chance of a crumb.
Now compare these two.One crumb from one pull, or fifty from a hundred.A lucky start, or solid evidence?
This reel tracks that difference with a belief, and lets the belief do the exploring.

thompson:2.t:
Here's how Pip pictures machine B before pulling it.Left to right, every chance the machine could have.Height is how plausible Pip finds it.
Pip knows nothing yet, so the line is flat.

thompson:3.t:
B's first pull drops a crumb.Watch the flat line tilt into a ramp.
A chance of point nine would drop a crumb nine times in ten.So it's now nine times as plausible as point one.
And chance zero is ruled out.

thompson:4.t:
The second pull drops nothing.Now a chance of one is ruled out too.Watch the ramp bend into a hill around one half.
Old height, times how likely each chance makes what happened.That's Bayes' rule.

thompson:5.t:
Keep pulling B. Watch the hill narrow.After ten pulls, it's centred near one half.After a hundred, it's a thin spike, right by B's true chance.
These curves are Beta distributions.The peak is the estimate. The width is how unsure Pip is.

thompson:6.t:
Here's Thompson sampling.Every turn, Pip draws one random chance from each machine's curve.
Then it pulls whichever draw came out highest, and updates that one curve.
At the start the curves are all flat, so the draws are just random.

thompson:7.t:
Let's follow one visit. Watch the dots on each curve.Pull one, A's draw is highest. A gives nothing.Its curve tilts low.
Pull two, C wins the draw. Nothing again.
The highest draw decides, every time.

thompson:8.t:
B gets lucky. Crumb after crumb.Its hill moves high, so its draws usually win.
Now look at C. No crumbs from two pulls.Its curve leans low, but it's still wide.That width keeps C in the game.

thompson:9.t:
Pull twenty two. C's wide curve throws a lucky high draw, just above B's.C drops a crumb!
Watch more chances follow. C's hill catches up with B's.
Nobody told Pip to explore. The width of C's curve did it.

thompson:10.t:
Back at pull forty. How often does each machine win the draw?B wins most of the time. C and D, about eight percent each.
That's the secret. Each machine gets pulled about as often as it might be the best.A share only shrinks as Pip grows sure that machine is worse.

thompson:11.t:
Fast forward to pull one thousand.C's curve has become a spike, near point seven.
A and D were barely pulled, so their curves stay wide.That's fine. Pip only needs to know they're unlikely to beat C.

thompson:12.t:
Now regret, averaged over two thousand visits.Teal, epsilon greedy. Gold, U C B one.And purple, Thompson sampling, the lowest. Eighteen.
It wastes far fewer pulls on D.Only a specially tuned U C B edges it here.

thompson:13.t:
Your turn. Tap a machine to pull it, and watch its curve change.
Or tap the button, and Thompson sampling chooses. You'll see its four draws first.
Try pulling one machine many times, and see how thin its curve gets.

thompson:14.t:
The fine print. It needs a starting belief.Flat is fine. But a strong wrong start, like this one on the right, can slow it down.
And its randomness is handy. When results come back slowly, its draws spread the waiting visitors out.

thompson:15.t:
William Thompson proposed it in nineteen thirty three, for medical treatments.Then it was mostly forgotten.
Around twenty ten it came back, for Bing ads, then Yahoo's ads and news.Proofs soon showed its regret grows only slowly.
Today it's common in website tests.

thompson:16.t:
So, Pip keeps a belief curve for each machine.Each turn, draw one chance from every curve, and pull the highest.
Wide curves get explored. Narrow low ones get dropped. No schedule, no bonus to tune.

valueiter:0.t: Value Iteration. Know the rules? Spread value outward from the goal, step by step.

valueiter:1.t:
Back in Pip's maze. Watch it draw itself.Cheese plus one, cat minus one, gamma point nine.
This time, we hold the rulebook. Where every move lands, and what it pays.
So we can plan at a desk, while Pip waits.

valueiter:2.t:
Here's the rule from the Bellman reel, with the best move instead of an average.Value here is the best score over all moves.
Start with every number at zero.Then sweep that rule over every cell, again and again.
That's value iteration.

valueiter:3.t:
Take the cell beside the cheese, in sweep one.Watch the four moves get scored.Right reaches the cheese, plus one. Down is the cat, minus one. The others score zero.
The best score, one, becomes the cell's number.And its arrow points right, at the winning move.

valueiter:4.t:
Now do that for every cell.Only the two cells beside the cheese reach one.
Beside the cat, the best is zero. Just don't step on it.Question marks mean several moves still tie.

valueiter:5.t:
Watch the sweeps run.Each one carries the good news one cell further from the cheese.A cell gets its arrow as soon as one move pulls ahead.
At sweep seven, the news reaches the start, point five three.Where two routes are equally short, both arrows stay.

valueiter:6.t:
Sweep eight changes nothing. We're done.On a dry floor, a number is final as soon as it appears.
The arrows form the best policy.Watch Pip follow them. Seven steps to the cheese.

valueiter:7.t:
Now someone mops the floor again.Watch Pip try right at the start.Eight times in ten it goes right. Otherwise it slides sideways.
Rewards and gamma don't change. Any new numbers come from slipping alone.

valueiter:8.t:
On a wet floor, a move's score is an average over where it might land.That's its Q.
Beside the cheese, right hits the cheese eight times in ten, and the cat one in ten.So its Q is point seven.
The cell takes the best Q. Pip picks the move, not the landing.

valueiter:9.t:
Watch the wet floor sweeps.Numbers grow out from the cheese again, but they don't stop after seven.
The start keeps creeping up, sweep after sweep.
Slides make walks longer, so each extra step adds a little more, and less each time.

valueiter:10.t:
This chart shows each sweep's biggest change.Each line down is ten times smaller.
Stop once it's below a thousandth. That's sweep sixteen.
The remaining changes shrink by point nine each time, so together they can't add up to much.

valueiter:11.t:
Watch the arrows, sweep by sweep.Teal cells mark arrows that just changed.
The arrows are final by sweep ten.The numbers keep creeping until sweep sixteen.
The best move often shows before its exact value. The next reel uses that.

valueiter:12.t:
Dry floor arrows on the left, wet floor on the right.Look at the circled cell, right below the cat.
Dry, the best move was right. Wet, it's down, away from the cat.And the ties disappear. Slipping makes one route better by a hair.

valueiter:13.t:
Why go down? Watch the slides from right below the cat.Going right risks a slide up, onto the cat.
Going down risks nothing. Its slides bump the rock or go right.
The detour is longer, but the averages favour it.

valueiter:14.t:
Does it matter? Watch one walk with the new arrows.
From below the cat, the old arrow sent two hundred and seven walks in a thousand onto the cat.The new one, only a hundred and fourteen.
The last step always carries some risk. The policy just stops adding more.

valueiter:15.t:
Your turn. Drag the slip chance.Value iteration reruns from zeros.
More slipping, more sweeps, and arrows that bend away from the cat.Tap a cell to send Pip from there.

valueiter:16.t:
The catch? Every sweep visits every cell, every move, every landing.Here that's sixteen cells.
Go has so many positions that just writing the count takes a hundred and seventy one digits.
And often there's no rulebook at all. Later reels learn from experience instead.

valueiter:17.t:
Richard Bellman called this dynamic programming, in the nineteen fifties.
It's still a standard solver when the rules are known and small.Inventory, maintenance, robots on a known map.
Q-learning aims at the same target, but learns it from experience.

valueiter:18.t:
So, value iteration sweeps the best move rule over every cell, from zeros.Stop when the changes are tiny.
The best arrows are the best policy. And on a slippery floor, they steer away from danger.

policyiter:0.t: Policy Iteration. Judge your plan, fix it, repeat, until nothing changes.

policyiter:1.t:
Pip's maze again, on the wet floor.Eight times in ten a move goes straight. Otherwise, a slide.
We hold the rulebook again.
But this time, instead of sweeping values, we'll improve a whole plan in rounds.

policyiter:2.t:
A plan puts one arrow in every cell.Let's start with a clearly bad one. Every arrow points up.
Watch Pip walk up to the top corner, and push against the wall.It only moves on when it happens to slide.

policyiter:3.t:
Round one. First, measure this plan.
Watch the notebook fill in, sweep after sweep, using only the plan's moves.
It takes twenty four sweeps to settle.And the start is worth just point oh one.

policyiter:4.t:
Let's read this bad notebook.Below the cheese, up is already right. Point seven seven.Beside the cheese, up pushes into the wall.
And below the cat, up walks straight into it. Minus point eight three.

policyiter:5.t:
Now fix the plan. Take the cell beside the cheese.Score every move by this notebook. That's its Q.
Up, the current arrow, scores point four.Right scores point seven four. Switch!
Ties keep the old arrow, so nothing flip flops.

policyiter:6.t:
Do that in every cell. Watch the teal ones change.Ten arrows flip.
The top row now runs right. Below the cat, the arrow turns away.Some look odd. They only win by the old plan's notebook. Next round rejudges them.

policyiter:7.t:
Round two. Measure the new plan.Watch the start jump, from point oh one to point three two.
Then improve again. Only three arrows change this time.Below the cat, it now goes down, around the cat.

policyiter:8.t:
Round three. Just one arrow changes.
Round four. Nothing changes at all. So we stop.
It's exactly the plan value iteration found on this floor, detour and all.

policyiter:9.t:
Here are the four rounds in one table.Each row is one plan, its sweeps, and what it makes the start worth.
Round two jumps the start to point three two.After that, it's fine tuning. Ten, three, one, then zero arrows changed.

policyiter:10.t:
Why does it never get worse?Beside the cheese, right once and then the old plan already beats the old plan.
And the new arrows wherever Pip lands passed that test too.Use them again and again, and you're still no worse. Every round, numbers rise. None fall.

policyiter:11.t:
Why does it stop at the best?Each change strictly improves, so no plan ever comes back.There are only finitely many plans, so the rounds must end.
And at the end, every arrow has its cell's best Q. Nothing can beat that.

policyiter:12.t:
Policy iteration on the left. Value iteration on the right.The same arrows.
Four rounds against sixteen sweeps. But each round hides a full evaluation.Counting all the work, they come out about the same.

policyiter:13.t:
Your turn. Pick a different first plan, and watch the rounds.All right takes three rounds. All down or all left take seven.
But every start ends at the same plan.Tap a cell to see its four Q values.

policyiter:14.t:
Evaluate, then improve. This loop is everywhere in R L.The gold arrow hands a notebook over. The teal arrow hands back a better plan.
Do each half only partly, and it's generalised policy iteration.Actor critic, later on, works just like this.

policyiter:15.t:
Ronald Howard described policy iteration in nineteen sixty.
It's still a standard tool when the rules are known. Inventory, maintenance, routes.
Its biggest legacy is the loop itself. Judge what you do, then nudge it toward better.

policyiter:16.t:
So, policy iteration starts from any plan.Evaluate it, then point each arrow at its best move.
Every round is at least as good as the last. When nothing changes, you've found the best plan.

mc:0.t: Monte Carlo Learning. Play to the end, then learn from what really happened.

mc:1.t:
Back in the maze, on a dry floor.Cheese plus one, cat minus one, and gamma at point nine.
The faint arrows are Pip's habit. One move in five goes random.

mc:2.t:
This time, nobody hands Pip the rulebook.So it can't work values out on paper. It can only walk.
And real Pip always starts in the corner.Learning from the complete walks it actually takes is called Monte Carlo.

mc:3.t:
Here's walk one. Cheese in seven steps.
When it ends, Pip writes a return into every cell it passed.Beside the cheese, that's one.Each step back gets one more times point nine, down to point five three at the start.

mc:4.t:
Each cell keeps two things. How many returns, and their average.
A new return nudges the average, by a share that shrinks as returns pile up.After walk one, each average is just that walk's return.

mc:5.t:
Walk two. Watch Pip step back down once, and bump the top wall.Some cells get passed twice. Only the first visit counts.
The start now averages point four six.Beside the cheese, point nine five.

mc:6.t:
Walk three starts along the same path.See the hourglasses? Mid walk, nothing can be written yet.
Then, beside the cheese, a random move. Onto the cat.Every return on the path turns negative.
A single walk can swing the notebook a lot.

mc:7.t:
Pip keeps walking from the start. Watch the numbers settle.
After a thousand walks, the start reads point four.The same as the values reel, because these are the same walks.
But every cell on the route got its own returns too, with no extra walking.

mc:8.t:
Along Pip's usual route, these numbers match the values reel closely.
But off the route, cells got far fewer returns.Below the cat, just three. And its average is way off.
Monte Carlo only learns where Pip goes.

mc:9.t:
Here are all thousand returns from the start.Gold bars reached the cheese, rose bars the cat.
They spread from minus point five three to plus point five three.Every random move changes the return. Only the average settles.

mc:10.t:
Your turn. Drag the slider to choose how many walks the notebook has seen.Tap a cell to see every return it collected.
Try the start, then a cell in the bottom right. With few walks, one return can pull an average a long way.

mc:11.t:
So far, the notebook only judged someone else's arrows.To improve them, Pip needs a number for each move.
Watch the four Q labels appear. One per cell and move.Pip picks moves by them, and they change after every walk.

mc:12.t:
Now Pip drops the arrows. Every Q starts at zero.It takes the biggest Q, and one move in five at random.
Walk one wanders for fifty one steps, and ends on the cat.Every move it used now averages negative. Watch the rose arrows.

mc:13.t:
Walk four takes almost five hundred steps.In the top left corner, Pip bumps the wall again and again.
Up looked least bad there, because the cat's penalty had shrunk to almost nothing.
And averages can't change until the walk ends. T D learning, coming later, fixes that.

mc:14.t:
So how did Pip get out?A walk that reaches the cheese gives every move it used a positive return.
On walk eight, Pip left the corner rightward and found the cheese.Now right has the corner's only positive average. A gold arrow appears.

mc:15.t:
Two hundred walks, sped up. Each bar is one walk's length.After about twenty walks, most take seven to ten steps.
Then watch Pip follow the arrows. The shortest route, seven steps.Cells it rarely visits keep rough arrows. They never mattered.

mc:16.t:
The name dates from the nineteen forties, and random sampling for physics at Los Alamos.
A classic R L example is blackjack. Play many hands to the end, and average the results.AlphaGo judged positions partly by playing fast games to the end.

mc:17.t:
So, Monte Carlo needs no rulebook.After each walk, every cell passed gets its return, and its average moves toward it.
Returns are real but noisy, rare cells stay rough, and nothing is learned until the walk ends.

td:0.t: Temporal-Difference Learning. Learn a guess from a slightly better guess, every single step.

td:1.t:
Welcome back to Pip's maze.Same cheese, same cat, and a dry floor, so every move goes where Pip points.
The faint arrows are Pip's habit.The numbers are what that habit is worth, worked out by the sweeps.Point eight seven beside the cheese.Point four at the start.Pip must now learn them the hard way.

td:2.t:
The sweeps had a cheat sheet.They knew where every move leads.
Monte Carlo didn't need that, but it had to wait until each walk was over.
Now Pip gets neither shortcut.Every guess starts at zero.And it has to learn while it walks.

td:3.t:
Picture driving home from the office.You expect the trip to take half an hour.
Ten minutes in, you're still on track.Then, a traffic jam.You don't wait until you're home to feel late. You update right there, to forty minutes.
Time so far, plus a fresh guess for the rest.That's the whole trick behind T D learning.

td:4.t:
Look at the start cell.The arrows show every move Pip might make, and how likely each one is.Mostly up.
The Bellman rule averages over all of them. That needs the rulebook.
Now watch Pip take one real step.T D uses just that: the reward, plus point nine times its guess where it landed.

td:5.t:
Here comes Pip's first walk.Watch the highlighted cell.After every step, Pip updates the cell it just left.
But nothing has happened yet.No reward, and every guess is still zero.So the target is zero, and nothing changes.
Six steps in a row, and the notebook stays blank.

td:6.t:
Watch the last step.Pip moves from the cell beside the cheese, onto it.Plus one!
The walk is over, so there's nothing to add. The target is just one.Pip's old guess was zero.
That gap, between what happened and what Pip expected, is the T D error. Think of it as surprise. Here, the surprise is a full one.

td:7.t:
Watch the cell beside the cheese. Pip doesn't jump to one.
It moves just a fifth of the way, to point two.That fraction is alpha, the learning rate.The match with one move in five is a coincidence.
Why so cautious? The next walk might end on the cat.Small steps let the good and bad walks average out.

td:8.t:
Walk two, sped up.Watch Pip step beside the cheese.
That cell already reads point two.So the cell Pip just left gets a little credit too.A guess learned from a guess. That's bootstrapping, the heart of T D.
Then a bump into the wall, and a small dip.Then the cheese lifts the guess to point three six.

td:9.t:
At each cheese, split the plus one in two.Yellow is what Pip expected.Orange is the surprise.
Watch the orange shrink.Then, on walk three, a random move sends Pip into the cat.A big negative surprise, and the guess drops.
So the next cheese surprises Pip all over again.

td:10.t:
Now Pip walks two hundred times.Look at the start cell around walk fifty. It already reads point three five, and the truth is point four.
Gold is the guess beside the cheese.Dashed is the true value, point eight seven.
The gold line hovers, dipping at every rose tick, every cat.

td:11.t:
Here are the two notebooks side by side.T D on the left.The exact sweeps on the right.
Beside the cheese, T D reads point nine eight.Why so high?The last cat scare was fifteen walks ago, and every good walk since nudged it up.
A fixed alpha never lets the guesses settle. They keep wobbling around the truth.

td:12.t:
Now Monte Carlo, on the left, trained on these very same walks.
Monte Carlo ends closer almost everywhere.Along Pip's usual route, it's within a hundredth of the truth.In rarely visited cells, T D is far off.
Why? These walks are short, so waiting for the end costs almost nothing. T D shines when walks are long, or never end.

td:13.t:
Look right of the start.The small numbers are visits.T D updated this cell nine times, more than Monte Carlo's eight returns.
But each update leaned on the next cell's guess, and that was still almost zero.The cheese's news never reached this far.
Give it the true values, and the same nine updates land on point four.

td:14.t:
Same walks, smaller step.Alpha is now point oh five.Watch the blue line grow over the pale gold one.
Blue is much calmer.But it's slow.At walk one hundred, the start reads only point oh eight.
Monte Carlo's one over n step is slower still. It shrinks so fast that the early zeros linger.

td:15.t:
Your turn. Drag the alpha slider, and the same two hundred walks replay with that learning rate.
Gold is beside the cheese.Teal is the start.Watch how far the lines jump around their dashed targets, and how long teal takes to climb.
Big alpha is quick but jumpy. Small alpha is calm, but slow.

td:16.t:
These dots are Pip's surprise at the cheese, across all two hundred walks. They sink, then jump after each cat.
Surprise also moves earlier.On walk two, Pip got a small lift one step before the cheese.
Wolfram Schultz saw monkey dopamine neurons do the same. They fired for surprise juice, then for the light that announced it.

td:17.t:
So T D filled in the notebook from experience alone.But notice, the habit itself never changed.
Say Pip stands here and wants a better move.Where does each arrow lead? Watch the question marks.Without the rulebook, Pip can't tell.
The fix is a number for each move. That's Q-learning, coming next.

td:18.t:
So that's T D learning.Pip learns what its habit is worth from experience alone, updating after every single step.
The target is one real step: the reward, plus gamma times the guess where Pip landed.Alpha sets how far to move.Big alpha learns fast and wobbles. Small alpha is steady, but slow.

qlearning:0.t: Q-Learning. Learn the value of every move, even while acting randomly.

qlearning:1.t:
Remember the T D reel? Pip learned how good each cell is, under its habit.Here's that notebook, with the habit's arrows.
Now Pip wants to do better than its habit. Can the notebook tell it which move is best?

qlearning:2.t:
Pip stands in the middle of the bottom row.Right looks worth more than left. But where does right actually lead?
Pip doesn't know the rules. No map.It only finds out after it moves.
Q-learning skips the map, and learns a value for each move directly.

qlearning:3.t:
Now Pip keeps four numbers in every cell, one per move.Here's the start cell, made big. Each triangle points its way.
Each is an action value. Make this move, then act as well as possible.That's Q star. All start at zero.

qlearning:4.t:
To move, Pip only looks at its own cell.It takes the biggest number. Here, that's up.
And one move in five is still random, so every move gets tried.That habit is epsilon greedy.

qlearning:5.t:
Watch Pip make a move.Then look where it landed, made big below.
The target is the reward, plus point nine times the biggest number there.Then the old number moves a fifth of the way toward it.
That fifth is alpha, the learning rate.

qlearning:6.t:
Here's the same rule in symbols.Each piece gets a label as it appears.
The key part is the max. The biggest of the four numbers where Pip landed.Gamma and alpha are the same knobs as in T D.

qlearning:7.t:
Walk one. Every number is zero, so every choice is a coin toss.Watch Pip wander, sped up.
Finally, a random move up, onto the cheese. Plus one!
So that one number, up below the cheese, becomes point two.Nothing else changes.

qlearning:8.t:
Walk three. Pip steps right, beside the cheese.The biggest number there is point two.
So the move Pip just made gets a little credit too.A guess learned from the next guess, stored on a move.

qlearning:9.t:
Walk seven. Pip steps beside the cheese, and updates right away.
The target uses the best move from there, right, worth point six seven.
Whatever Pip actually does next plays no part.

qlearning:10.t:
And what does Pip do next? A random move. Down, onto the cat.Minus one.
Only that one number, down, drops.Right keeps its point six seven.
Four numbers keep a bad move apart from a good one.

qlearning:11.t:
This chart tracks two numbers beside the cheese, walk by walk.Gold is right, onto the cheese. Rose is down, onto the cat.
Watch gold climb, close to one after twenty walks.It never drops. Its target is always exactly one.

qlearning:12.t:
Three hundred walks, sped up.The bars below are walk lengths. They shrink fast.
At the end, arrows show Pip's best guesses.Along the route they're right. In rarely visited cells, some are wrong.

qlearning:13.t:
Follow the arrows back from the cheese.One, then point nine, point eight one, down to point five three at the start.
Those are the best possible values, learned from walks alone.The max makes every target assume the best next move.

qlearning:14.t:
In the T D reel, the guesses kept wobbling. Here they sit still. Why?
Take right, beside the cheese. Its target is one, every single time.And the max ignores Pip's random next move.
Same target every time, so nothing is left to wobble.

qlearning:15.t:
But those numbers describe a Pip that never moves at random.Each dot is one of the real Pip's last hundred walks.
A few hit the cat. The average is point three nine, not point five three.
Q-learning learns the best way to act, not how Pip acts while learning.

qlearning:16.t:
Your turn. Drag epsilon, how often Pip moves at random.At every setting, the start reaches point five three.
More randomness visits more cells, so more arrows come out right.Tap a cell to drop Pip there.

qlearning:17.t:
Chris Watkins introduced Q-learning in nineteen eighty nine.A few years later, he and Peter Dayan proved it works, under some conditions.
In twenty fifteen, D Q N swapped the table for a network that read Atari screens.

qlearning:18.t:
So, Q-learning keeps a number for every move.Pick the biggest, and explore now and then.
After each move, aim at the reward plus gamma times the best number where you landed. Because of that max, Pip learns the best way to act.

sarsa:0.t: SARSA. Learn the value of what you’ll actually do next.

sarsa:1.t:
Pip has a new room. Six wide, four tall, no rocks.Start bottom left, cheese bottom right.And in between, along the bottom row, four sleeping cats.
The old rules still hold. Plus one for cheese, minus one for a cat.

sarsa:2.t:
Two ways across.The short way runs right along the cats. Seven steps, worth point five three.One row higher takes nine steps. Point four three.
But Pip moves at random one time in five. Next to the cats, that's risky.

sarsa:3.t:
First, Q-learning, just like the last reel. Five hundred walks.Its arrows take the short way, right along the cats.
That fits. Every target assumes the best next move, as if Pip never slipped up.

sarsa:4.t:
SARSA changes one thing.When Pip lands, it first picks its next move, with its usual habit.
Then it updates using that move's number, the move it will really make.Not the biggest one.
The name lists the pieces. State, action, reward, next state, next action.

sarsa:5.t:
Here's SARSA's rule, with Q-learning's below it.The only difference is underlined.
SARSA uses the number of the next move Pip picked. Q-learning uses the biggest.And that next move is sometimes random.

sarsa:6.t:
Watch one SARSA update.Pip steps right, onto the cell above a cat.And picks its next move. A random one, down.
That move's number is negative, so the move Pip just made drops, to point three.Q-learning would have raised it instead.

sarsa:7.t:
And SARSA commits. Pip steps down, onto the cat.Minus one.
Picking the move in advance makes SARSA honest about Pip.Its targets contain the random moves Pip really makes.

sarsa:8.t:
After five hundred walks, compare one cell above the cats.
Q-learning says right is worth point six six. The perfect value.SARSA says only point one five.
Walking on along the cats, a random move will sometimes hit one. For SARSA, up is best here.

sarsa:9.t:
Now follow each learner's arrows from the start.Q-learning hugs the cats.SARSA climbs two rows, keeping a gap.
With Pip still random one move in five, SARSA's route is worth more.

sarsa:10.t:
Is that one run a fluke? Let's run both a hundred times.
This chart shows what Pip actually earned while learning.Orange is Q-learning. Teal is SARSA.
Watch the dots appear, walk by walk.

sarsa:11.t:
SARSA earned more per walk.Its route is longer, but far fewer of its walks met a cat.
Early on, both wander. Then SARSA settles away from the cats.
Q-learning picked the cat side route in most runs. SARSA, never.

sarsa:12.t:
So who's right? Both, about different Pips.
Never random, Q-learning's route is better.While Pip still explores, SARSA's is.
If mistakes while learning cost something real, use SARSA. If only the final route matters, Q-learning.

sarsa:13.t:
Your turn. Drag epsilon.Each setting reruns both learners a hundred times, and shows their most common routes.
The more random Pip is, the more SARSA steers clear of the cats.
At zero, the two rules are the same.

sarsa:14.t:
SARSA was described in nineteen ninety four. Richard Sutton gave it its name.A room like this is the classic cliff walking test.
The lesson carries over. A real robot near stairs should learn about the behaviour it actually has.

sarsa:15.t:
So, SARSA picks its next move first, then aims at that move's number.Its numbers include Pip's own random moves.
Near danger, it learns a safer route. Q-learning learns the best route for a Pip that never slips.

onoff:0.t: On-Policy versus Off-Policy. Learn only from your own behaviour, or from anyone’s?

onoff:1.t:
In the last two reels, Pip learned four numbers per cell, while moving epsilon greedy.
Such a learner really has two rules.On the left, the behaviour policy. It picks the moves.On the right, the target policy. The rule the numbers describe.

onoff:2.t:
Take SARSA first.Its target uses the move its habit really picks next, random moves and all.
So both boxes say the same thing, epsilon greedy.Same rule. That's on policy. You learn about exactly what you do.

onoff:3.t:
Now Q-learning. It acts epsilon greedy too.But its target assumes the best next move every time.
So its numbers describe a greedy Pip, one that never moves at random.Different rules. That's off policy.

onoff:4.t:
Why can Q-learning do this?Look at its target. The reward and landing come from the maze, whoever chose the move.
Then the max fills in the best way to carry on.SARSA's target needs the walker's own next move.

onoff:5.t:
Remember the Wanderer, whose every move is random?Pip finds a diary of a hundred of its walks.
Watch them flash by. Most end on the cat.
Can Pip learn the best route from this, without taking a single step?

onoff:6.t:
Pip replays the diary, applying Q-learning's update as if it had made each move.Watch the start cell, made big.
After just two readings, the start reaches point five three. Perfect.
The best arrows appear, though the Wanderer never walked those routes.

onoff:7.t:
Now replay the same diary with SARSA.Compare the start cell. Q-learning on the left, SARSA on the right.
SARSA learns the Wanderer's own values, all close to zero.
Correct, but useless for Pip.

onoff:8.t:
Learning one rule while following another opens doors.
Pip can reuse old experience, again and again.Learn from other walkers, a random mouse, a human, an older self.
And explore wildly, yet still learn the best way to act.

onoff:9.t:
But here's a risk. Another diary, from a careful mouse.A hundred walks, all the same seven steps.
Q-learning learns that route perfectly, and nothing else.Drop Pip off the route, and it has no clue.
Off policy data only teaches about moves someone actually tried.

onoff:10.t:
Another risk. Off policy numbers describe a rule that never acted.
At scale, a network replaces the table, so changing one guess shifts others.Guesses chasing guesses can run away.
Network, bootstrapping, off policy data. Sutton and Barto call it the deadly triad.

onoff:11.t:
Your turn. Pick whose experience Q-learning learns from.Pip's own walks, the Wanderer's diary, or the careful mouse.
Then tap a cell, and Pip follows the arrows.Where the data never went, Pip has no clue.

onoff:12.t:
Off policy methods include Q-learning, and D Q N, which replayed old Atari moves from memory.
On policy, there's SARSA, and P P O, used to fine tune chatbots.P P O gathers fresh experience, learns briefly, then throws it away.

onoff:13.t:
So, the behaviour policy acts. The target policy is what the numbers describe.Same rule, on policy. Different rules, off policy.
Off policy learners can reuse experience and learn from others, but only about moves the data contains.

traces:0.t: Eligibility Traces  and  T D(lambda). Give credit to recent steps, fading into the past.

traces:1.t:
Pip follows its habit again, learning each cell's value.Watch walk one, seven steps to the cheese.
T D updates every step, from the next cell's guess.Monte Carlo waits for the real return.
Can we get the best of both?

traces:2.t:
Here's what walk one teaches each method.With T D, only the cell beside the cheese learns anything.
With Monte Carlo, every cell on the path moves.One walk reached the whole path. But only after it ended.

traces:3.t:
Which earlier moves earned the cheese? That's the credit assignment problem.
Watch T D over ten walks. The news crawls back about one cell per walk.After ten walks, the start has barely moved.
Monte Carlo credits everything at once, but one unlucky ending shakes it all. Is there a middle ground?

traces:4.t:
T D looks one step ahead. Monte Carlo looks to the very end.Watch the three arcs. One step, three steps, the whole walk.
In between is the n step target.A few real rewards, then a guess for the rest.

traces:5.t:
Here's a smoother idea. Give each cell a fading mark.Watch the teal bars as Pip walks.
The cell Pip just left gets a full mark. The older ones shrink, step by step.A dial called lambda sets how fast they fade.

traces:6.t:
Pip reaches the cheese. Plus one, a surprise of one.
Now every marked cell moves, in proportion to its mark.Watch the whole recent path light up.Point two beside the cheese, smaller and smaller back to the start.

traces:7.t:
Now turn the dial.At lambda zero, marks vanish after one step. Plain T D. One cell changed.
