Turn it up, and more of the path learns.At one, it behaves like Monte Carlo.
In between, it's a blend of all the n step targets. This is T D lambda.

traces:8.t:
Let's race them fairly. Every lambda learns from the very same walks.
Each is scored by its error on the seven route cells, against the true values.
And we average over two hundred sets of walks, to avoid a lucky draw.

traces:9.t:
Here are the first fifty walks. Lower is better.After ten walks, T D is still far off.Lambda point eight, much closer. Lambda one, closer still.
Spreading surprises makes early learning much faster.But watch the rose line creep back up.

traces:10.t:
These bars show the error after twenty walks, and after two hundred.At twenty walks, a big lambda wins.After two hundred, plain T D wins.
Why? A big lambda leans on the real rest of the walk, so one cat ending jolts many cells.

traces:11.t:
But was one step size fair? Big lambda might want smaller steps.Now each lambda gets its best alpha.
Early, a big lambda still wins.Later, a middle value, one half, edges ahead.
T D's late win was partly the shared step size.

traces:12.t:
Your turn. Drag lambda.The maze shows this run's notebook after ten walks.
At zero, the news stays near the cheese. At one, it reaches the start at once.The bars show the error for your setting.

traces:13.t:
The cost? Watch walk two.Every marked cell gets updated, not just one.
The card counts them as Pip goes.On a long walk, that can be fifteen cells per step. And lambda is one more dial to tune.

traces:14.t:
Richard Sutton introduced T D lambda in nineteen eighty eight.T D Gammon used it to learn backgammon by playing itself.
The same lambda lives on in G A E, which the popular P P O method commonly uses.

traces:15.t:
So, an eligibility trace is a fading mark on cells Pip recently left.Each surprise updates every marked cell, so it reaches the whole recent path.
Lambda zero is T D, lambda one is like Monte Carlo. In between is often a good compromise.

funcapprox:0.t: Function Approximation. Too many states for a table? Learn a function that generalises.

funcapprox:1.t:
Pip has left the maze, for an open meadow.No cells, no inside walls. Its position is just two numbers, x and y.
Same rules. Cheese circle plus one, cat circle minus one.And gamma is still point nine.

funcapprox:2.t:
Pip still has four moves. Watch three steps to the right.Each carries it about point one five, plus a little random wobble from the bumpy grass.
And the fence stops Pip at the edge.

funcapprox:3.t:
Pip follows a fixed habit again. Watch the arrows.Up at first, then toward the cheese.And one move in five, a random direction.
Here's walk one. Ten moves, ending in the cheese.We want this habit's values, from every spot.

funcapprox:4.t:
In the maze, each cell got visited again and again.Here, every landing spot is new. Watch the blue dots.
In ten thousand walks, Pip never stood on exactly the same spot twice.A notebook page per spot would never be read again.

funcapprox:5.t:
We could cut the meadow into squares.Sixteen by sixteen, one number each.
But look at these two neighbours. Almost the same place, learning separately.Neither teaches the other anything.

funcapprox:6.t:
Here are the habit's true values. Gold is good, rose is bad.Pip can't see this. It has to learn it.
Notice the dark band below the cat. From there, the habit climbs straight into it.
But mostly, nearby spots have similar values.

funcapprox:7.t:
So instead of naming the spot, Pip describes it with a few measurements.Its x and y. Its distance to the cheese. Its distance to the cat.
Close spots have similar measurements, so a rule built on them treats them alike.That's generalisation.

funcapprox:8.t:
The simplest rule. Multiply each measurement by its own knob, and add them up.That's a linear recipe, with five knobs.
All start at zero, so every guess is zero.And one recipe guesses for every spot, even ones never visited.

funcapprox:9.t:
Walk one's last step, into the cheese.Target one, guess zero. The error is one.
Now each knob moves by step size, times error, times its measurement.Watch them change, one by one.
That's a gradient step. Bigger measurements sway the guess more, so they move more.

funcapprox:10.t:
That one nudge changed the guess everywhere. Watch the meadow warm up.
The start, far away, moved. The spot below the cat moved too, though nothing happened there.
That sharing is the whole point. And its danger.

funcapprox:11.t:
Now train on all ten thousand walks.Watch the colours settle.
The chart below tracks the average gap from the true values.It drops from point four seven to about point two, then wobbles.

funcapprox:12.t:
True values on the left. The trained recipe on the right.It gets the big picture.
But look at the ring below the cat. The truth is strongly negative. The recipe says about zero.
The recipe can only add. Near the cat's x and below it needs an and.

funcapprox:13.t:
So, a tiny neural network.The four measurements feed eight hidden units.Each adds them up with its own weights, then squashes the result.
The output adds those up again. That's the guess.Forty nine knobs in all.

funcapprox:14.t:
The nudge works the same way.Each knob moves by how much turning it would change the guess.
Watch the error flow back through the network, output first.That's backpropagation.
A single nudge more than doubles this guess.

funcapprox:15.t:
Train the network on the same walks.Blue is its average gap. Gold, the recipe's.The network ends lower.
And the band below the cat appears.But it's too wide. It spills onto spots that are actually fine.

funcapprox:16.t:
Here's the catch. Walk fifty six was one move into the cheese.The colour shows what that one nudge changed.
The far off start moved too. And T D targets use the same knobs, so they move as well.
Add data from a different policy, and that's the deadly triad.

funcapprox:17.t:
Your turn. Tap a spot to teach Pip, this spot is worth one.Watch which other spots change with it.
Slide between the recipe and the network.The recipe moves near and far alike. The network moves nearby spots more.

funcapprox:18.t:
T D Gammon used exactly this mix in nineteen ninety two.A network for the values, trained with T D, from games against itself.
Today almost every large R L system uses a network instead of a table. The next reel, D Q N, does it for Atari.

funcapprox:19.t:
So, when states never repeat, describe them with features.Then learn a function with a few knobs that guesses for any state.
Shared knobs mean every lesson generalises. And sometimes, it spills where it shouldn't.

dqn:0.t: Deep Q-Network (D Q N). Q-learning plus a neural network: superhuman Atari from pixels.

dqn:1.t:
Back on the meadow.Last reel, a network learned how good each spot was, under Pip's habit.
But to do better, Pip needs a number for each move. Watch the four arrows.That's Q-learning. And spots never repeat, so a table won't work.

dqn:2.t:
Quick reminder of Q-learning.After each move, nudge its number toward the reward, plus point nine times the best Q where Pip landed.
And Pip acts epsilon greedy. One move in five at random.

dqn:3.t:
The fix is a network, as in the last reel. Watch it build.This one has four outputs, one Q value per move.
One pass gives all four. That's a Deep Q Network, D Q N.Its knobs start random, so for now its numbers are pure noise.

dqn:4.t:
First, the simple way. One nudge after each move.Watch move thirty seven. A step left, straight into the cat.
One nudge lowers left a little.Each nudge is small, so one bad moment can't wipe out everything.

dqn:5.t:
Pip learns this way for eight thousand moves.Every so often, thirty test walks check how it's doing.
The chart counts walks that reach the cheese.It hardly learns. Mostly near zero.
Only the very last test scores well. Nothing to rely on.

dqn:6.t:
Problem one. The target comes from the same network.At a spot only a step away.
Watch the bars. Nudge the guess up, and the target rises too.So the gap barely closes.

dqn:7.t:
Problem two. Moves arrive in order.Watch the rose dots. Sixty moves in a row, hugging one patch.
The network bends toward each patch in turn.Random old moves, the blue dots, would mix the whole meadow into each lesson.

dqn:8.t:
D Q N adds two fixes.First, a replay memory. Pip learns from thirty two random old moves at a time.
Second, a target network. A frozen copy, refreshed now and then, sets the targets.
Same network, same knobs, same meadow.

dqn:9.t:
Now run it again, with both fixes. Blue is D Q N.Watch the test walks turn teal.
By the end, all thirty reach the cheese.The faint rose line is the simple version, far behind.

dqn:10.t:
Here's what the network learned.Each arrow is its best move. Colour is how good that move looks.
Mostly it rounds the cat, though a few spots right below still point into it.Watch the teal walk from the start. Twelve moves. Good, not perfect.

dqn:11.t:
Inside the trained network, with Pip at the start.Up scores highest, so Pip goes up.
But the numbers are rough. Left, a wasted bump into the fence, scores above right.It ranks the best move here, but the values are only approximate.

dqn:12.t:
Your turn. Tap a spot to drop Pip there.It walks by its biggest Q, no random moves.
Slide to pick how long D Q N trained.Early networks wander. Later ones round the cat, from almost anywhere.

dqn:13.t:
D Q N made its name on Atari games.The input was the last four frames of the screen, so motion showed.The outputs, one Q per joystick action.
In twenty fifteen, one network with the same settings played forty nine games.

dqn:14.t:
Forty nine games, one recipe.
It reached at least three quarters of a human tester's score on twenty nine of them.It failed where rewards are rare, like Montezuma's Revenge.
And it needed far more practice than a person.

dqn:15.t:
So, D Q N is Q-learning with a neural network.Measurements in, one Q per move out.
Done naively, it flounders. Replay memory and a target network make it learn, on the meadow and on Atari.

replay:0.t: Experience Replay. Store experiences, then learn from random old memories.

replay:1.t:
Here's Pip's meadow again, with the cheese, the cat, and Pip at the start.
And here's the same little network. Four measurements go in, and one value per move comes out.Last time, two fixes rescued it. This reel tests just the first one, on its own.

replay:2.t:
Watch Pip walk, and watch the cards pile up below.Every move becomes one card: where Pip was, what it did, what it got, and where it landed.
The simplest plan is to learn from the newest cards, in order. Each update looks at the latest thirty two.

replay:3.t:
Now look at where those thirty two cards sit.They're all bunched up in one corner, near the fence.
Read the cards below. They tell almost the same story.Moves that follow each other are alike. So the network hears one lesson, over and over.

replay:4.t:
Watch the ringed spot just below the cheese.It should be worth about one.
Pip is far away, in its corner. Yet watch the gold line slide down.It ends near point two nine.
Every spot shares the same knobs. Tuning them for the corner quietly rubs out what Pip knew about the cheese.

replay:5.t:
Here's the fix. A shoebox for cards.Every move drops a new card in, and it stays a while.
When the box is full, the oldest card falls out.So at any moment, the box holds moves from many walks, from all over the meadow.

replay:6.t:
Before each update, Pip shakes the box and pulls out thirty two cards at random.
Watch the teal dots appear.They're scattered all over the meadow.The faint orange ones, the latest thirty two, sat in one corner.
On average, two random cards lie about point six oh apart. Two recent ones, only point three one.

replay:7.t:
Now a fair race. Both versions get the same moves, the same seeds, and the same size of update. The only difference is which cards they learn from.
These dots are thirty test spots.Every so often, Pip tries to reach the cheese from each one, with no random moves.The chart below will count its successes.

replay:8.t:
Watch the lines grow.Teal is replay. Orange learns from the latest cards.The thin lines are single runs, and they jump around a lot.
Follow the thick lines, the averages.At the end, replay reaches the cheese from about 25 point eight spots out of thirty. The other, about 7 point eight.Same work. Only the cards differ.

replay:9.t:
Why does shuffling help? A random handful covers the whole meadow fairly. So each update nudges everywhere a little, instead of bending toward one corner.
Look at the spot below the cheese again, late in training.Orange swings wildly.Teal stays much steadier.

replay:10.t:
Here are the two finished networks, as maps. Gold is good, rose is bad.
On the left, replay.Watch Pip follow it from the start. It goes along the bottom, up the right side, and finds the cheese.
On the right, the latest cards only. Watch where that Pip ends up.

replay:11.t:
One worry. The cards in the box came from an older Pip, with older habits.
D Q N doesn't mind.Its target always asks about the best move from the landing spot, whoever made the card.A method like SARSA, which studies today's habit, would be learning about a Pip that's gone.

replay:12.t:
Remember the deadly triad? A network, targets built from guesses, and data from other habits. Replay has all three.
Here it stayed calm anyway.The box only keeps recent moves, so its cards come from Pips much like today's.The next reel adds more safety.

replay:13.t:
Your turn. Drag the memory size, and watch the race replay.
With a tiny box, even a random handful is full of near-duplicates.A few hundred cards already work much better.
Surprisingly, keeping all eight thousand did worse here.The box decides which spots get lessons. Old cards point at places today's Pip rarely visits.

replay:14.t:
Experience replay goes back to Long-Ji Lin, in nineteen ninety two.
D Q N made it famous in twenty fifteen, with a memory of a million moves.Without replay, its Breakout score fell from about three hundred and seventeen to about ten.Later, prioritised replay drew the surprising cards more often.

replay:15.t:
So, moves that follow each other are near-duplicates. Learning from them in order bends the network toward one corner, and old lessons fade.
Experience replay keeps a box of recent cards, and learns from random handfuls.Varied lessons, each card reused many times, and much less forgetting.

targetnet:0.t: Target Networks. Stop chasing your own tail: freeze the target for a while.

targetnet:1.t:
Pip keeps its replay memory from last time. Now we zoom in on the other problem.
Here's Pip's network.To build a target, it needs the best value where Pip landed.And who supplies that value? The very network being trained.

targetnet:2.t:
Let's run a small experiment, with one single card.
Watch Pip step right, from here to the landed spot. No reward.
The network values that move at minus point oh four.Its target is point nine times the best value where Pip landed.Now we train on this card alone, and watch both numbers.

targetnet:3.t:
Watch the two lines.Gold is the move's value. Teal is its target.Gold climbs toward teal, but teal climbs too.
Gold ends near point one four, and nothing new was learned at all.The landing spot is close by, and shares the same knobs. Raise one, and the other rises too. Pip is chasing its own shadow.

targetnet:4.t:
The fix is simple. Keep a second network, a frozen copy, just for targets.
The live network on the left learns and acts.The copy on the right stays still.
Now the target reads the copy's best value instead.

targetnet:5.t:
Same card, same steps, but now the target comes from the frozen copy.Watch teal. It stays flat.Gold reaches it in 27 steps, and stops.
With the target held still, it's just ordinary fitting. Hit a fixed number.

targetnet:6.t:
A copy frozen forever would never learn. So every so often, we refresh it with the live knobs.
Watch the staircase.The target holds, gold catches up, then the target jumps.
The drift is still there, just slower. Gold ends at point oh seven.In real training, other cards bring real information to anchor it.

targetnet:7.t:
Now back to full training, with replay, and the same seeds. Once with live targets, once with a copy.
We'll track one number, the best value at Pip's start spot.
Watch the lines draw.Orange uses live targets. Teal uses the copy.

targetnet:8.t:
Here's the second half of training, four runs each.Orange jitters. Teal is calmer.
On average, live targets jump about point oh five between readings, the copy only point oh two.Reaching the cheese, they're close. Replay did most of the work here. The copy mainly steadies things.

targetnet:9.t:
Your turn. Drag N, how many updates pass before the copy is refreshed.
Watch the start value as you change it.Refresh too often, and the chase comes back.
Refresh too rarely, and the targets go stale.At a thousand, the numbers are calmest, but only 16 point oh spots out of thirty reach the cheese.

targetnet:10.t:
D Q N, in twenty fifteen, refreshed its copy every ten thousand updates.Without it, its Breakout score fell from about three hundred and seventeen to about two hundred and forty one.
Later methods, like D D P G and sack, blend instead. The copy slides a tiny bit toward the live network after every update.

targetnet:11.t:
When a network builds its own targets, every update moves the thing it's chasing.
A frozen copy, refreshed every so often, holds the target still.Refresh too often, and the chase returns. Too rarely, and learning goes stale.

doubledqn:0.t: Double D Q N. Taking a max over noisy guesses is too optimistic.

doubledqn:1.t:
Pip now trains the full D Q N, with replay and a frozen copy.
Look at the target. It takes the largest of the copy's four values.That one word, largest, hides a problem.
To see it, let's leave the meadow and play with plain numbers.

doubledqn:2.t:
Imagine a spot where every move is truly worth zero.Pip doesn't know that. Its guesses each carry a random error.Watch them appear, one by one.
Now pick the largest. It's above zero.So the target says this spot is worth something, when it's worth nothing.

doubledqn:3.t:
Roll again, and again. Watch the yellow box in each row, the round's largest guess.
Now the averages.A single guess is right on average, close to zero.But the largest one averages point one oh.
The max keeps picking the lucky errors. An error that always leans one way is a bias. Here, an overestimation bias.

doubledqn:4.t:
Back in the meadow, Pip's values are noisy too. The network is still partly wrong. So the max in its target leans high.
And it doesn't stay put.Watch the labels walk backwards along the route.Each spot learns from the inflated one after it.

doubledqn:5.t:
The fix needs two independent sets of guesses.
Set A chooses the move, the one with A's largest guess.Then set B scores that same move.
B's error has nothing to do with A's luck.So B's number is just a fresh random error. No longer lucky on purpose.

doubledqn:6.t:
Here are the averages over all the rounds.The single guess and the largest, as before.And now, A picks, B scores. Right back near zero.
This trick is Double Q-learning. Hado van Hasselt proposed it in twenty ten, with two tables that pick moves for each other.

doubledqn:7.t:
Here's the neat part. D Q N already has two networks.
Double D Q N uses them as A and B.The live network chooses the move. The copy scores it.
The copy only lags a little behind, so their errors are partly shared. The bias shrinks, but maybe not all the way.

doubledqn:8.t:
Here's one real card, landing in the corner.
The copy favours up. The live network prefers down.So D Q N and Double D Q N read different numbers from the copy.
Check the simple route at the bottom. Double D Q N can err low, too. It underestimates here.

doubledqn:9.t:
Does any of this matter in the meadow? Let's measure it.
At each of these thirty spots, compare what the network expects with what Pip really gets.
The gap is estimate minus reality.Above zero means too optimistic.

doubledqn:10.t:
Watch the two lines, averaged over eight runs.Orange, D Q N, starts point two three too high.Teal, Double D Q N, drops near zero, sometimes below.
The gap is mostly early. By the end, both are close.Reaching the cheese, they score about the same.

doubledqn:11.t:
Your turn. Drag the number of moves, all truly worth zero.
Watch the rows. More boxes, more chances for one lucky error.
So the largest guess climbs higher.A picks, B scores stays near zero every time.

doubledqn:12.t:
On Atari games, D Q N's value estimates sat far above the scores it really earned. Double D Q N brought them down, and played better on many games.
The same worry shaped later methods.T D 3 keeps two critics and trusts the smaller one.Rainbow bundles Double D Q N with other upgrades.

doubledqn:13.t:
The largest of several noisy guesses is too high, on average. D Q N's target takes exactly that max, and the optimism spreads backwards.
Double D Q N lets the live network choose, and the copy score.Same two networks, one line changed.

pg:0.t: Policy Gradient Methods. Skip the values: directly tweak the policy to win more.

pg:1.t:
Welcome to a new way of learning.
On the left, the old way. Pip learned a value for every move, then mostly took the biggest.
On the right, the new way. Pip keeps its choices as chances, and adjusts them directly.Moves that turned out well become more likely. These are policy gradient methods.

pg:2.t:
To see the idea clearly, let's shrink the world to one decision.
Three doors. Pip picks one, walks through, and the episode is over.Sometimes a crumb appears. Sometimes nothing.Each door has its own hidden chance, and Pip can't see it.

pg:3.t:
Pip's policy is just a chance for each door.The pie shows it.Right now it's a third each. Pip has no idea which door is best, so it tries them all.
With only one situation, this pie is the whole policy.

pg:4.t:
Where do the chances come from? Pip keeps a preference for each door, any number at all.
Softmax turns them into chances.All zero gives a third each.
Now watch door C's preference rise to one.Its chance grows to point five eight.

pg:5.t:
Why preferences, and not chances directly? Pip can push them anywhere, and softmax still gives proper chances. Every door keeps a little chance, so Pip keeps exploring.
Now watch all three preferences go up by one.The pie doesn't change. Only the differences matter.

pg:6.t:
Let's peek behind the doors. C is the best, at point eight.Pip still doesn't know this. We use it only to score the policy.
The score is the expected return, the average reward per episode.With a third each, that's one half.Always choosing C would give point eight.

pg:7.t:
Which way should Pip nudge its preferences? The gradient tells it. Same idea as in machine learning, but climbing uphill.
Watch the curve draw. It's the expected return, as C's preference changes.The red arrow shows the slope. Then the dot steps uphill.

pg:8.t:
Here's the gradient for all three doors at once.
Watch the arrows appear.A points down. B, right at the average, gets nothing for now. C points up.
The rule is simple. Each door's chance, times how much it beats the current average.

pg:9.t:
Now Pip climbs. Add the gradient, a small step at a time, then look again.
Watch the dots rise.The gains are big at first, then shrink near the top.After 20 nudges, the expected return is point seven eight.
And the pie leans heavily toward C.

pg:10.t:
Why bother with chances at all? First, they change smoothly.
On the left, Pip always picks the biggest guess.A tiny shift, and the choice flips completely, from B to C.
On the right, the same tiny shift in preferences.The chances barely move. Learning slides, instead of jumping.

pg:11.t:
Second, actions don't have to be a short list.
Say Pip must jump a gap, with any strength it likes.The policy can be a bell curve over strengths.Watch its centre slide toward the cheese ledge.
Nudge the centre toward jumps that landed better. Later reels show how.

pg:12.t:
Third, sometimes being random is the best plan.
Take rock, paper, scissors.Any fixed choice gets beaten once it's spotted. The best play is a third each.
Always picking the biggest guess can't learn that mix.A policy of chances can.

pg:13.t:
Back in the maze, every cell gets its own four preferences, and its own softmax.The arrows show the chances. All start equal, a quarter each.
Now watch one cell. Raise its up preference, and the up arrow grows.

pg:14.t:
Now the catch. Every gradient so far used the hidden crumb chances.
Watch the numbers on the doors vanish.Pip never gets to see them.
So it must estimate the gradient from its own tries.That's the next reel, REINFORCE.

pg:15.t:
Your turn. Tap a door to raise its preference. Tap the floor to start again.
Watch the pie, and the arrows that point uphill.
Try raising A a few times, then C. Or tap all three once, and notice that nothing changes.

pg:16.t:
Policy gradient methods are everywhere.
They steer robots, where actions are motor strengths.A method called P P O trained OpenAI Five, which beat the Dota 2 world champions in twenty nineteen.And similar training fine-tunes chatbots from human feedback.

pg:17.t:
So, a policy gradient method keeps the policy itself as numbers, and nudges them uphill.
Preferences become chances through softmax.The gradient points toward doors that beat the average.Chances move smoothly, handle any action, and can stay random on purpose.

reinforce:0.t: REINFORCE. The simplest policy gradient: weight actions by the episode’s return.

reinforce:1.t:
Welcome back to the door room.
Last time, Pip climbed using the hidden crumb chances.Watch them disappear. Pip never had them.
REINFORCE needs no secrets.Pip just tries a door, sees what happens, and nudges its preferences.

reinforce:2.t:
Every door starts at a third.
Watch Pip roll its dice and walk to door C.A crumb! Plus one.
Now the rule. A choice followed by a good return becomes more likely.So C goes up, and the other two dip a little.

reinforce:3.t:
How big is each nudge? It's the step size, times the return, times a factor.
For the chosen door, the factor is one minus its chance. Here, about two thirds.The other doors drop by their own chance.
And if the reward had been zero? Nothing would change at all.

reinforce:4.t:
That factor measures how surprising the choice was.
On the left, a door picked nine times out of ten. Its factor is small.On the right, a rare pick. Its factor is big.
Why? Likely doors get nudged often, rare ones seldom.Scaling by surprise evens that out, exactly.

reinforce:5.t:
One try is a rough guess. So let's try many times, without changing anything, and average the nudges.
Watch the three lines settle.They wobble wildly at first, then close in on the dashed lines, the true gradient.
Noisy, yes. But on average, REINFORCE points uphill.

reinforce:6.t:
Now, the maze. Cheese plus one, cat minus one, and all arrows start equal.
REINFORCE waits for the walk to end, like Monte Carlo.Then each move gets the return that came after it.A move can't change rewards that already happened.

reinforce:7.t:
Here's walk one. Watch Pip wander.It bumps into walls, and finally steps onto the cat. Minus one.
Now every move gets its return.The closer to the cat, the bigger the blame.Pip's first move only gets minus point two three.

reinforce:8.t:
Every return was negative. So every move Pip made becomes a little less likely.
Watch the cell below the cat. Its up move led straight into the cat, so pushing it down is fair.But the start cell's up move was fine. It gets pushed down too, just because this walk ended badly.

reinforce:9.t:
Walk 5 is the first to find the cheese.Watch the arrows shift.
The last move gets a full one.But the first move gets very little. The cheese was too far away.
So learning starts near the cheese, and spreads back toward the start.

reinforce:10.t:
Now Pip walks 300 times.Watch the arrows in the maze line up.
Below, each dot is one walk's return. Gold for cheese, rose for cat.Early walks are long, and score near zero.Then the gold line climbs, close to the best possible.

reinforce:11.t:
Follow the biggest arrows from the start.Watch the teal route. It reaches the cheese in 7 moves, the shortest way.
Along the way, some walks hit the cat, and some were stopped. Stopped walks changed nothing.Cells off the route were rarely visited, so their arrows stay rough.

reinforce:12.t:
Same recipe, different dice. Does it always go the same way?
Each thin line is one run.Some learn early, some late.
The thick line averages many runs. It climbs smoothly.A single run is a very noisy copy of it.

reinforce:13.t:
Why so noisy? One walk's luck colours every move in it.
A detour into the cat punishes the good moves before it. A lucky walk rewards its bumps.
These bars count Pip's walks by return. They're spread wide, so the nudges swing just as wide.That's high variance. The next reel calms it.

reinforce:14.t:
Your turn. Drag alpha, the step size, and the same dice replay.
Watch the thick line.Small alpha learns slowly, but steadily.
Big alpha starts faster. But keep an eye on the count of stuck runs.

reinforce:15.t:
With alpha at one, 8 runs get stuck.Look at this one's arrows. Early cat walks pushed them hard, away from the cheese.
Now Pip wanders until the walk is stopped. Return zero, so no nudge.Nothing left to learn from. Big steps on noisy estimates can wreck a policy.

reinforce:16.t:
Ronald Williams published REINFORCE in nineteen ninety two.
AlphaGo used it, with games against older versions of itself. Win or lose, every move got nudged.
Today it still helps fine-tune language models on a reward score.Usually together with the noise-calming tricks coming next.

reinforce:17.t:
So, REINFORCE learns from complete episodes. Each action gets nudged by the return that followed it.
Surprising choices get bigger nudges, so on average it climbs the true gradient.But each episode's luck colours every action. Updates are noisy, and big steps can wreck the policy.

baseline:0.t: Baselines  and  Advantage. Not “was it good?” but “was it better than usual?”

baseline:1.t:
Back in the door room, with plain REINFORCE. A few lucky crumbs made B the favourite, though C is better.
Now Pip opens A, the worst door. A crumb!Watch A's chance grow.
An empty door changes nothing. So a picked door only ever goes up, or stays put.That seems a bit off, doesn't it?

baseline:2.t:
Think of grading on a curve.
A score of seventy five is great, if the class usually gets sixty.And poor, if the class usually gets ninety.
So Pip keeps a yardstick, a usual reward. It nudges by the reward minus the yardstick.Better than usual, push up. Worse, push down.

baseline:3.t:
That difference has a name, the advantage. How much better this try went than usual.
A simple yardstick is Pip's average reward so far. Here, about one half.
A crumb is now worth plus a half, a push up.An empty door, minus a half, a push down.

baseline:4.t:
Does the yardstick bend Pip's direction? No. It's the same, whatever door Pip picks.
Take door A. When it's picked, the yardstick pulls it down a bit.When it's not picked, it pushes it up a bit.Weighted by how often each happens, they cancel exactly.

baseline:5.t:
So the average nudge stays the same. What changes is the spread.
Each dot is one possible nudge to C. Bigger dots happen more often.Plain nudges sit far apart. With the yardstick, they huddle closer.
Over all doors, the spread drops from point five six to point three eight.

baseline:6.t:
Now many runs, each 200 picks, with and without the yardstick.The line shows Pip's chance of picking C. The shading covers most of the runs.
Grey, plain, climbs slowly, with a wide band.Teal, with the yardstick, climbs faster, and the band is much narrower.

baseline:7.t:
Now look at single runs at the very end.
Plain REINFORCE leaves 32 runs out of 500 still preferring the wrong door.Lucky crumbs pushed them off, and empty doors never pushed back.
With the yardstick, just 3.Empty doors now push down, so a wrong lead gets corrected.

baseline:8.t:
Your turn. Drag the yardstick. Try fixed numbers, or Pip's running average.
Watch the teal line against the grey one, plain REINFORCE.Almost any yardstick beats none here.
The running average isn't the very best. But it needs no tuning at all.

baseline:9.t:
Back to the maze. Here, one average won't do.
Look at the numbers. From the start, Pip's usual return is small.Right beside the cheese, it's large.
So each cell gets its own yardstick, its value.The usual return from that cell, under Pip's current chances.

baseline:10.t:
How does Pip learn these yardsticks? Just like Monte Carlo, from returns. No rulebook.
Watch the numbers fill in, walk after walk.After each walk, every visited cell moves a tenth of the way toward the return that followed.
Preferences and yardsticks learn side by side.

baseline:11.t:
Watch the cell left of the cheese.In one walk, Pip steps straight onto the cheese. Better than usual, so a gentle push up.
In another, Pip takes a detour, and gets the cheese three moves later. The return is still positive, point eight one.But it's worse than usual, so that move is pushed down.Plain REINFORCE would have pushed it up.

baseline:12.t:
How much calmer are the nudges? We freeze Pip at three moments and measure.
Grey is plain. Teal uses yardsticks.Early on, the young yardsticks actually make it worse.Later, they divide the noise by about 8 point three.
Poor yardsticks add noise. Good ones remove it.

baseline:13.t:
Now an honest result.
Watch the two curves. They almost overlap.Over many runs, the gain in the maze is small.
Why? Most learning happens early, when returns are near zero and the yardsticks are poor. Baselines help most when returns share a large common level, like in the door room.

baseline:14.t:
Nearly every modern policy gradient method subtracts a baseline.
Actor-critic methods learn the value with a second network, and nudge by the advantage.
For language models, methods like G R P O sample several answers to one question. Their average reward is the yardstick.That's the door room idea, almost exactly.

baseline:15.t:
So, a baseline is a yardstick for the usual return. Nudge by the advantage, the return minus the baseline.
Better than usual goes up. Worse goes down.The direction stays the same, only the noise shrinks. Next, Pip learns the values step by step.

actorcritic:0.t: Actor-Critic. One network acts, another grades every move.

actorcritic:1.t:
Welcome back to Pip's maze.
Same cheese, same cat, same dry floor.The arrows are Pip's chances. Every one starts at a quarter.
And there's still no rulebook. Pip learns only from what happens.

actorcritic:2.t:
REINFORCE has to wait until the walk is over.
Watch Pip's first walk.15 steps, then the cat. Until that last step, nothing is learned.
Then every move takes the blame.Even the very first step up, fourteen moves before the cat.

actorcritic:3.t:
Here's the idea. Split Pip in two.
The actor is the arrows. It picks the moves.The critic is a notebook of numbers, one guess per cell, of the return to expect from there.
Think of an athlete and a coach.The athlete tries a move. The coach says at once, better than I expected, or worse.

actorcritic:4.t:
The critic learns just like in the T D reel.
Watch Pip take one step up.
The target is the reward, plus point nine times the guess where Pip landed.The gap between the target and the old guess is the T D error, delta.The guess moves a fifth of that gap.

actorcritic:5.t:
Here's the clever part. The critic's T D error also grades the move.
REINFORCE waited for the whole return.Actor-critic uses one real reward, plus the critic's guess for the rest.
Better than expected, the move becomes more likely. Worse, less likely. And it happens right away.

actorcritic:6.t:
Let's see it in numbers. Walk one's last step.
Watch Pip step up, onto the cat. Minus one.Every guess was zero, so delta is minus one.
Up's preference drops. The other three rise a little.Up's chance falls to point one one.

actorcritic:7.t:
What about the steps before that?
Watch Pip wander through walk one.Every reward is zero, and every guess is zero. So delta is zero. No push at all.
A blank critic needs news from the cheese or the cat. That news spreads back slowly, so actor-critic starts slow.

actorcritic:8.t:
Now walk 11. The critic has learned a little.Watch the cell right of the cat. Its guess is negative, from past meetings.
Pip steps up into it. Delta goes negative, a push away, right there, mid-walk.
The dots mark each grade. Gold is better than expected, rose is worse.And finally, the cheese.

actorcritic:9.t:
Let the pair learn for 300 walks.Watch the arrows straighten along the short path.And the critic's numbers fill in behind them.
At the end, the critic's guess at the start is point five two.The best possible is very close. Most recent walks take just seven steps.

actorcritic:10.t:
Let's compare the two kinds of grade for a single move.
Freeze Pip, and send it up from the start, forty times.
Each dot is the grade REINFORCE with a baseline would give that move.They're spread wide. Each one carries the luck of the rest of its walk.

actorcritic:11.t:
Now the critic's grade. It's point oh eight, every single time.No slips, a frozen critic, so no noise.
But the dots average somewhere else.That average is the honest grade. The critic's guess above lags behind Pip's progress.
Returns are unbiased but noisy. The critic is steady, but can be wrong. That's bias.

actorcritic:12.t:
Time for a fair race. Actor-critic against REINFORCE with a baseline.
Same maze, same seeds, a hundred runs each.
The chart shows the return from the start. Dashed is the best possible.Watch the first few walks.

actorcritic:13.t:
REINFORCE with a baseline gets going sooner.The blank critic is why. Its grades stay near zero, until news from the cheese reaches the start.
But watch the lines cross.From walk 69 on, actor-critic leads, and it finishes ahead.

actorcritic:14.t:
Each dot is one run. Its average return over the last walks.
Top row, REINFORCE with a baseline.4 runs fall below the dashed line.In most of them, Pip just wanders. Its walks get stopped, every grade is zero, and pushes fade away.
Bottom row, actor-critic.None at all.

actorcritic:15.t:
Were the step sizes fair? The yardstick and the critic learned at different speeds. So we swapped them.
Here's the table.Same picture either way.
REINFORCE with a baseline starts faster, but leaves more runs behind.

actorcritic:16.t:
Your turn. Drag the actor's step size, and both methods rerun on the same seeds.
Watch the two curves, and the count of runs left behind.
Big steps learn fast, but trust every push. Which method copes with a step of two? Which is quicker with small ones?

actorcritic:17.t:
The critic is only a guess. How fast should it learn?
Look at the top bars. A rushed critic spreads news faster.
But the bottom bars show the cost.With step point five, 7 runs fall behind.A wrong critic steers the actor wrong.

actorcritic:18.t:
The idea is old.
In nineteen eighty three, Barto, Sutton and Anderson balanced a pole on a cart.One part chose the pushes. An adaptive critic graded them.
Today, A 2 C, P P O, D D P G and sack are all actor-critic methods.

actorcritic:19.t:
So, actor-critic splits Pip in two. The actor holds the chances. The critic learns values by T D.
After every step, the critic's T D error grades the move, and the actor nudges it.No waiting, and steady grades. The price is bias, when the critic is wrong.

gae:0.t: n-step Returns  and  G A E. How far should you look before trusting the critic’s guess?

gae:1.t:
Welcome back to the maze, with an actor and a critic.
The actor needs a grade for each move. How much better did it go than the critic expected?
Actor-critic looked one real step ahead. REINFORCE looked at the whole walk.Is there something in between? And is it better?

gae:2.t:
Freeze Pip after walk fifty, and send it up from the start, two thousand times.
The teal line is the one-step grade. It's the same every time.The dots are whole-walk grades. They swing all over.
The gold line is the true grade, worked out from the rulebook.Notice which one sits closer to it.

gae:3.t:
The one-step grade has no noise at all. But it's always too low. The critic's guess for the next cell lags behind. Leaning one way every time is bias.
The whole-walk grade is right on average.But each walk's luck pushes it around. That jumping is variance, or noise.

gae:4.t:
Here's the in-between. Take a few real steps, then trust the critic.
Watch the arcs. The teal one takes one step, then reads the guess.Orange takes three steps first.Rose goes all the way to the end, with no guess at all.
The number of real steps, n, becomes a dial.

gae:5.t:
Let's turn the dial, and watch the grades change.
As n grows, the arc reaches further.
The dots creep toward the true grade. But they spread out more.More real steps, less bias, more noise.

gae:6.t:
Why pick just one n? Generalised advantage estimation, or G A E, blends them all.
Each bar is one n's weight. They fade as n grows.Lambda sets how fast. At point five, they fade quickly. At point nine, slowly.
The weights add up to one, so it's still an average.

gae:7.t:
The blend has a neat shortcut.
Watch Pip walk. Each move leaves its T D error, its little surprise.One of them was a bump into the wall.
The G A E grade just adds them up, each later one faded a bit more.For this walk, it comes to point two eight.

gae:8.t:
Your turn. Drag lambda, and watch the grades of the same move.
At zero, the dots stack on one wrong spot.At one, they centre on the truth, but spread wide.
The typical miss combines both. How far one grade usually lands from the truth.

gae:9.t:
Which lambda is best? Here's the whole picture.
Rose is the bias. It falls as lambda grows.Blue is the spread. It rises.Black, the typical miss, combines them.
With this young critic, the miss is smallest at lambda 1. The critic still lags, so trusting it less pays.

gae:10.t:
Now freeze Pip a bit later, after walk eighty. The critic has caught up.
Watch the black curve again.Now the best lambda is 0.
The best lambda depends on how much you can trust the critic.

gae:11.t:
Now Pip actually learns with G A E. After each walk, every move gets its grade.
Each line is one lambda, averaged over many runs.Watch which ones climb first.
The table below sums up the race.

gae:12.t:
Lambda zero starts slowest. Its grades lean on a blank critic.Lambda one starts fast, but stays noisy, and leaves more runs behind.
The ones in between strike a compromise.And once the critic is good, small lambda ends best.

gae:13.t:
There's a price. A G A E grade needs the surprises that come after the move.
Watch Pip walk. Each move's grade has to wait.Only at the cheese can every move be graded.
Real systems cut experience into chunks, and let the critic's guess stand in for the rest.

gae:14.t:
John Schulman and colleagues introduced G A E in twenty fifteen.
A lambda of point nine five became a common default.The P P O paper used exactly that.
It's the same dial as T D lambda, now grading moves for the actor.

gae:15.t:
So, an n-step grade takes n real rewards, then trusts the critic. Small n is steady but biased. Large n is honest but noisy.
G A E blends every n, with weights that fade by lambda.The best lambda depends on how far the critic can be trusted.

ppo:0.t: P P O. Improve the policy, but not too much at once.

ppo:1.t:
Welcome back to the maze. Pip starts from scratch again.
Watch the arrows appear, a quarter each.Most test walks hit the cat, or wander until they're stopped.
Its score, the expected return from the start, is low.The best possible is point five three.

ppo:2.t:
Each update, Pip walks 10 times. That's a batch.Watch the walks, one after another.The tally keeps count of how each one ends.
Then each move gets its advantage. The return that followed, minus what the critic expected.Good moves are pushed up, bad ones down.

ppo:3.t:
Those ten walks were used once, then thrown away.
In a real game or robot, collecting walks is the slow, expensive part. Computing is cheap.
So why not go over the same walks several times?Ten passes, though, could push ten times too far.

ppo:4.t:
After one pass, Pip's chances have changed. But the walks came from the old Pip.
So P P O compares, new chance over old chance. That's the ratio.
Look at the cheese step, from the gold cell.After one pass, the new Pip makes it about 1 point two nine times as often.

ppo:5.t:
Each pass climbs an objective. The ratio, times the advantage, averaged over the batch.
Watch the line. For a good move, a bigger ratio gives a bigger objective.At ratio one, the first pass is exactly the ordinary update.
Moves the new Pip makes more often simply count more.

ppo:6.t:
Now ten passes over the first batch, with no brake.
Watch the arrows twist, pass after pass.
Every test walk now gets stopped. Pip just wanders and bumps, meeting neither cat nor cheese.The score barely changes, to about zero. Looks harmless. It isn't.

ppo:7.t:
Why would Pip stop finishing?
Look at the batch. Some walks hit the cat, some the cheese, and some were stopped, with return zero.
The critic expected less than zero everywhere. So zero looked better than expected!Pushed ten times, keep wandering beat reach the cheese.

ppo:8.t:
And now Pip is stuck for good.
Every walk gets stopped. Every return is zero, and the critic expects zero.No surprises, so nothing to learn.
Watch the score over forty more updates. It stays flat.

ppo:9.t:
P P O, proximal policy optimization, adds a brake. It clips the ratio to a band, usually from point eight to one point two.
Watch the line for a good move.Past one point two, it goes flat. No reward for pushing further.Below the band, the line keeps falling. Making a good move rarer is still penalised.

ppo:10.t:
For a bad move, it mirrors.
Lowering its ratio helps, but only down to point eight. Then it's flat.Raising a bad move's chance still costs, with no cap.
P P O removes the reward for going too far. Never the penalty.

ppo:11.t:
Flat means no slope, so the move stops pushing.
Watch the cheese step over ten passes.Without the clip, its ratio climbs to 2 point five oh.
With the clip, it overshoots a little on the first pass, then stays put.The first pass starts inside the band, so the clip can't catch it yet.

ppo:12.t:
Same batch, ten passes, now with the brake.
The brake limits the bad advice, but doesn't undo it. Fewer walks finish than before.
But watch the blue line. Later batches correct it.After forty updates, it reaches point five two. The unclipped rose line stays stuck.

ppo:13.t:
One run could be luck. So here are fifty, averaged.
Teal takes one ordinary pass. Rose takes ten passes, unclipped. Blue takes ten, clipped.
Watch how many runs get stuck.Ten passes cost ten times the computing, but the same number of walks.

ppo:14.t:
Ten passes at once is like one giant step. What if we just take a giant step?
Rose takes one pass, thirty times bigger. Many runs crash.Teal takes ten tiny passes. Safe, but slow.
Blue, the clipped passes, gets both. Fast, and nothing stuck.

ppo:15.t:
Your turn. Drag epsilon, the width of the band, and the same fifty runs replay.
Watch the blue line against the pale one.A tight band is safe, but slow. A wide band lets more through.
With no clip at all, count the stuck runs.

ppo:16.t:
A warning. The clip is a brake, not a wall.
It stops a move from pushing itself. But other moves in the same cell still shift its chance.So some ratios end up outside the band. The rose bars.
Practical versions often also stop early, once old and new chances drift too far apart.

ppo:17.t:
Schulman's team at OpenAI introduced P P O in twenty seventeen. Easy to code and tune, it became a common default.
A scaled-up P P O trained OpenAI Five, which beat the Dota 2 world champions.
And InstructGPT used P P O to steer a language model toward answers people preferred.

ppo:18.t:
So, reusing a batch squeezes more learning out of every walk. But unchecked passes push too far, and a wrecked policy may never recover.
P P O clips the ratio, new chance over old, to a narrow band.Once a move has moved enough, it stops earning credit.

sac:0.t: Entropy  and  Soft Actor-Critic. Reward the agent for keeping its options open.

sac:1.t:
Welcome back to the door room.
Three doors, each with a hidden crumb chance. C is the best, at point eight.Pip's policy is a pie of chances, a third each to start.

sac:2.t:
This time Pip is an actor-critic.
The critic keeps a score for each door.It learns by replaying old picks from memory, like D Q N.
The actor nudges toward doors that score above the pie's average.No sampled returns needed.

sac:3.t:
Why can old picks still teach Pip something?
The memory holds picks from any old policy.The critic learns what each door pays. A crumb behind C is news about C, whoever picked it.And the actor learns from those scores.
Learning from old data like this is called off-policy.

sac:4.t:
Here's Pip's first run.
Watch the picks.B pays a few crumbs early on, and its score climbs.C never gets a try.
Once B looked good, the actor raised its chance, and Pip tried the others even less. Luck chose the start. The rule did the rest.

sac:5.t:
Now watch four hundred picks.
B's line climbs, and C's stays flat near the bottom.
The critic only learns about doors Pip actually picks.So C's score stays far below its true value. Pip is stuck on B, with almost no way out.

sac:6.t:
Was that just one unlucky run? Let's run it two hundred times.
Each dot is one run. Teal means Pip ended up favouring C.Rose means it got stuck on a worse door.
It's the old exploration trap. A learner that stops trying a door never finds out it was wrong.

sac:7.t:
We need a way to measure how spread out a pie is.
A door's surprise is high when its chance is small.Entropy is the average surprise.
Watch the three pies.A third each has the most entropy. A sure thing has none.

sac:8.t:
Now Pip aims for more than crumbs. It aims for reward, plus alpha times entropy.
Alpha is the temperature. How many crumbs one unit of spread is worth.
Each door is worth its score, plus a bonus for being rare.So rare doors don't sink forever.

sac:9.t:
Why not just pick a random door now and then, like epsilon-greedy?
Those random picks would go to good and bad doors alike, forever.
With the bonus, staying spread is part of the aim.Pip keeps spare chances where they cost little, on doors close to the best.

sac:10.t:
What's the best pie at each temperature?
Watch the pies, from cold to hot.Near zero, it's always C.As alpha rises, the pie spreads toward a third each.

sac:11.t:
Let's rerun Pip's first run, same dice, with alpha at point two.
It starts the same way.But watch C's line. The bonus keeps C in play, and C climbs.
Over two hundred runs, far fewer get stuck.

sac:12.t:
Curiosity has a price. Even after finding C, Pip keeps a few percent on A and B.
Look at the averages.Crumbs per visit come out about even, with or without the bonus.
So for now, curiosity roughly pays for itself. The big payoff comes when the world changes.

sac:13.t:
After pick four hundred, door A suddenly starts paying, ninety five times out of a hundred.
On top, the certain Pip. It never tries A, and never finds out.
Below, the curious Pip. It keeps trying A now and then. Watch A take over.

sac:14.t:
Your turn. Drag the temperature, and rerun the two hundred runs.
The pie is the best one for that temperature.The numbers are what real learning Pips did.
Too cold, and Pip gets stuck. Too hot, and it wastes visits. Which bar is tallest?

sac:15.t:
Now a new task, with no menu. Pip picks a jump strength, any number.
The cheese is point seven metres out.The gold curve shows the reward for each strength. A near miss still pays a bit.
The policy is a bell curve, with a centre and a spread.

sac:16.t:
Bell curves have entropy too. Wider bells have more.
Without a bonus, the bell narrows toward one strength.With it, the bell keeps some width.
Watch the close-up. A bigger alpha keeps a wider bell.

sac:17.t:
In longer tasks, the bonus joins the reward at every step.
So a spot with three good ways on is worth more than a spot with just one.The agent learns to keep its options open.
Why soft? The best pie is a softmax of the values, a soft maximum.

sac:18.t:
sack, soft actor-critic, brings all this to continuous actions. It came from Haarnoja and colleagues in twenty eighteen.
Its actor tries a few strengths from its bell, and asks the critic which way to move.It replays old experience, and keeps two critics, trusting the lower one.

sac:19.t:
sack is a standard choice for continuous control.
Its authors taught a four-legged robot, Minitaur, to walk with about two hours of real experience.That's short, for real hardware.
Many other methods add a small entropy bonus too, just to keep exploring.

sac:20.t:
So, entropy measures how spread out the chances are. Add it to the reward, and Pip stays curious.
An unlucky start, or a changing world, no longer traps it.Alpha sets the price of curiosity. sack puts it all into an actor-critic.

ddpg:0.t: Continuous Control: D D P G  and  T D 3. D Q N for steering wheels and robot joints.

ddpg:1.t:
Welcome back to Pip's ledge. This time, every action is a number.
Pip picks how hard to jump. Watch a few tries.Too soft, too hard, and then just right.
The gold curve shows the reward for each strength. It peaks at point seven metres.

ddpg:2.t:
Now a row of ledges, and a stream between them.
Watch the first jump land, and Pip jump again.Then a jump that's too long. Splash. The run is over.
Wind nudges each landing, and crumbs vary in size. So rewards are noisy, too.

ddpg:3.t:
D Q N kept one score per move, and took the biggest. Four numbers to compare.
But a strength can be any number at all.Point seven? Point seven one? There's no end to the list.
Even chopping into steps fails. A robot arm with seven joints has ten million combinations.

ddpg:4.t:
So the critic scores any strength. How much reward to expect from this jump, and every jump after.
Watch the dashed curve. It's the true score, if Pip always jumps point seven.The peak is about 9 point oh six.Past the cliffs on either side, Pip falls.
The critic has to learn this curve.

ddpg:5.t:
The actor is simpler still. It answers each situation with one strength. No dice, no chances.
Here, the actor is just one number, starting at point three metres.Watch the jump. Too short. Pip falls.
A strength is already a smooth number, so a small nudge makes a small change.

ddpg:6.t:
The critic learns like D Q N. Its target is the reward, plus point nine times its score for the next jump.
Watch this jump land.The next jump comes from the actor, not from searching for the best.
Here the target beats the critic's old score, so its curve rises at that spot.

ddpg:7.t:
If the actor always gives the same answer, the critic only ever sees one strength. It can't tell if harder or softer is better.
So in training, every jump gets a little random noise.Watch the bell. Jumps scatter around the actor's answer.

ddpg:8.t:
How does the actor improve, without trying every strength? It asks the critic.
If I jumped a little harder, would your score rise?That's the slope of the critic's curve, at the actor's strength.
So the actor steps uphill, here from point four seven to point five oh.

ddpg:9.t:
Real actors are networks, with many knobs.
The critic says how much the score changes per metre.Each knob says how many metres it moves the strength.
Multiply the two, and each knob knows which way to turn.That's the chain rule. So it's still a policy gradient.

ddpg:10.t:
Two tricks from D Q N keep this steady.
A replay buffer. After every jump, the critic studies eight random old ones.
And target copies. Slow copies of the critic and the actor build the targets, so they hold still.

ddpg:11.t:
Put it all together, and you get D D P G, deep deterministic policy gradient. Lillicrap and colleagues, twenty fifteen.
Here's Pip's first run, sped up. Early jumps often end in the stream.
Watch the actor's dot climb the gold curve, and settle near point seven.After that, Pip rarely falls.

ddpg:12.t:
The actor finds a good jump fast. The critic takes longer.
Gold is the critic's score. Dashed is the true worth.Watch gold climb slowly, one reward at a time, like T D.The dips are when the actor drifted.

ddpg:13.t:
But look closer. This critic ends up too optimistic. It believes in reward that never comes.
Why? The actor seeks the critic's highest point.Including spots that look high only by luck.
Every target leans on that inflated score, and the error is copied back, jump after jump. Double D Q N saw the same thing.

ddpg:14.t:
Was that bad luck? Let's run D D P G eight times.
The line shows the critic's score minus the true worth.Above the dashed zero, too optimistic.D D P G stays above zero.

ddpg:15.t:
In twenty eighteen, Fujimoto, van Hoof and Meger proposed T D 3, with three fixes.
Fix one. Train two critics, and build the target from the smaller score.
Two critics rarely share the same lucky guess. Watch the new line drop toward zero.

ddpg:16.t:
Fix two. Update the actor only every second jump, and let the critics settle in between.
If the critic still wobbles, the actor chases the wobble.
In this small task, it makes no real difference.It matters more for large networks, whose critics take longer to settle.

ddpg:17.t:
Fix three. Jiggle the next jump inside the target a little.
Then a narrow false peak can't lift the target.
The new line sits a bit lower. That's mostly by design. The critic now values a slightly clumsier jumper.Measured against the jumper it really values, T D 3 is very close.

ddpg:18.t:
Your turn. Add T D 3's fixes one at a time.
The thin lines are the eight runs. The thick line is their average.
Notice Pip jumps about equally well in all four. With one simple hump, false optimism has nowhere to lure the actor. In big tasks, it can.

ddpg:19.t:
D D P G learned over twenty simulated physics tasks, like swinging up a pole, walking, and driving.
T D 3 clearly beat it on standard robot benchmarks.Today T D 3 is a common starting point for continuous control. Soft actor-critic also uses two critics.

ddpg:20.t:
So, when actions are numbers, you can't take a max over them all.
D D P G lets a deterministic actor climb the critic's slope, with noise, replay, and slow copies.The critic turns optimistic. T D 3 trusts the smaller of two critics, delays the actor, and blurs the target.

modelbased:0.t: Model-Based R L. Learn how the world works, then plan in your head.

modelbased:1.t:
Welcome back to Pip's maze. Cheese, cat, and a dry floor.
But Pip still has no rulebook. It can't tell where a move will land.
In the Q-learning reel, it learned from experience alone. Its first walks were long, very long.

modelbased:2.t:
Here's that first walk again, sped up.
Watch the numbers in each cell. Nothing moves.Every update nudges zero toward zero.
Only the very last step, onto the cheese, changes one number.Pip saw 24 steps of the maze, and almost all of them left no trace.

modelbased:3.t:
What if Pip also wrote down what each move did?
In this cell, this move landed there, and paid this much.Watch the notes fill the maze. Bumps count too.
This notebook is a learned model. Pip's own copy of part of the rulebook.

modelbased:4.t:
Pip's floor is dry, so one look per move is enough. But on a wet floor, moves can slip.
Remember the wet floor? Try right from the start, again and again.Count where Pip lands.
The counts, divided by the tries, land close to the true chances.

modelbased:5.t:
Now Pip can plan with its notebook, just like value iteration.
Each cell's value is the best noted move, its reward plus point nine times the value where it lands.Watch the values spread out, sweep by sweep.
Pip only uses moves it has noted. Untried moves are a mystery.

modelbased:6.t:
Now follow the best noted move from each cell.Pip reaches the cheese in 7 steps, the shortest way.After just one real walk!
Plain Q-learning, after the same walk, knew one single move.Learning more from each real step is called sample efficiency.

modelbased:7.t:
But planning isn't free. Each plan sweeps the whole notebook, again and again.
Here that's cheap.In a world with millions of states, it's not.
So Richard Sutton's Dyna spreads the planning thin. A little after each real step.

modelbased:8.t:
Here's how Dyna-Q works. Part one is plain Q-learning.
Pip makes a real move.Its number moves a fifth of the way toward the reward, plus point nine times the best number where it landed.
And one new thing. Pip writes the move into its notebook.

modelbased:9.t:
Part two. Before its next real move, Pip practises in its head, 10 times.
It picks a random note, reads where the move landed and what it paid, and updates, as if it were real.
Imagination takes no real step. And it only replays moves Pip has really tried.

modelbased:10.t:
How do the first walks compare?
Walk one is identical for both. Every number is zero, so imagining changes nothing.
But by the end of walk two, Dyna-Q has far more nonzero numbers.On walk three, Q-learning wanders 28 steps. Dyna-Q walks 7.

modelbased:11.t:
One run could be lucky. So let's race twenty runs, with the same dice for both.
Across is the walk number. Up is how many steps it took.Grey is Q-learning. Teal is Dyna-Q.Watch which line falls faster.

modelbased:12.t:
Over the first ten walks, Dyna-Q used about half the real steps.
Later, both settle at the same level, above the shortest route, because one move in five is still random.
The price is thinking. Ten imagined updates for every real one.

modelbased:13.t:
Now the catch. What if the world changes?
After fifty walks, Pip's arrows take the bottom route.Then the cat wakes up, and moves right onto it.
The notebook doesn't know. Pip follows its confident plan, and meets the cat.

modelbased:14.t:
The note for that move gets overwritten. Right here, lands on the cat.
On walk two, Pip bumps up and down in that cell, again and again.Those numbers come from the old route, and shrink only slowly.
Only after walk 2 do the arrows go over the top.

modelbased:15.t:
Look at the rose tags. These notes still say the old cat cell costs minus one.
The plan stays away, so nothing checks them. And imagination keeps replaying them, making the mistake stronger.
One fix, Dyna-Q plus, adds a small bonus for moves not tried in a while. So Pip goes back to check.

modelbased:16.t:
Your turn. Drag how many imagined steps Pip takes per real step. Zero is plain Q-learning.
Watch the teal line against grey.The first walks shrink as Pip imagines more, then stop shrinking.
Once the notebook is mostly learned, extra imagining adds little.

modelbased:17.t:
Richard Sutton introduced Dyna in nineteen ninety.
Learned models matter most where real experience is slow or costly, like robots.In twenty eleven, PILCO learned to swing up a real cart-pole in a handful of trials.
Next, searching ahead with a model, and learning models from pictures.

modelbased:18.t:
So, a model says where each move lands, and what it pays. If no one hands you one, write down what really happened.
Then plan with it, or practise in your head between real steps.That halved Pip's real steps. But a wrong model gives confident, wrong plans.

mcts:0.t: Monte Carlo Tree Search. Grow a search tree toward the most promising moves.

mcts:1.t:
Welcome to a game night. Pip and the cat play noughts and crosses.
Pip draws cheese, the cat draws paws. Three in a row wins.
We keep score in Pip's points. A win is one, a draw is a half, a loss is zero.The cat wants Pip's points low.

mcts:2.t:
Here's a game two moves in. Now it's Pip's turn, with seven empty squares.
Pip knows the rules exactly. Where each move puts a mark, and when the game ends.
That rulebook is a model. So Pip can play moves out in its head before choosing.

mcts:3.t:
Picture every possible future as a tree.
Under the board, a branch for each of Pip's seven moves. Under each, the cat's replies, and so on, until the games end.
Here that's 6,900 nodes, few enough to check. In Go, the tree is unimaginably bigger.

mcts:4.t:
Here's a cheap way to judge a move. Play it, then let both sides move at random until the game ends.
Watch this playout. Pip tries bottom left, and the random game ends in a win.
One playout is a coin flip. But average many, and you get an estimate. That's what Monte Carlo means.

mcts:5.t:
So let's run two thousand random games after each of Pip's moves.
Each number is the average of Pip's points.The centre looks best, at point six nine.
Should Pip play the centre?

mcts:6.t:
Not so fast. Check every line backwards from the end, with both sides playing their best.
Only top right wins.Watch why. Top right threatens the column, the cat must block, then the centre makes two threats at once.
The playouts missed it, because their random cat rarely defends.

mcts:7.t:
Monte Carlo tree search grows a tree on top of the playouts.
At every node, both sides choose with U C B, like the cheese arcade from the bandits reel. The cat uses its own points, one minus Pip's.
So the search aims its effort where the real choices are decided.

mcts:8.t:
Each loop has four steps.
Select. Follow the best U C B scores down the tree, to an untried move.Expand. Add it as a new node.Simulate. One random playout.Back up. Add its points along the path.

mcts:9.t:
At first, the top node has untried moves. So each loop just adds one of Pip's moves, and plays it out once.
Watch the seven moves appear, one per loop.Each gets one coin flip of a result.
The card explains the numbers under each move.

mcts:10.t:
Loop eight is the first real choice.
Every move has been tried once, so the exploration bonuses are equal.The winners tie, and the earliest one, bottom left, gets the visit.
The search adds a cat reply, and plays it out. This time the cat wins.

mcts:11.t:
Now loop after loop, the same four steps.
Watch the tree grow. Bigger dots mean more visits.Moves that keep scoring well get walked often, so their branches grow deeper.
Weak moves still get an occasional look. Their bonus creeps up while they're ignored.

mcts:12.t:
After a thousand loops, here's the tree.
Top right got by far the most visits.292 of the thousand.
M C T S plays the move it visited most. A lucky average can fool you, but visits only pile up on moves that keep scoring.

mcts:13.t:
Where did the effort go?
Top right's branch runs deep. Weak moves stay shallow.A thousand loops built only 796 nodes.
Value iteration sweeps everything. M C T S goes deep where it matters, so it handles games too big to search fully.

mcts:14.t:
Was a thousand loops just lucky? Let's run the search a hundred times, at several budgets.
Across, the number of loops. Up, how many runs chose each move.Gold is top right, the winning move.With few loops, it's a guess. With many, gold rises to the top.

mcts:15.t:
Teal is the centre. With a few hundred loops, M C T S often picks it.
A shallow tree's averages are mostly playout averages. So it believes them too.
Only deeper trees discover the cat's one good answer to the centre. Then top right takes the lead.

mcts:16.t:
Your turn. Drag the number of loops per decision.
The board shows one search, with the share of loops through each move.
Below, the result over a hundred searches.Notice the centre peak at a few hundred loops, then fade away.

mcts:17.t:
Here's the weak spot. Random playouts judge crudely.
They rated the centre above the only winning move, and that cost M C T S about a thousand loops.
In Go, random games say very little about who's ahead. The next reel learns a better replacement.

mcts:18.t:
In two thousand six, Rémi Coulom named Monte Carlo tree search, in his program Crazy Stone. Kocsis and Szepesvári published UCT, the rule used here.
For a decade, the strongest Go programs used M C T S.They reached strong amateur level. Then AlphaGo added learned networks.

mcts:19.t:
So, M C T S grows a search tree, one node per loop. Select, expand, simulate, and back up.
Both sides choose with U C B, so the search expects good replies. It goes deep where moves look strong.Its weak spot is the random playout.

alphazero:0.t: AlphaZero. Self-play plus tree search plus one neural network.

alphazero:1.t:
Welcome back to Pip's puzzle. Only top right wins.
Random playouts liked the centre better, and the search needed about a thousand loops to see past them.
What if Pip could learn to judge a position, instead of playing it out at random?

alphazero:2.t:
AlphaZero uses one small neural network.
It reads the board, and gives two answers.The value, Pip's expected points from here.And the prior, how promising each move looks.
Before training, its knobs are random.

alphazero:3.t:
The search loop stays. Select, expand, back up. But there's no random playout anymore.
When a loop reaches a new node, the network looks at it once.Its value is backed up the path, and its priors are kept for later.
At a finished game, the rules report the real result instead.

alphazero:4.t:
The prior steers the exploration bonus.
A move the network likes gets tried early.One it dislikes waits its turn, but its bonus grows while it's ignored.
Unlike U C B, this rule has no proof. It was chosen because it works.

alphazero:5.t:
Where do the lessons come from? No human games, no hints.
The network plays against itself, with search choosing every move for both sides.That's self-play.
A little randomness early on makes games differ, so disliked moves still get tried.

alphazero:6.t:
Here's game one, with an untrained network.
Under each board, the share of visits for the move played.Watch the cat ignore Pip's diagonal. A random opening draw.
Each position becomes a lesson. The search's visit shares, and how the game ended.

alphazero:7.t:
Why copy the search? Because search plus network chooses better than the network alone. It looks ahead, and checks the guesses.
Training the prior toward the visits makes the network's instinct more like its own careful thinking.
The value just learns how whole games turned out.

alphazero:8.t:
Here's the full loop.
Each generation plays 50 games against itself, then trains on the lessons.Older games, played by a clumsier network, get dropped.
We run 12 generations in all. Each nudge moves the knobs a little toward the lessons.

alphazero:9.t:
Is it learning? We check against an answer key of best moves.
The chart shows how often the prior's favourite is a best move.Watch it climb, generation by generation.
Nobody ever showed it a good move. Truth comes in only through the rules, from how games end.

alphazero:10.t:
After training, the network looks at Pip's puzzle.
Its prior already leans toward top right.But its value is unsure. The truth is a sure win.
So the instinct points the right way. Next, the search checks it.

alphazero:11.t:
Now search with just fifty loops.
Watch where the loops go. Top right gets the most, and its average climbs.
Random playouts needed about a thousand loops. Here the value judges each new position directly.

alphazero:12.t:
Does the teacher stay ahead of the student?
The bars count best moves found, by the network alone, and with search.Search still finds more.
That gap is what keeps the loop improving.

alphazero:13.t:
Now a real test. Play against a perfect player, thirty games on each side. Perfect play always draws.
Untrained, even with search, it loses games on both sides.One wrong early move is enough.
Trained, the losses almost vanish.

alphazero:14.t:
Your turn. Drag through the generations.
The board shows the network's prior on Pip's puzzle.
The chart marks how often its favourite is a best move. Watch when top right takes the lead.

alphazero:15.t:
Even this toy took 600 games of self-play.AlphaZero played tens of millions of games, on thousands of special chips.
And there's a deeper catch. Every loop plays moves by the rules.Atari games and the real world come with no rulebook. That's the next reel.

alphazero:16.t:
In twenty sixteen, AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, a top Go player, four games to one. It learned from human games first.
A year later, AlphaGo Zero learned by self-play alone, and beat that AlphaGo a hundred to nothing.Then AlphaZero learned chess, shogi and Go, given only the rules.

alphazero:17.t:
So, AlphaZero swaps random playouts for a network, with a value and a prior.
The search uses the value at new nodes, and the prior to pick which moves to try.It learns by self-play. Better network, better search, better lessons. But it still needs the rules.

worldmodels:0.t: World Models  and  Dreamer. Learn to dream the game, then practise inside the dream.

worldmodels:1.t:
Welcome back to the open meadow.
Pip's position is just two numbers, x and y. Each move goes a little way, plus a random wobble.Cheese pays plus one, the cat minus one.
D Q N needed eight thousand real moves here. For a robot, every real move costs time and wear.

worldmodels:2.t:
In the model-based reel, Pip kept a notebook of what each move did, and practised in its head.
But here Pip never stands on the same spot twice. No notebook can list them all.
The fix is the same as for values. A network, that can guess for spots it has never seen.

worldmodels:3.t:
Pip's world model is two small networks.
The move predictor guesses where a move will land.The reward predictor guesses what the landing pays.
Together, they're a learned simulator of the meadow.

worldmodels:4.t:
First, some real experience. Pip wanders at random, 500 real moves in all.Watch the dots. Very few land on the cheese or the cat.
Then each network learns the usual way. Guess, compare with what really happened, and nudge the knobs, thousands of times over.

worldmodels:5.t:
How good are its guesses?
Teal arrows are the predicted moves to the right. Grey is the move without wobble.Near the right fence, teal pokes through. It rarely saw that bump.
Elsewhere it's close. The leftover error is mostly the wobble, which nobody can predict.

worldmodels:6.t:
Now the reward predictor.
Gold squares are where it says cheese. Rose, where it says cat.It covers about two thirds of the cheese circle, but only about a third of the cat.
It saw very few cat landings to learn from.

worldmodels:7.t:
Now Pip can dream. It picks a move, asks the model where it lands, and carries on from there. No real step taken.
Dashed is a dream of ten fixed moves. Solid is the same moves, for real.Watch them drift apart.

worldmodels:8.t:
How fast do dreams drift? Make fifteen random moves, real and dreamed, from many spots.
Teal is the gap for Pip's model. It grows, step after step.Each dream step builds on the last guess, so errors pile up.
Grey, a perfect predictor, grows too, as the wobble adds up.

worldmodels:9.t:
Now train the D Q N network entirely in the dream. Zero real moves.
Each dream starts where Pip really was, and lasts at most 15 moves, since long dreams drift.Watch the dreams. Some stray past the fence, where real Pip never goes.

worldmodels:10.t:
Time to wake up. The dream-trained network now steers the real Pip.
Watch it set off from the thirty test spots.Most reach the cheese.
And all it ever saw of the real meadow were 500 random moves.

worldmodels:11.t:
Was that luck? Four runs, with different dice.
Plain D Q N, on the same few real moves, does far worse.So does a network fed those moves directly, with just as many updates.
It's not just more practice. The model fills the gaps those few moves left.

worldmodels:12.t:
Here's the catch. The dream's cat is only a third of the real one.
Watch where dream-trained Pip meets the real cat.At some of those spots, the dream said grass. Practice never warned against them.
The policy inherits the dream's mistakes.

worldmodels:13.t:
Your turn. Drag how many real moves the model learns from.
Watch the dream of ten moves.And the drift chart below.
More real experience makes the dream more trustworthy. But grey shows a floor no model beats.

worldmodels:14.t:
Real agents often see pictures, not positions. Predicting every pixel is wasteful.
In twenty eighteen, Ha and Schmidhuber squeezed each frame into a short list of numbers, and learned to predict the next list.
In a Doom game, their controller trained only in the dream, and still worked for real.

worldmodels:15.t:
Danijar Hafner's Dreamer learns such a model from pixels. Its actor and critic train on short dreams, starting from real moments, like Pip's.
It keeps collecting real experience, so the dream is checked against reality.DreamerV3 even collected diamonds in Minecraft, from scratch.

worldmodels:16.t:
So, when the world is too big for a notebook, learn a world model with networks. Where a move lands, and what it pays.
Then practise in the dream, almost for free.Keep dreams short, and check them against reality. The policy inherits the dream's mistakes.

shaping:0.t: Reward Shaping. Add hints so the agent isn’t searching in the dark.

shaping:1.t:
Welcome to a bigger maze.
Eight cells across, six up, and five rocks. The cheese is far away, top right.No cat this time, to keep it simple.
Same rules. Plus one for the step onto the cheese, and nothing for every other step.

shaping:2.t:
Pip learns with Q-learning, just like before.
Four numbers per cell, one per move, all starting at zero.It takes the biggest, with one move in five at random.
After each move, its number moves a fifth of the way toward the target.

shaping:3.t:
Every number starts at zero, so every choice is a coin toss.
Watch Pip's first walk.It takes 207 steps, and every update says zero stays zero.
Only the very last step changes anything. A reward that almost never shows up is called a sparse reward.

shaping:4.t:
How slow is this? Let's run twenty Pips, thirty walks each.
The line shows how many steps each walk took, averaged. Lower is better.The first ten walks average about 151 steps.
The shortest way takes just twelve.

shaping:5.t:
We, the designers, know how far each cell is from the cheese. Pip doesn't.
So we add a hint, like the game hot and cold.A little bonus for a step closer. A little penalty for a step away.
Adding extra rewards like this is called reward shaping.

shaping:6.t:
Teal is the same twenty Pips, now with hot and cold hints.The first ten walks drop to about 20 steps.
Why? Every step now carries a little news. The numbers start pointing toward the cheese long before Pip ever reaches it.

shaping:7.t:
A designer has an idea. Why punish steps away at all?
Just reward progress, and make it stronger. Point three for every step closer.
It sounds like the same hint. Watch what Pip learns.

shaping:8.t:
After thirty walks, Pip follows its biggest numbers from the start.
It runs toward the cheese.Then it steps back and forth, right beside it. It never eats.
Most of the twenty Pips do this dance.

shaping:9.t:
Why does dancing pay?
Beside the cheese, Pip can eat now. One, plus point three, then the walk is over.Or it can step away for free, and step back for point three, again and again.
Add it all up, and the dance is worth more. The hint changed what's best. Pip is farming our reward.

shaping:10.t:
So why was hot and cold fine?
