A step away takes back what the step closer gave. Out and back sums to almost nothing.
Think of each cell as having a potential. Each hint is just the change in potential. Along any walk, the middle terms cancel out.

shaping:11.t:
In nineteen ninety nine, Andrew Ng, Daishi Harada and Stuart Russell made this exact.
Give each cell any potential. The hint is point nine times the new potential, minus the old one.
Every move from a cell shifts by the same amount. So the best plan stays best. That's potential-based shaping.

shaping:12.t:
Any potential is safe. A good one also helps.
A natural choice is a rough guess of the reward to come.Ours is low at the start, and high beside the cheese.
On the final step, Pip gets the cheese, and the guess is cashed in.

shaping:13.t:
What do these hints feel like?
From a cell partway there, a step closer pays a little.A bump costs a tiny bit. A step away costs more.
These costs never change the plan. The cheese step repays them, so every plan totals the same.

shaping:14.t:
Let's check that. Three walks from the start.
The shortest route. Pip's first wandering walk. And a thousand steps of dancing.
Their hints all add up to the same thing, zero.Dancing earns nothing extra. Only the cheese makes a difference.

shaping:15.t:
Gold is twenty Pips with the potential hint.Almost as fast as hot and cold.The teal line hides right under the gold one.
And all 20 Pips end up on a twelve-step route. Fast, and safe.

shaping:16.t:
But safe doesn't mean fast.
Use hot and cold's potential in the exact recipe. Now even a bump earns a little.So tried moves beat untried ones, and learning slows down.
The best plan doesn't change. But since Pip's numbers start at zero, the speed does.

shaping:17.t:
Your turn. Pick a hint, and watch twenty Pips learn with it.
Watch the maze for dancing.And the card for the speed.
Which hint is fast and safe?

shaping:18.t:
The word comes from animal training. B. F. Skinner taught pigeons by rewarding small steps toward a trick.
In nineteen ninety eight, a simulated bicycle was rewarded for nearing a goal, and never penalised for riding away.It learned to ride in circles, just like Pip's dance.

shaping:19.t:
So, sparse rewards make learning slow. Shaping adds hints, so every step carries news.
Careless hints change what's best, and get farmed.Hints built from a potential never change the best plan. And a good potential makes learning fast.

hacking:0.t: Reward Hacking. You get what you reward, not what you meant.

hacking:1.t:
Welcome back to Pip's maze. Today there's a chore.
Three crumbs are lying around.We want Pip to tidy up, then go to the cheese.
But Pip knows nothing of what we want. It only feels the rewards we hand out.

hacking:2.t:
So we write a reward.
Every step that ends on a crumb pays a little bonus.Cheese and cat stay the same.
Our sensor only checks where Pip stands. So a crumb never disappears.

hacking:3.t:
After training, Pip follows its biggest numbers from the start.
It walks to the crumb on the left.And then it bumps into the rock beside it, again, and again.
Each bump ends on the crumb. Bonus, every single step. Pip never goes near the cheese.

hacking:4.t:
Why does bumping win? A bonus every step, forever, adds up.
Even with the discount, it's worth more than the cheese.
Even right beside the cheese, the best move is to turn away.

hacking:5.t:
Pip broke no rule. It found the best way to collect exactly what we rewarded.
What we meant, tidy up and then eat, was never in the numbers.
Scoring well by a route the designers didn't intend is called reward hacking, or specification gaming.

hacking:6.t:
Here's every training walk.
Each bar shows its points. Gold means it reached the cheese.The scores are high from the very first walk.
Watch the gold bars. Only a few early walks reach the cheese, then hardly any.

hacking:7.t:
Economists know this as Goodhart's law. When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
Touching crumbs was a fine sign of tidying, as long as nobody pushed on it.
Once Pip optimised it, the sign and the goal came apart.

hacking:8.t:
Let's patch the loophole. Each crumb pays once, then it's gone.
Now watch Pip. It picks up crumbs along the way, and eats.
But it skips the left one. The detour would delay the cheese too much.

hacking:9.t:
Patching worked because we watched Pip, and saw the trick.
In a big world, we can't list every loophole ahead of time.A hard-searching agent finds the ones we missed.
And each patch is a new reward, with its own gaps.

hacking:10.t:
This happens with real agents, too.
In twenty sixteen, an agent learned the boat racing game CoastRunners.It found a lagoon where targets kept coming back, and circled there forever, crashing and catching fire.
It never finished the race, but it scored more than finishing would.

hacking:11.t:
Researchers at DeepMind keep a public list of cases like this.
A robot arm, rewarded for the height of a block's bottom face, just flipped it over.A simulated hand only looked like it was grabbing, to the camera.And a Tetris program paused the game forever, so it never lost.

hacking:12.t:
Pip found its trick in a tiny maze. Stronger agents search harder, and find gaps weaker ones miss.
Researchers found more capable agents exploit bad rewards more.
Chatbots tuned on a reward model feel the same pull. An answer can score well, yet be no better for people.

hacking:13.t:
There's no complete cure.
Watch what the agent does, not just its score. Test it in new situations. Patch the loopholes you find.
And don't push too hard on a reward you don't fully trust.

hacking:14.t:
Your turn. Choose what each crumb step pays.
Then watch where trained Pip goes.
How small does the bonus have to be before Pip heads for the cheese? Below a point, Pip still bumps, but that's unfinished exploration, not hacking.

hacking:15.t:
So, an agent optimises exactly what you reward, not what you meant.
Pip bumped a rock on a crumb. A boat circled for points.
The stronger the optimiser, the more this matters. Watch behaviour, test widely, and patch.

curiosity:0.t: Curiosity  and  Intrinsic Motivation. Reward the agent for being surprised.

curiosity:1.t:
Welcome to a much bigger maze.
A hundred and eight cells, with walls between them.The cheese is top right, 21 steps away by the shortest route. The gold dashes show it.
No cat here. Just one plus one, on the step onto the cheese.

curiosity:2.t:
Until Pip first finds the cheese, every step pays nothing. A sparse reward.
Why not add hints? With walls everywhere, closer as the crow flies can point into dead ends. And the designer may not know the maze at all.
So everything depends on how Pip explores before that first cheese.

curiosity:3.t:
Pip learns with Q-learning, one guess per cell and move.
One move in ten is random. The rest follow the best guess.
Every guess starts at zero, and stays zero without reward. So at first, every choice is a tie, broken at random.

curiosity:4.t:
Watch a thousand steps of this random walk, sped up.
The darker the cell, the more often Pip stood there.Look how it piles up near home.
Random steps keep undoing each other, so Pip circles near the start.

curiosity:5.t:
Pip keeps wandering.
It finally finds the cheese at step 2274.More than a hundred times the shortest route.
Unlucky? A bit. But over many runs, a typical Pip still needs well over a thousand steps.

curiosity:6.t:
Children explore because new things are interesting, not because someone pays them.
So let's give Pip the same drive. An intrinsic reward, a bonus it pays itself for going somewhere new.
The cheese is an extrinsic reward, from the world. Pip learns from the sum.

curiosity:7.t:
The simplest novelty bonus counts visits.
Watch the bars. The first visit to a cell pays the most.Each later visit pays a bit less. Familiar cells get boring, but slowly.
Cells Pip has never visited keep the full bonus.

curiosity:8.t:
Here's a subtle point. An untried move doesn't start at zero. It starts at one.
Why? Endless new cells, each paying a bonus, add up to exactly one.
So untried means maybe fresh ground. That's optimism, like in the bandit reels.

curiosity:9.t:
Same maze, same luck, now with the counting bonus.
Watch the shading spread, like a flood.Pip's guesses keep pointing toward the least visited parts of the maze.
This Pip finds the cheese at step 348. The random walker needed 2274.

curiosity:10.t:
One run proves little. So let's average many.
Across is steps taken. Up is how many cells Pip has seen.A line that reaches the top has seen the whole maze.
Grey shows the fastest possible case, one new cell every step.

curiosity:11.t:
Gold is the random walker. It creeps along.Teal is the counting explorer. It sees almost every cell in a thousand steps.
Being pulled toward rare cells turns wandering into a sweep.

curiosity:12.t:
Now the race to the first cheese.
Each bar is the middle run of many.The counting explorer is more than five times faster.
Is it just the hopeful start? Without the bonus, those hopes fade once each move is tried. The bonus keeps pulling Pip onward.

curiosity:13.t:
In twenty seventeen, Pathak and colleagues paid for surprise instead.
Pip keeps chances for where each move will land. The less it expected what it saw, the bigger the bonus.
A new move is a full surprise. Then a half, then a quarter, as Pip learns.

curiosity:14.t:
Same seed, the surprise explorer finds the cheese at step 738.Over many runs, it's slower than counting, but far faster than random.
Here, surprise is basically a count per move, halving each try. It fades faster than counting does.

curiosity:15.t:
Now a twist. A TV sits in the maze, showing random static.
On that cell, Pip must also predict the picture. And no one can predict static.
So the surprise never fades. Watch Pip reach the TV, and stay.

curiosity:16.t:
In three thousand steps, this Pip spent 2333 on the TV cell.It saw only a small part of the maze, and never found the cheese.
Counting isn't fooled. It counts cells, not pictures. But count each picture as a new place, and static would trap counting too.

curiosity:17.t:
After the hacking reel, a fair question. Can Pip farm its own bonus?
A count bonus fades. Farming it pays less and less, until the cheese wins.
A surprise bonus fades only if the world is predictable. Noise never is. The noisy TV is reward hacking of an inner reward.

curiosity:18.t:
Your turn. Tap a cell to put the TV there. The slider picks the explorer.
Watch Pip replay three thousand steps.
Try the TV far away, or in a dead end. When does surprise get hooked? Does counting ever care?

curiosity:19.t:
Pathak's curiosity let agents explore Doom and Super Mario with little or no game reward.
Bellemare and colleagues stretched counting to game screens, with big gains on Montezuma's Revenge, where D Q N scored zero.
And in twenty eighteen, Burda and colleagues demonstrated the noisy TV trap.

curiosity:20.t:
So, when reward is sparse, random exploring wanders in circles. A bonus for novelty sends Pip toward fresh ground.
Count visits, or pay for surprise.But beware the noisy TV. Pure randomness stays surprising forever.

imitation:0.t: Imitation Learning. Skip the reward: just copy an expert.

imitation:1.t:
Meet Mo, an old mouse who has lived in Pip's maze for years.
In every cell, Mo knows a good move.
Pip could learn by trial and error, but that means many walks, and many meetings with the cat. Here's a shortcut. Watch Mo, and copy. That's imitation learning.

imitation:2.t:
The floor is wet again. Pip's moves slide sideways, two times in ten.
Mo's old paws grip. Mo never slides.
The rewards are as usual. But a copier never looks at rewards, only at what Mo does.

imitation:3.t:
Mo walks to the cheese, and we write down every step.
Each step is a pair. The cell Mo was in, and the move Mo made.Mo's walk takes 7 steps, up the left side, then along the top.
One recorded walk is called a demonstration.

imitation:4.t:
Mo walks the route three times. Mo never slides, so every walk is the same.
All the examples sit in the same few cells.Everywhere else, nobody has ever seen Mo. Those cells get a grey question mark.

imitation:5.t:
Each example is like a quiz question with its answer. In this cell, which move? Up.
Learning a rule from answered questions is supervised learning.
Used on demonstrations, it's called behaviour cloning. In each cell, give Mo's answer.

imitation:6.t:
But Pip's rule has to answer in every cell.
Our copier just borrows the answer from the nearest cell with an example.These are only guesses. Some push into rocks or walls.
And beside the cat, one guess steps right onto it.

imitation:7.t:
Pip walks with its copy.
On this walk, no slides. Pip follows Mo's route, step for step, to the cheese.
On the route, the copy is perfect. If Pip never slid, cloning would be all it needs.

imitation:8.t:
Another walk. Watch the very first move.
Pip tries up, and slides right, into a cell Mo never stood in.The copy guesses up. Pip slides again, then bumps into the rock. Bump, bump.

imitation:9.t:
Pip bumps around until a lucky slide puts it back on Mo's route.
Near the end, it slides beside the cat. The guess says right. Onto the cat.
That's compounding error. A slip reaches a cell Mo never showed. Guessing there leads further off, and nothing shows the way back.

imitation:10.t:
Now a thousand walks each, with the same dice.
On top, Pip with Mo's whole rule card, perfect everywhere. Below, the clone.Gold means cheese, rose means cat.
The clone walks that strayed off Mo's route rarely made it to the cheese.

imitation:11.t:
Would more demonstrations help? Thirty walks by Mo give many more examples.
But they're all in the same cells. Mo never leaves the route.
The trouble isn't how much data, but where it comes from. That mismatch is called distribution shift.

imitation:12.t:
In twenty eleven, Ross, Gordon and Bagnell proposed a fix.
Let Pip walk, and ask Mo about the cells Pip actually reaches.For every cell Pip stood in, Mo says, here, I would go this way.
Add those answers, clone again, and repeat. It's called dagger.

imitation:13.t:
Round one. Pip walks five times with its clone, slides and guesses included.
Mo labels every step.Several cells get Mo's answer for the first time.
With them, the clone reaches the cheese more often.

imitation:14.t:
Here's how the score changes, round by round.
Rounds two and three add examples, but no new cells. No change.By round four, every cell holds Mo's answer, and the clone all but matches Mo's card.
That's the ceiling. A copier matches its teacher, but never beats it.

imitation:15.t:
The price? An expert on call, for places it would never go itself. And the learner practises for real, mistakes included.
In return, a better guarantee.A clone's extra mistakes can grow with the square of the walk's length. dagger's grow only in proportion.

imitation:16.t:
Your turn. Slide through the dagger rounds.
Plum arrows are Mo's examples. Gold arrows with a dot are the clone's guesses.
Tap a cell to drop Pip there, and watch one walk with that round's clone. Each tap rolls new dice.

imitation:17.t:
Around nineteen ninety, a van called ALVINN learned to steer by copying a human driver.
In twenty sixteen, NVIDIA added off-centre camera views, labelled with how to steer back.That's dagger's recovery idea, without an expert on call.
Chatbots, too, begin by imitating human-written text.

imitation:18.t:
So, behaviour cloning copies the expert's move in each state. Plain supervised learning, no rewards needed.
But small slips lead to states the expert never showed, and errors compound.dagger asks the expert about the states the learner actually visits.

irl:0.t: Inverse R L. Watch the expert, figure out what they want.

irl:1.t:
Welcome back. Last time, Pip copied Mo, move by move. That breaks when the maze changes.
Look at the two lines.Normal R L starts from a reward and finds behaviour.Inverse R L runs the other way. It watches behaviour, and asks what reward would explain it.
So the question becomes, not what does Mo do, but what does Mo want?

irl:2.t:
Think of a friend who always takes the long road home.The short road is jammed with traffic.
So you guess what they care about. Traffic costs them more than distance.Now, in a city they've never driven, you can still predict their route.
Moves belong to one place. A goal travels anywhere.

irl:3.t:
Here's Mo, on a dry floor.Watch Mo walk up the left side, then along the top. Seven steps to the cheese.
Pip knows the maze. It knows where every move leads.What it doesn't know is the rewards.
That's the usual setup. The learner can plan, but has to find out what's worth planning for.

irl:4.t:
Pip describes each step with three simple questions.Did it reach the cheese? Did it reach the cat? And, was a step taken? That one is always yes.
A guessed reward is just one weight per question.The usual rewards are plus one for the cheese, minus one for the cat, and nothing for a step.

irl:5.t:
Now add up Mo's walk, one feature at a time.Watch the small numbers on the route. Each step of delay multiplies by point nine.
The cheese comes on the last step, so its total is point five three.No cat, so zero.
Weight each total, and add. With the usual weights, Mo's return is point five three.

irl:6.t:
So which rewards make Mo's walk a best walk?
The usual ones fit. So does cheese only.And look at all zero.Every walk scores nothing, so Mo's is as good as any. It explains every behaviour at once.
Rewarding steps doesn't fit. The best walk would then never end.Ng and Russell pointed out this ambiguity back in 2000.

irl:7.t:
Pip needs a rule to pick one reward.Here's the idea. Under a good guess, Mo should beat every rival clearly.That gap is the margin. Make it as wide as possible.
All zero gives a margin of zero, so it's out.And doubling every weight would double every gap, so the size of the weights is fixed.

irl:8.t:
Round one. A single rival, the Wanderer, who moves at random.Compare the step totals. Mo takes far fewer steps.
So the widest margin reward mostly says, steps are bad.The cheese weight is tiny. Step totals are about five, while a cheese total is at most one.How the features are scaled sways the choice.

irl:9.t:
Now Pip plans the best walk under guess one.Watch where it goes. With steps that costly, the quickest ending wins.Pip runs to the cat in 5 steps.
That's not what Mo does, so guess one is wrong.But it's still useful. The cat run joins the list of rivals.

irl:10.t:
Round two. Now Mo has to beat both the Wanderer and the cat run.The new guess looks far more sensible.Cheese is good, the cat is bad, and steps cost a little.
Watch Pip plan with it.It takes exactly Mo's route, seven steps to the cheese.
Nothing is left for Mo to beat, so the search stops.

irl:11.t:
Scale guess two so the cheese is worth exactly one.The cat comes out near minus one.And steps carry a small cost, which Mo's walk can't rule out.
Now compare the totals. Pip's plan matches Mo's.
Why is a match enough? It earns Mo's return under every reward built from these features, Mo's true one included.

irl:12.t:
Now the maze changes.The cheese moves to the bottom right, the cat sits nearby, and the rocks shift.
Watch Pip copy Mo's card.Up and along the top, to the corner where the old cheese was.There's no arrow there, so the nearest arrow says right. Into the wall, again and again.
Copying never reaches the cheese.

irl:13.t:
Now Pip plans in the new maze, with guess two.Watch it go up and around the cat. 8 steps to the cheese.
That's exactly the best route under the maze's real rewards.
The moves didn't transfer. The goal did.

irl:14.t:
Your turn. Pick a reward guess with the slider, and tap a cell to move the cheese.
Pip plans with that guess, and walks it.Guess one runs for the cat whenever the cat is nearer. All zero just sits there.
Guess two finds the cheese anywhere in this small maze.

irl:15.t:
Real experts aren't so tidy. They vary their routes.
Here are two routes, equally good.Maximum entropy inverse R L gives each one an even chance.
Match the expert's feature totals, and otherwise stay as uncommitted as possible.Brian Ziebart's team used it on taxi traces, to learn how drivers weigh roads.

irl:16.t:
Inverse R L has flown real helicopters. Pieter Abbeel's team learned aerobatics from a pilot's demonstrations.
The costs are on the card.A full plan in every round, features picked by hand, and ambiguity that never quite goes away.
gale skips writing the reward. A second network tells expert from learner, and the learner is rewarded for fooling it.

irl:17.t:
So that's inverse R L.Watch behaviour, and work out the reward behind it.
A reward is a goal you can carry to a new maze, where copied moves fail.Many rewards fit, so a rule has to choose, like the widest margin.

offline:0.t: Offline R L. Learn from a fixed log of data, with no new trials.

offline:1.t:
Here's a new rule for Pip. It gets a fixed record of old experience, and no new walks, ever.
Everything it learns has to come from this diary.
That's offline R L.Think of hospitals. You can't test random treatments on patients, but there are years of records.

offline:2.t:
Watch the walks flick by. Fifty of them, from long ago, on the wet floor.Pip followed Mo's rule card, and slipped now and then.
Most walks reached the cheese. Forty six of the fifty.
Now look at the plum arrows.Slips carried Pip everywhere, but each cell only ever saw one move. Mo's arrow.

offline:3.t:
First, replay the diary into a table, four numbers per cell.Moves that were never tried simply stay at zero.
Every tried move scores above zero, so Pip just follows Mo's arrows.It reaches the cheese 861 times in a thousand tests.
No harm done, at least with a table.

offline:4.t:
Big problems don't fit in a table. So Pip uses a network instead.
It takes the cell's column and row, and gives back four numbers, one per move.
Here's the catch. Every move gets a number, even moves nobody ever tried.

offline:5.t:
The replay works as before.Each diary step gets a target. The reward, plus point nine times the biggest of the four numbers where Pip landed.Then the knobs take small steps toward those targets. Thirty rounds of it.
Notice the max. It looks at all four moves, tried or not.

offline:6.t:
After thirty rounds, look at the start cell.Only up was ever tried there. Yet left, never tried, reads two point eight eight.
That can't be true.The cheese pays one, once, and the discount only shrinks it. No walk can earn more than one.
That number is pure invention.

offline:7.t:
This line is the start cell's biggest number, round by round.Watch it climb past one, the most any walk can earn.
Why? The max in each target grabs the most hopeful made-up number. The next round builds on it, and so on.That's extrapolation error.

offline:8.t:
Online, this would fix itself. Pip would try left, bump the wall, and lower the number.
Offline, nobody checks.Watch Pip at the start. It pushes into the wall, again and again.
In a thousand tests, it never reaches the cheese.The rose arrows are choices the diary never tried.

offline:9.t:
The fix sounds simple. Don't trust moves the diary never tried.
Learn from the plum moves, the ones in the data.For everything else, assume it's not great.
Offline methods do this in different ways. Next, one of them.

offline:10.t:
Meet C Q L, conservative Q-learning, from 2020.Look at one cell. At every diary step, it adds a little push.The diary's move, up, gets pushed up. All four numbers get pushed down, the biggest hardest.
Tried moves are held up by their targets, so only the untried ones sink.Alpha sets how hard. Here it's point five.

offline:11.t:
Same diary, same network, same rounds, now with C Q L.Watch the gold line. It stays down, far below one.
At the start, the diary's move is back on top.Pip reaches the cheese 845 times in a thousand, against none without C Q L.
One invention survives, near the cat, so it still trails the diary's own rule.

offline:12.t:
So how hard should C Q L push? Here are five strengths.Too gentle, and the inventions survive. Pip reaches the cheese only a hundred and forty one times.
In between, the numbers are sane.Push very hard, and Pip just copies the diary, but the start's number climbs past one again.
With one move per cell, C Q L can't beat the diary's rule here.

offline:13.t:
Your turn. Slide alpha, from zero, plain offline learning, up to five. Each setting trains its own network.
Rose arrows are choices the diary never tried.Tap a cell to drop Pip there, and watch one walk, slips and all.

offline:14.t:
There are other ways to stay close to the data.I Q L never asks about untried moves at all. Its targets use only logged moves.
Before that, BCQ kept the learner to moves that looked like the data's.
They all share one idea. Offline, don't trust what the data doesn't show.

offline:15.t:
Offline R L shows up wherever logs are plentiful and trials are costly.Treatment records, click logs, recorded robot runs.
Often it's a careful warm start, followed by a little cautious practice in the real world.

offline:16.t:
So that's offline R L. Learn from a fixed record, with no new trials.
A network invents numbers for untried moves, and the max hunts down the most hopeful one.Nobody checks, so it grows.
The cure is to stay close to the data.

rlhf:0.t: R L H F. How chatbots are tuned with human preferences.

rlhf:1.t:
Meet Bot. Pip asks it the way to the cheese.Bot is a tiny stand in for a language model.
A real one writes word by word. Bot just picks one of eight whole answers, each with its own chance.It learned those chances by copying answers people wrote. Some are good. Many aren't.

rlhf:2.t:
Watch the route trace out. Up three, then right four, just above the cat.
So which answers help? Could a simple rule in code decide?
Counting words fails. The longest answer is wrong.Direction words fail too.For real questions, writing down helpful and honest is far harder still.

rlhf:3.t:
But comparing is easy.Bot answers twice, and a person just picks the one they prefer. Here, Mo picks A.
The people are simulated. Each answer has a hidden taste score that drives their choices.Bot never sees it. Only the comparisons.

rlhf:4.t:
People are noisy, though.Watch the curve. Across is the taste gap, and up is the chance of picking A.Equal taste, and it's a coin flip.
A gap of three gives point nine five. Likely, but not certain.
This is the Bradley Terry model.

rlhf:5.t:
Now Bot answers twice, four hundred times over, and Mo picks each time.Watch the counts in the table climb.
Keep an eye on the last row.Bot's rare repeated answer turns up in only eleven pairs. Too few to learn much from.

rlhf:6.t:
Next, a reward model. A program that scores any answer, trained to agree with the comparisons.
Ours counts just three things. Every word, every up or right, and every down or left.Watch the weights slide as training goes.
Each comparison nudges them, so the chosen answer scores above the rejected one.

rlhf:7.t:
Here are the trained scores, next to the hidden taste.The two good answers score above the rest. So far, so good.
But look at the last row.The repeated answer scores highest of all, four point three one.It says up and right four times, and the scorer just counts.

rlhf:8.t:
Now the reward model is the judge, and judging costs nothing.
Bot answers thirty two times. Each answer gets its score.Above the batch average, its chance goes up. Below, it goes down.
That's P P O, from the P P O reel, with the usual clipping.

rlhf:9.t:
Two charts will track Bot.On top, the reward model's average score. That's what P P O pushes up.
Below, people's verdict. How often a person prefers the new Bot over the original.Point five means no better.Only the simulation can compute this. Bot can't.

rlhf:10.t:
First, run P P O with the score alone.
Watch both lines rise at first. Bot learns the good answers.Around update thirty four, people's verdict peaks at point eight seven.
Then Bot stumbles on its repeated answer, and P P O piles on.By the end, Bot says it almost every time, and people like it less than the original.

rlhf:11.t:
Why did that happen?The scorer learned that up and right are good. In Bot's usual answers, that's true.
Repeating them isn't. But eleven comparisons were too few, and three weights can't say repeating is bad.
Push hard on a learned score, and you find exactly such gaps. That's reward hacking.

rlhf:12.t:
The fix is a leash, tying the tuned Bot to the original.Watch it stretch.
Each reward pays a penalty for drifting from the original's chances.Beta sets how strong the leash is.On average, that penalty is the K L divergence, a measure of how far Bot has moved.

rlhf:13.t:
Same run, with beta equal to one.The blue score rises less.But people's verdict climbs to point six five. People now prefer the tuned Bot about sixty five times in a hundred.
The repeated answer still grows. The leash holds it back, but doesn't erase the blind spot.

rlhf:14.t:
Your turn. Drag beta, the leash strength. Each setting reruns P P O.
The bars show Bot's final chances. Black ticks mark the original's.Too loose, and Bot hacks the scorer. Too tight, and it barely changes.
Beta of one does best with people here.

rlhf:15.t:
Here's every run on one line of people's verdict.Leash off, worse than the original. Leash on, point six five.The best possible Bot would reach point nine one.
So the leash is safer, not perfect. A reward model is only as good as its comparisons.Real teams keep collecting fresh comparisons, and retrain the scorer.

rlhf:16.t:
In 2017, Christiano and colleagues taught simulated robots from people comparing short clips.A backflip took about nine hundred comparisons.
In 2022, InstructGPT did the same for a language model. Comparisons, a reward model, then P P O on a leash.That recipe, R L H F, shaped later chat assistants.

rlhf:17.t:
So that's R L H F.When good is hard to write down, ask people to compare. Fit a reward model to their choices.
Then tune with P P O, on a leash to the original. A learned scorer has blind spots, and an unleashed optimiser will find them.

pomdp:0.t: Partial Observability (P O M D P). What to do when you can’t see the whole picture.

pomdp:1.t:
Here's a new maze, built to show one problem.A corridor of seven cells, with three rooms below.The cheese sits under the middle cell. Cats wait under both ends.
The usual rules apply. And each walk starts in a random corridor cell.

pomdp:2.t:
Now the fog rolls in.Pip can no longer see the cheese, the cats, or even the cell numbers.
All it can feel is which sides of its own cell are walls.
What Pip senses is its observation. Where it really is, is still the state. Pip just can't see it.

pomdp:3.t:
Walk the corridor, and Pip can feel only four different things.The left end. The right end. The junction above the cheese.
And this one, corridor. Four cells all feel exactly alike.
Seven cells, but only four feelings.

pomdp:4.t:
Look at cells three and five.From three, the cheese is to the right. From five, it's to the left.
Yet they feel exactly the same.Same feeling, opposite best moves.
So the observation alone is not Markov. What happens next depends on more than what Pip can sense.

pomdp:5.t:
Underneath, nothing changed. It's still an M D P.
Add one thing, what each state lets Pip sense, and you get a partially observable M D P.A P O M D P, said pom dee pee.
Pip gets corridor, never cell three. The true state is still there, just hidden.

pomdp:6.t:
The simplest rule maps what Pip feels straight to a move. No memory at all.
Three entries are easy. Left end, go right. Junction, go down. Right end, go left.But corridor gets just one entry.
So all four corridor cells must share the same move.

pomdp:7.t:
Try corridor means right.
Start in cell five and watch.Right, right, the end turns Pip around. Then it feels corridor again, and goes right.Pip shuttles back and forth, forever.
It reaches the cheese from only four of seven starts. Corridor means left fails the same way, on the other side.

pomdp:8.t:
One trick helps a little. In the corridor, flip a coin.
Now every start reaches the cheese, with some dithering.Average return rises from point four nine to point six two.Seeing its cell, Pip would score point eight four.
Under fog, a random rule can beat every fixed one.

pomdp:9.t:
Fix one. Give Pip a tiny memory, the move it just made.
Now corridor going right and corridor going left are different situations.
Watch from cell five. Right, right, the end turns it around, then left, left, left, and down.Cheese in six steps.Now every start reaches the cheese.

pomdp:10.t:
Can Q-learning find a good rule by itself?
Watch the chart. The grey dashed line is Pip learning while seeing its cell.Rose learns from feelings only.
Rose stalls, near point three seven.Its one corridor entry mixes twins that need opposite moves.

pomdp:11.t:
Teal learns from feelings plus the last move.At first it's no better. There are more situations to fill.Then it pulls ahead, to point five four.
After three hundred walks, teal's best moves reach the cheese from almost every start.

pomdp:12.t:
Fix two needs more knowledge. Give Pip the map, but not its own position.
Now it can keep a belief, its chance of being in each cell. Shading shows it.At first, every cell is equally likely.
Then Pip feels corridor. Only four cells fit, so each gets one in four.

pomdp:13.t:
Pip moves right.It doesn't know from where, so every chance shifts one cell right.
Then it feels corridor again.Cells that don't feel like that are wiped out. Two remain, at one half each.
Move, then look. That's the whole update.

pomdp:14.t:
Pip moves right once more.Now it feels the right end. Only one cell feels like that.The belief collapses. Pip is certain.
Watch it follow the map. Left, left, left, and down.
Moving right earned nothing directly. But it told Pip where it was.

pomdp:15.t:
Real whiskers are shaky. Say each feeling is right nine times in ten.
Now a look lowers chances, instead of wiping them out.With the same readings, Pip is point nine six sure of cell seven.
If the middle reading had been wrong, cell seven still leads, at point six six.

pomdp:16.t:
Your turn. Pip starts in a hidden cell. Tap left, right or down to move it.
Watch the belief shift after each move, then sharpen after each feel.
Use the slider to make the whiskers unreliable, and see how much longer it takes to be sure.

pomdp:17.t:
So, memory or belief?A belief holds everything the history says about Pip's place, so choosing from it is Markov again.But it needs the map, and a number for every state.
Memory needs no map. Deep R L often uses a recurrent network that learns what to keep.

pomdp:18.t:
You meet fog everywhere.
In poker, you can't see the other cards, so you keep a belief about your opponent's hand.A self driving car must remember the cyclist hidden behind a bus.
And the Atari player in the D Q N reel looked at four recent screens, a short memory.

pomdp:19.t:
So that's a P O M D P. The agent sees observations, not the state.
Twins look the same, so a rule on observations alone can loop forever.
Two fixes. Remember what you saw and did. Or keep a belief, and update it with every move and look.

hrl:0.t: Hierarchical R L. Think in sub-goals, not individual muscle twitches.

hrl:1.t:
Pip moves into a bigger house. Four rooms, joined by four doors.Pip starts in the top left corner. The cheese sits in the bottom door, between rooms three and four.
No cat this time. The shortest route, in teal, takes thirteen steps.

hrl:2.t:
First, plain Q-learning, just as before. Every number starts at zero, so the first walk is pure wandering.
Watch the dots pile up.This walk took eight hundred and forty steps to stumble onto the cheese.
The shortest route is only thirteen.

hrl:3.t:
You don't plan a trip to the kitchen one footstep at a time. You think, leave this room, go down the hall, into the kitchen.
Pip can do the same. First, go to door B.Then, go to door D.Two big steps instead of thirteen small ones.

hrl:4.t:
A big step needs its own little policy.Here's go to door B. Every arrow leads to that door.
It can start anywhere in the shaded zone, and it stops at door B.A mini policy, a start zone and a stopping rule. That's an option.
We drew eight of them by hand.

hrl:5.t:
Now Pip's menu grows.Four moves, plus any option that can start here.
Watch Pip pick go to door B.One decision, and it follows the arrows all the way to the door.
Nobody says which choice is good. Options are just extra choices.

hrl:6.t:
How does Pip learn a number for an option?
Watch the last option of walk one, go to door D.The cheese comes on its fourth step, so the reward is discounted three times, to point seven two nine.
Alpha moves the number a fifth of the way, to point one four six.

hrl:7.t:
Same seed, same rules, walk one, side by side.Gold is plain Q-learning. Teal uses options.
Watch teal reach the cheese in thirty nine steps, while gold keeps wandering.
Why so fast? A random option carries Pip a whole room at a time.

hrl:8.t:
Now sixty walks per run, averaged over twenty runs.Up is how many steps each walk took. The dashed line is the shortest route.
Gold needs many walks to come down.Teal is near the bottom almost at once.

hrl:9.t:
After sixty walks, follow the best choices.With options, Pip makes just two decisions, the gold dots. Door B, then door D.
Think of a manager who picks the next big step, and a worker who takes the small ones.Plain Q-learning makes thirteen decisions for the same route.

hrl:10.t:
Why does news travel faster?In plain Q-learning, the cheese's reward creeps back about one cell per walk. A chain of thirteen links.
With options, the chain has just two links.The start learns of the cheese after about five walks, instead of about twenty three.

hrl:11.t:
But options can get in the way.Move the cheese to the far corner of room four, well away from any door.
Watch Pip. Every option ends on a door, so it keeps getting yanked back.
Nineteen of twenty runs hit the step limit.Plain Q-learning does far better here.

hrl:12.t:
Options only help when their stopping points suit the task.We drew ours knowing where the doors were.
Getting an agent to discover good options by itself is the hard, still open problem.
Some methods look for bottlenecks, like doorways. Others learn options from reward alone.

hrl:13.t:
Options came from Sutton, Precup and Singh, in 1999. Others split the work differently.
In feudal designs, a manager hands out goals, and the worker is rewarded just for reaching them.
In goal conditioned versions, one worker learns to reach any target the manager picks.

hrl:14.t:
Your turn. Slide to move the cheese, from door D to the far corner. Both learners rerun.
Watch the two lines.Where do options shine, and where do they hurt?
Look at how close the cheese is to a door.

hrl:15.t:
Robots often chain skills like reach, grasp and place.A higher level policy picks the next skill, and the skill does the moves.
DeepMind's FeUdal Networks used a manager and a worker on hard Atari games.It helps most when tasks are long and rewards are rare.

hrl:16.t:
So that's hierarchical R L. Plan with big steps and small ones.
An option is a mini policy with a start zone and a stopping rule. Picking one is a single decision.
Options that fit the task help a lot. Bad ones hurt. Finding good ones automatically is the hard part.

marl:0.t: Multi-Agent R L. When several learners share one world.

marl:1.t:
In every reel so far, Pip learned alone. Everything else followed fixed rules.
Now meet Tam, a second mouse, with a pink bow.Tam learns too.
Several learners sharing one world. That's multi-agent R L.

marl:2.t:
From Pip's side, Tam is just part of the world, like the floor.And for Tam, Pip is part of its world.
But the floor never changes its habits. Tam does, as it learns.So Pip's world keeps shifting under its feet. That's called non-stationary.

marl:3.t:
Let's shrink things to one room and two doors.Each round, both mice pick a door at once, without seeing each other.
Watch the big door. It opens only if both push, and then each gets a big cheese.Push alone, and you get nothing.The small hole always has a crumb, worth point three.

marl:4.t:
Here's the payoff table. Pip's door picks the row, Tam's the column.
Both at the big door is best for both. They're a team.But it's a gamble. It only pays if the other comes too. The hole is safe.Game theorists call this a stag hunt.

marl:5.t:
Each mouse keeps two numbers, a guess for each door. Both start at zero.
It picks the bigger number, but one round in five, it picks at random.After each round, it moves that door's number a fifth of the way toward the payoff.
Neither knows the other is learning. They're independent learners.

marl:6.t:
Watch the first rounds.Both toss coins and land at the hole. Each gets its crumb, and the hole's number rises.
Now the hole leads, so both stay there.
Then one random round sends Pip to the big door alone. Tam's at the hole, so it stays shut. Nothing.

marl:7.t:
Pip keeps trying the big door, but only in random rounds.Eleven tries alone, every one paid zero.
Is Pip wrong? Not really. Tam only comes along about one round in ten.So the big door pays about point one on average, less than the crumb.

marl:8.t:
Round one hundred. By luck, both pick the big door at random.It opens! Their big door numbers jump to point two.
Then a second lucky double.The number climbs to point three three, just above the hole.Now both prefer the big door.

marl:9.t:
Here's the world from Pip's side.The line is the chance the big door pays Pip. That's just Tam's chance of picking it.
The door never changed. Tam did, jumping from point one to point nine.Pip's lessons can go stale at any moment.

marl:10.t:
Now a hundred pairs, each with its own dice.Gold dots share the big door. Teal dots share the hole.
After two hundred rounds, forty seven pairs are still at the hole.They're stuck, but sensibly. Whoever switches alone gets nothing.

marl:11.t:
Teammates share a goal. Opponents don't.
New game. Pip runs to one of two doors, and the cat waits at one.Same door, Pip is caught. Different doors, Pip eats.
What one wins, the other loses. That's zero sum.

marl:12.t:
Pip and the cat learn just like the two mice.
The strips show each one's favourite door, round by round.The cat learns where Pip goes, and waits there. So Pip switches. Then the cat follows.
Pip's favourite flipped nineteen times. Neither settles.

marl:13.t:
The best play here is a coin toss, like rock, paper, scissors.If both play that, neither gains by changing. That resting point is an equilibrium.
Our learners never hold it.Each has a favourite, which the other exploits.

marl:14.t:
Your turn. You're the cat. Tap a door to wait there.
Pip keeps learning. Its two numbers are on the card.A coin tossing cat catches about half. Can you catch Pip more often?

marl:15.t:
One popular fix. Train together, act alone.
During practice, a helper sees everything.It learns the value of each pair of doors, and nudges each mouse toward good ones.
When it's time to act, the helper's gone. Each mouse decides from its own view.

marl:16.t:
When both sides share the rules, like chess, an agent can train against a copy of itself.As it improves, so does its opponent. Practice is never too easy, or hopeless.
That's self play. It taught AlphaZero chess and Go.Big systems also play older copies, to avoid chasing in circles.

marl:17.t:
In 2019, OpenAI Five beat the Dota 2 world champions, trained mostly by self play.
The same year, AlphaStar reached Grandmaster in StarCraft Two, with a whole league of agents.
Both took enormous practice. A shifting world is one reason it's hard.

marl:18.t:
So that's multi-agent R L. Several learners, one world.
To each one, the others are part of the world, and they keep changing.
Teams can settle on a safe but poor habit. Rivals can chase each other forever.

sim2real:0.t: Sim-to-Real  and  Domain Randomisation. Train in simulation, then deploy on a real robot.

sim2real:1.t:
Pip has a new job, on a real running track, with cheese at the end.Practice here is slow, and the cat sleeps just past the cheese.
So engineers build a simulator, a computer copy of the track.In the copy, Pip can practise thousands of walks in seconds, and nobody gets hurt.

sim2real:2.t:
Here are the rules. Each step, Pip either walks one cell, or runs two.
Watch Pip run three times, straight onto the cheese.That's worth point eight one. Walking all the way takes six steps, and earns only point five nine.
Go past the cheese, and you land on the cat.

sim2real:3.t:
In the simulator, the floor is perfectly dry. A run always goes exactly two cells.
Watch the habit appear, one choice per cell.Run everywhere, except right next to the cheese.
From the start, three runs, point eight one. Perfect, for this exact floor.

sim2real:4.t:
But the real track is polished.Watch the run on the bottom track. Sometimes it skids one cell further, and Pip loses a step getting up.
Nobody knows the slip chance. The engineers only guess it's somewhere up to point four.
The difference between copy and real thing is the reality gap.

sim2real:5.t:
Pip takes its dry habit onto the real track. Say the slip chance is point two.
Run, run, fine. Now watch the run from cell four.It skids, past the cheese, onto the cat.
The simulator never made a skid, so the habit never planned for one.

sim2real:6.t:
One walk could be bad luck. So the engineers test a thousand.
Each dot is a walk. Gold reached the cheese. Rose met the cat.
A hundred and thirty three walks met the cat.The average return falls to point five eight, far below the promised point eight one.

sim2real:7.t:
The dry habit isn't stupid. It's perfect for its practice floor.
Look at the run from cell four.It counts on landing exactly two cells on.
Whatever the copy gets slightly wrong, the habit may lean on. And no copy is ever perfect.

sim2real:8.t:
A different idea. Domain randomisation.
Before each practice walk, the simulator picks a random slip chance.Pip is never told which.
Now the best habit is the one with the best average across all of these floors. It can't rely on any single one.

sim2real:9.t:
Here's the winner.Run until two cells from the cheese, then walk.From cell four, a skid could carry Pip past the cheese, so it walks.
On a dry floor, this caution costs one step. Point seven three instead of point eight one.

sim2real:10.t:
Back on the real track, a thousand walks again.
Watch the dots. All gold.Not one walk meets the cat.
The average is point seven three, against point five eight for the dry habit.

sim2real:11.t:
Your turn. Drag the real slip chance, and both habits face a thousand real walks.
Watch the chart below.On a dry floor, the dry habit wins. From point one up, the randomised one wins.

sim2real:12.t:
Why is the randomised line flat?In this toy, its walks always take four steps, skid or no skid.
Real robots aren't so tidy. Outside the practised range, a policy can break.
And too wide a range can make policies slow, cautious, or hard to learn.

sim2real:13.t:
In 2017, Josh Tobin's team trained on simulated images with random colours, textures and lighting.It worked on real images, well enough for a robot to grasp objects.
Then OpenAI trained a robot hand in randomised simulation, first to turn a block, then a Rubik's cube.

sim2real:14.t:
So that's sim to real. A simulator makes practice fast and safe, but it's never exact.
A habit tuned to one exact copy can break in reality.
Randomise the copy, and the real world is just one more version. The price is a little caution.

rainbow:0.t: Rainbow: Dueling  and  Distributional D Q N. Six fixes for D Q N, stacked into one strong agent.

rainbow:1.t:
Back to the meadow. Pip's D Q N already has a few upgrades, each from a different paper.
In 2017, a DeepMind team stacked six of them into one agent, and called it Rainbow.This reel opens up two new ones, then lists all six.

rainbow:2.t:
Start with a question. Does the move really matter?
Here are Pip's four Q-values at the start.They're very close. From way out here, every move leaves a long way to go.
Now watch the gold squares. Where Pip stands changes the value far more than which move it picks.

rainbow:3.t:
So split each Q-value in two.A part for the spot, called V. And a part for the move, its advantage, A.
But you could shift a little from V to every A, and no Q would change.So there's a rule. Subtract the average advantage. Then V is just the average of the four Q-values.

rainbow:4.t:
A dueling network builds this split into its shape.One hidden layer feeds two heads. One output for V, and four for the advantages.
At the start, the four advantages are averaged and subtracted.What's left is Q equals V plus A, minus the average A.

rainbow:5.t:
Why bother? Think about one replay card, about one move.
In a plain network, it mostly teaches that one move's output.In a dueling network, V sits inside every Q-value. So every card trains V, whatever the move.
The advantage head only has to learn the differences.

rainbow:6.t:
Here's what the two heads learned.On the left, V. It rises toward the cheese, and dips behind the cat.
On the right, how much the move matters.Strongest around the cat, where one wrong step costs a lot. Pale where moves are about equally good.

rainbow:7.t:
Does it learn faster? Eight runs each, with matching seeds.
Watch the thick lines, the averages.Orange is plain D Q N. Teal is dueling.
They end up about equal. Single runs spread widely, so the gap is within the noise.On Atari, with more moves to choose from, the gains were clearer.

rainbow:8.t:
Now the second upgrade.From one spot, below and right of the cat, Pip walks a thousand times, with some random moves.
Watch the paths. Most reach the cheese. Some meet the cat.Each walk's return depends on how it ended, and how long it took.
Same spot, same habit, different luck.

rainbow:9.t:
Now sort all thousand returns into a histogram.Across is the return, from minus one to plus one. Height is how many walks landed there.
The gold bars on the right reached the cheese, spread by how long they took.The rose bars on the far left met the cat.

rainbow:10.t:
A Q-value keeps just one number, the average return.Watch the teal band. Only a small share of walks land anywhere near that average.
And the average hides the risk.It can't tell a sure thing from a gamble.

rainbow:11.t:
Now force the first move.Up first, past the cat's edge.Then down first, away from it.
The two averages are almost the same.But up meets the cat far more often. Nearly equal averages, very different risks.

rainbow:12.t:
Distributional R L learns the whole histogram, for every move. The C 51 network gives each move the chances of fifty one return values.
Here's a target. Pip moved right, and landed here.Take the histogram from where it landed.Squeeze it toward zero by point nine, and add the reward.

rainbow:13.t:
Now the squeezed bars sit between the fixed return values.So each one is split between its two neighbours, more to the nearer one.
Then the network's histogram is nudged toward that target.The loss measures how far apart the two histograms are.

rainbow:14.t:
Pip still picks moves by the average. The histogram contains it.
Yet on Atari, learning the whole shape scored clearly better. Why is still debated.Perhaps each card simply teaches more.
It also opens the door to risk aware choices.

rainbow:15.t:
Your turn. Tap any spot on the meadow.Pip walks from there four hundred times, and the histogram appears below.
Try open grass, then spots touching the cat's circle.Where is the average a fair summary, and where does it hide a cat?

rainbow:16.t:
Here are all six upgrades.You've now seen four. Double D Q N, prioritised replay, dueling heads, and distributional learning.
The other two. Multi step targets use a few real rewards before trusting a guess.And noisy networks explore with learned wiggles, instead of random moves.

rainbow:17.t:
On fifty seven Atari games, Rainbow beat every one of its parts alone.It also needed far less experience than D Q N.
Remove one part at a time, and prioritised replay and multi step targets hurt most.Small, compatible upgrades can add up.

rainbow:18.t:
So that's Rainbow.
A dueling network splits each Q-value into the spot's value and each move's advantage. V learns from every card.
Distributional R L learns the whole spread of returns. And six upgrades, stacked together, beat any one alone.

a2c:0.t: A 2 C  and  A 3 C. Many players learning at once beats one player alone.

a2c:1.t:
Back in the actor critic maze.Pip is an actor, the arrows, and a critic, the notebook.
After every move, the critic's T D error grades that move.Everything Pip learns comes from one walk, one move after another.

a2c:2.t:
Here's the trouble with one walk.Watch the teal cells as Pip makes eight moves in a row.It barely leaves its corner.
Moves in a row look alike, so updates keep pushing the same few cells.In a neural network, where everything shares numbers, that can drag it one way.

a2c:3.t:
The fix. Run many copies of the maze at once.Each copy has its own Pip, a worker, with its own dice. Here, eight.
But they all share one set of chances, and one critic.Whatever one worker learns, every worker uses.

a2c:4.t:
Now take one move from each worker, at the same moment.The workers have drifted apart, so their cells differ.
Compare the bars.Eight workers cover far more cells than one worker's eight moves in a row.Varied data. That's the first reason for workers.

a2c:5.t:
Here's A 2 C.Each worker plays five moves, then waits for the others.Then all forty moves make one shared update.
Each move's push uses its T D error, just as before.A 2 C stands for advantage actor critic. Everyone moves in lock step, so it's synchronous.

a2c:6.t:
Why average across workers?One worker's five moves carry one walk's luck. Eight workers cancel much of it.
So each update can take a bigger step, and stay safe.A single worker with that step would overshoot. It would need smaller, slower steps.

a2c:7.t:
Now add a clock. A move takes one tick, but some moves take two.
In A 2 C, the fast workers wait for the slowest.Watch the dots. That's waiting time.
The chart below will track how good Pip's habit is, tick by tick.

a2c:8.t:
Here's the race, a hundred runs each.Grey is one worker. Teal is eight workers, same step size.
Watch teal climb faster, and end far higher.The dashed line is one worker with smaller steps. Steadier, but slow.

a2c:9.t:
Same runs, but now count moves instead of ticks.Across is every move gathered by all workers together.
Now one worker is ahead.So workers don't help Pip learn from fewer moves. They save time on the clock, and steady the updates.

a2c:10.t:
Your turn. Drag the number of workers, from one up to eight.
Watch the curve, and how many runs stay stuck below point four.Going from one worker to two helps a lot. Four helps more. Eight gains nothing here.

a2c:11.t:
A 3 C never waits.Each worker copies the shared numbers, plays its moves, and sends its update the moment it's done.
Compare the lanes. Top is A 2 C, with waiting.Bottom is A 3 C. Every black dot is one worker's update, arriving on its own.

a2c:12.t:
The catch. While a worker plays, others update, so its copy goes stale.The white numbers count the missed updates.
Why does it still work? Each push is eight times smaller, so eight of them add up to about one A 2 C update.Watch the two lines finish close together.

a2c:13.t:
A 3 C ran on an ordinary computer's cores, with no graphics card.On Atari, it beat earlier agents in about half the time.
A year later, OpenAI found that A 2 C did just as well. Its one big batch suits graphics cards.Real speed depends on the hardware.

a2c:14.t:
Running many copies of the world in parallel became standard practice.
P P O, coming next, is usually trained this way. From eight copies on a laptop, to thousands in big labs.
The asynchronous style lives on in systems like IMPALA.

a2c:15.t:
So that's A 2 C and A 3 C. Workers run copies of the world, and share one actor and one critic.
Their moves are more varied, and averaging steadies each update.
A 2 C waits for everyone. A 3 C doesn't. Either way, workers save time, not moves.

trpo:0.t: T R P O: Trust Regions. Improve the policy, but never jump too far at once.

trpo:1.t:
Same maze, same dry floor.The arrows are Pip's chances in each cell. Longer means more likely.
After a little learning, Pip's score is point three six.The best possible is point five three, seven steps straight to the cheese.

trpo:2.t:
Here's one update. Pip walks ten times with its current chances. That's a batch.Watch the walks pile up.
For each move, Pip asks, did things go better than usual from here?That's the move's advantage. The return after the move, minus the critic's value of the cell.

trpo:3.t:
Look at the start cell. Each bar is one time Pip made that move there.
Up often went fine, but twice that walk later met the cat.Down and left just bump a wall. Yet by luck, some of those walks went better than usual.
So the batch says, less up, and more of two useless moves.

trpo:4.t:
Now take a normal step in that direction.Watch the start cell. Up shrinks a little, down grows a little.
The rest of the maze improves too.The score rises, from point three six to point three nine.

trpo:5.t:
If a small step helps, surely a bigger one helps more?
Same batch, same direction, but a step about thirty three times bigger.Watch the start cell. Up almost vanishes. Down takes over.
Pip now mostly walks into the wall. The score crashes to almost zero.

trpo:6.t:
Watch what happens next.Pip bumps into the bottom wall, again and again.
In its next batch, eight of ten walks hit the step limit, and score nothing.And those poor walks are exactly what it must learn from next.

trpo:7.t:
Now both policies keep learning with the normal step.Teal continues from the normal step. Rose from the big one.
Watch rose crawl along the bottom, while teal climbs.Bad walks bring slow news.

trpo:8.t:
Why did the batch mislead?Its advice is a slope, measured at the old policy. A slope is only reliable nearby.
Watch the line. Small steps along the advice help, up to about five.Further out, the very same advice hurts.

trpo:9.t:
So limit how far one update may move. But measure it in behaviour, not numbers.
Watch both cells get the same plus two for up.On the left, up jumps from a quarter to about seventy one percent. On the right, it was already near certain, and barely changes.

trpo:10.t:
First, a way to score one choice. Its surprise.
A sure thing surprises zero.Watch the dots. Chance one half gives point six nine. One tenth gives two point three.
Rarer choices surprise more, without limit.

trpo:11.t:
The batch came from old Pip. How much less likely is new Pip to make old Pip's moves?
Averaged over old Pip's choices, that's the K L divergence. Zero for identical policies.
At the start cell, new Pip almost never goes up, which old Pip did often. That alone makes the K L large.

trpo:12.t:
T R P O, trust region policy optimization, turns this into a rule.Improve as the batch suggests, but keep the average K L under a limit.
Watch the bars. The big step blows far past the limit.Even the normal step goes over, though harmlessly here.

trpo:13.t:
Real T R P O computes a step that just fits. Our toy simply halves the big step until it fits.
Watch the rows. Each halving shrinks the K L.Six halvings later, it fits.
The score rises a bit less than the plain step. Safety costs some speed.

trpo:14.t:
Now forty updates from a blank policy, averaged over fifty runs.Rose takes big plain steps. Teal takes small ones. Blue is T R P O.
Watch rose stall. Many of its runs get stuck near zero.T R P O starts slower, but ends near the best, with no run stuck.

trpo:15.t:
T R P O here does two things. It halves the step, and checks the K L. Which one prevents the crashes?
Rose keeps the halving, but drops the K L check.Watch it stall, as badly as plain big steps.
The K L limit does the work.

trpo:16.t:
Your turn. Drag the K L limit. Each setting reruns the same fifty runs.
Tiny limits are safe, but crawl.Big limits let the big steps through, and runs start getting stuck.

trpo:17.t:
Why bother with a limit at all, when a small fixed step also worked?
Because the safe step changes as Pip learns.Watch the bars. Early on, only small steps fit. Later, the full big step fits.
The price is heavy maths, slow and fiddly for big networks.

trpo:18.t:
In 2015, T R P O taught simulated robots to swim, hop and walk.It also played Atari games straight from the screen.
Two years later, the same group introduced P P O. It keeps the idea of not moving too far, with a much simpler trick.

trpo:19.t:
So that's T R P O.
A step that's too big can wreck a good policy. And then the wreck collects poor walks to learn from.
So measure each step by how much the chances change, the K L, and only accept steps within a limit.

muzero:0.t: MuZero. Plan like AlphaZero, without being told the rules.

muzero:1.t:
Remember AlphaZero's search. Every loop, it played moves by the real rules.
But Atari games, robots, and most real problems come with no rulebook.
So can Pip still search ahead? MuZero says yes. Learn your own model of what moves do, and search inside it.

muzero:2.t:
What should that model predict? The next board, exactly?For a game screen, that's every pixel, mostly irrelevant details.
MuZero predicts only what the search uses.The reward a move pays, the value of where it leads, and a prior over next moves.

muzero:3.t:
It uses three small networks.h reads the real board once, and turns it into a hidden state. Eighteen numbers, shown as bars.
g takes a hidden state and a move, and imagines the next state, plus the move's reward.f gives a prior and a value, just like AlphaZero's network.

muzero:4.t:
First, what do rewards and values mean here?
A move that ends the game pays Pip's points as its reward. One for a win, a half for a draw. Other moves pay nothing.The value is the points still to come. So a move's worth is its reward, plus the value after it.

muzero:5.t:
Here's the model imagining a line from Pip's puzzle.h reads the board, then g imagines five moves, one after another.
MuZero never sees those boards. We just draw them faded, for you.Watch the last move. It completes Pip's diagonal, and the predicted reward jumps to point nine five.

muzero:6.t:
Now MuZero runs AlphaZero's search, with the model in place of the rules.Each new node gets its state and reward from g, and its prior and value from f.
Only the top is real. Everything deeper is imagined.Nobody tells the model when an imagined game ends. It has to learn that rewards stop.

muzero:7.t:
How does the model learn? Replay a real game's next three moves, inside the model.
At each imagined step, check it against reality. The reward paid, how the game ended, the move played.
Errors flow back through all three networks. Nobody says what the hidden numbers mean.

muzero:8.t:
Our toy takes a shortcut.Real MuZero learns from its own search's games. That's too slow in a browser.
So ours learned ahead of time, from three thousand recorded games by a player who's perfect half the time.Either way, it never sees the rules.

muzero:9.t:
Did it learn what matters?Check every winning move. g predicts a high reward for most of them.
And for moves where play goes on, it mostly predicts low.Nobody explained three in a row. It learned it from the rewards.

muzero:10.t:
Back to the puzzle, now searched entirely in its head.The numbers show how many of fifty loops went through each move.
Top right gets the most, eighteen.That's the winning move. Every position below the top was imagined.

muzero:11.t:
How good is it, really? Two hundred random positions where the choice matters.
The prior alone finds a best move a hundred and thirty eight times. Searching in the model, a hundred and forty eight.Search the same networks with the real rules, and it's a hundred and ninety seven.
So the model's errors cost the most.

muzero:12.t:
Your turn. Tap squares to imagine moves from Pip's puzzle, Pip and cat taking turns.
Each tap runs g once. You'll see the predicted reward, and the value after it.
Try a move onto a taken square. The model was never told that's impossible.

muzero:13.t:
MuZero came from DeepMind, published in 2020.
Given legal moves but no rules, it matched AlphaZero in chess, shogi and Go.It also set a new best on fifty seven Atari games.
A later version was even trialled compressing YouTube videos.

muzero:14.t:
So that's MuZero. It searches like AlphaZero, but inside a model it learned.
h makes a hidden state. g imagines moves and rewards. f gives a prior and a value.
The model never draws the board. It keeps only what matters for choosing moves.

successor:0.t: Successor Features. Know where you’ll go, and new goals cost almost nothing.

successor:1.t:
Welcome back to the T D maze. Same habit, same rules.
Here's the notebook T D learned from two hundred walks.About point three four at the start, and point nine eight beside the cheese.A bit noisy. The true values are point four and point eight seven.

successor:2.t:
Now, tomorrow, someone swaps the cheese and the cat.Walls, habit, everything else stays the same.
But Pip's notebook is now wrong almost everywhere.Each number mixes two things. Where Pip tends to go, and what it finds there.

successor:3.t:
So keep those two apart.
Question one. From here, where will I go? That depends on the maze and the habit.Question two. What does each cell pay? That's the part that changed.
Like knowing your town's streets. The errand changes, but the streets stay the same.

successor:4.t:
Answer question one by counting visits.Watch walk one. Each cell Pip steps into gets a score.
One for the next step, point nine for the one after, and so on, shrinking each step.It's just like discounting rewards.

successor:5.t:
One walk is luck. Average over all walks from the start, and you get Pip's map.
The cell above the start scores over one, because Pip can come back to it.The cheese gets about point four three. The cat, almost nothing.
This is the successor representation, from Peter Dayan, in 1993.

successor:6.t:
Now question two. What does each cell pay?The cheese pays plus one. The cat pays minus one. Everything else, nothing.
Multiply each cell's visits by its pay, and add them up.You get point four. Exactly the start's true value.

successor:7.t:
Without the rulebook, Pip learns the map by T D.
After each step, the row of the cell it left moves toward one at the landing cell, plus point nine times the landing cell's row.
It's T D, with I arrived here as the reward.

successor:8.t:
Watch the start's row fill in over two hundred walks.Close to the true map on the usual route, rougher elsewhere.
Multiply by the pays, and it matches the T D notebook exactly, in every cell.So with fixed rewards, the map buys nothing. It pays off when rewards change.

successor:9.t:
Now the swap.Pip keeps its map, and just rewrites the pays. Plus one at the old cat cell, minus one at the old cheese.
Multiply again, and every value updates instantly, with no new walk.The start now reads minus point three four.

successor:10.t:
Plain T D only has its old notebook. Let it walk two hundred more times.
Watch the gold line, its error. It falls slowly.The start value doesn't even turn negative until walk thirty four.
The dashed teal line is the map, right from the first moment.

successor:11.t:
Rewards can change anywhere, not just at the ends.
Put back the cheese and cat, and drop a crumb on Pip's usual route.It's worth half a point every time Pip steps on it.
The map says Pip visits that cell often and early.So the start's value jumps to point eight six, at once.

successor:12.t:
Your turn. Tap a cell to drop a crumb there. Tap again to take it away.
Values come straight from the map, times the new pays.Crumbs on the usual route lift many cells. Crumbs in rarely visited corners barely matter.

successor:13.t:
Here's the catch. The map belongs to the habit.
After the swap, Pip's arrows still march toward the old cheese corner, now the cat's.A better habit would mean a new map, which has to be learned.
So the map makes new rewards cheap, but not new habits.

successor:14.t:
Big worlds have too many cells to map.So successor features map a few features instead, like food or water.
A task weights each feature. Keep several old habits' maps, and for a new task, follow whichever looks best at each spot.

successor:15.t:
Maybe brains do this too.
The hippocampus has place cells, neurons that fire at a particular place.One proposal says they hold a predictive map, firing for where the animal will likely go.
It fits some recordings. How far it goes is still debated.

successor:16.t:
So that's the successor representation.
Split value into a map of where Pip will go, and what each cell pays. Value is visits times pay.
The map is learned by T D. New rewards give new values instantly. A new habit needs a new map.

contextual:0.t: Contextual Bandits. Same slot machines, but now you know who’s playing.

contextual:1.t:
The cheese arcade now stays open late, from ten in the morning to ten at night.
But there's a new rule. The chances drift with the hour.Watch the numbers under the machines as the clock runs. C fades through the day. D wakes up.

contextual:2.t:
Here are the four chances through the day.Across is the hour. Up is the chance of a crumb.
The dots mark the best machine each hour.C in the morning, B briefly, then D in the evening.Pull the best one every hour, and you'd get a crumb sixty three percent of the time.

contextual:3.t:
Now each pull comes at a random hour.A plain bandit ignores the clock, and hunts for the best machine on average. That's B.
But even B, found perfectly, pays only half the time.The dashed line is the best for the hour plan. One winner for everyone leaves crumbs on the table.

contextual:4.t:
Information you see before choosing is the context. Here, it's the hour.
A contextual bandit sees the context, picks a machine, and gets a reward.It learns the best machine for each kind of situation.
And Pip's pull doesn't change the next hour. That's what keeps it a bandit, not full R L.

contextual:5.t:
The simplest fix. Keep separate tallies for each part of the day.
Two rows. Morning, and evening.Each row runs its own U C B, as if it were its own arcade.
Watch the clock, and which row gets highlighted with each pull.

contextual:6.t:
After a thousand pulls, look at the two rows.
The morning row mostly pulls C. The evening row mostly pulls D.Each row found its own winner.
At three in the afternoon, B is best, but only by a hair. Lumping that hour into the morning costs very little.

contextual:7.t:
Now regret compares each pull with the best machine at that hour.
Grey is the clock blind bandit. It keeps piling up regret.Gold is two rows. Much lower.
Almost all of gold's regret is the cost of learning.

contextual:8.t:
Why not one row per hour?Each row would be exactly right about its hour. But each sees only one pull in twelve, and starts from scratch.
Watch teal. Twelve rows do worse than two.More rows, less data in each.

contextual:9.t:
Instead of rows, give each machine a straight line.Chance equals a start, plus a slope times the lateness of the hour.
Every pull of D, at any hour, helps place D's line.Watch the dots. Top for a crumb, bottom for nothing. The solid line fits them.

contextual:10.t:
To explore, add a bonus, like U C B.The shaded bands show each line's doubt. Narrow where pulls pile up. Wide where they're few.
Score each machine by its line, plus half its band.That's Lin U C B, from 2010.

contextual:11.t:
Here's the race again, now with Lin U C B in purple.Watch it come in far below both kinds of rows.
But be fair to the rows. Here, the true chances really are straight lines.When the truth is curved, a line can be wrong however much data it gets.

contextual:12.t:
Your turn. Drag the hour, and see Lin U C B's lines, scores and pick.
A and B were barely pulled, so their lines sit at zero. Only their wide bands keep them in the running.
Try three in the afternoon. B is truly best, but Lin U C B picks something else.

contextual:13.t:
Here's the fine print. A bandit only sees the result of the machine it pulled.
If Pip never pulls A in the evening, it has no evening data on A.A line can guess from morning pulls, but only if a line is the right shape.
Old logs have the same gap. They only show what the old strategy chose.

contextual:14.t:
In 2010, Lin U C B chose which news stories to show on the Yahoo front page.It earned about twelve and a half percent more clicks than ignoring the context.
Today contextual bandits choose ads, songs, notification times, and are studied for personal treatments in medicine.

contextual:15.t:
So that's the contextual bandit. Look at the context before choosing.
Few contexts, keep a row of tallies for each. Many, learn a shared model, like Lin U C B's line plus bonus.
Either way, the pull doesn't change the next context.

dt:0.t: Decision Transformer. What if R L were just predicting the next word?

dt:1.t:
Pip finds a box of forty old diaries.Each one records a walk by the Wanderer, who moves at random.
Pip may not walk itself. It can only learn from these pages.Only two of the walks reached the cheese.

dt:2.t:
New scoring for this reel. Every move costs a little, point oh five.The cheese pays one, the cat minus one, and rewards just add up.
So shorter is better.Watch the green route. Seven moves, for a total of point six five.The best diary in the box only scored minus point one.

dt:3.t:
The key number is the return to go. The total still to come.
Here's the box's best diary. Twenty two moves, with lots of bumps into walls.Watch the number on the card. Each move's cost is paid, so it creeps up a little.
On the last move, the cheese arrives, and nothing is left to come.

dt:4.t:
Now write each diary step as three tokens.The return to go, the cell, and the move.
A whole walk becomes a sentence.A transformer, the network behind chatbots, learns to predict the next move, the way a chatbot predicts the next word.

dt:5.t:
Training is just prediction. No values, no Bellman updates.So nothing feeds on its own guesses, which caused trouble in the offline R L reel.
Our stand in is a simple lookup.In this cell, copy the move whose return to go is closest to the total still wanted.

dt:6.t:
Now ask for the best total, point six five.
Watch Pip. At each cell, it copies the closest diary step, then subtracts its reward from the total still wanted.
Seven moves, straight to the cheese.It beats every single diary in the box.

dt:7.t:
How can it beat every diary?Watch the colours. Its moves come from two different diaries, the only two that reached the cheese.
Pieces of different walks make a better one. That's called stitching.

dt:8.t:
The number you ask for is a dial.
Ask for zero, and Pip reaches the cheese the long way, in twenty moves.Ask for minus one and a half, and it wanders until it's stopped.
Nobody wants a bad walk. But it shows the model really listens.

dt:9.t:
Here's every request, played from the start.Across is the total asked for. Up is the total got.
In the middle, the dots sit right on the diagonal. Pip gets what it asks for.At the top, they go flat. Ask for one, and you still get point six five. There's no better walk to copy.

dt:10.t:
Here's another box. In this one, no diary ever reached the cheese.
Ask for point six five, and Pip just wanders until it's stopped.No total, however high, can produce cheese steps that were never written down.

dt:11.t:
A third box holds every piece of the seven move route.
But watch. Asked for point six five, Pip takes nine moves.In one cell, the closest return to go came from a diary going the long way.
Value learning finds the seven move route. Good endings flow back through shared cells.

dt:12.t:
Now a hundred boxes of each size.Up is how many boxes give the seven move walk.
Grey is a single diary that already was the best walk. Rare.Blue is the lookup. Green is value learning.Both stitch far beyond any single diary. But the lookup is less reliable.

dt:13.t:
Your turn. Drag the total to ask for, and Pip plays it from the start.
Tap the maze to switch to the third box, where the pieces don't line up.Watch what happens when you ask for more than the maze allows.

dt:14.t:
The Decision Transformer came from Lili Chen and colleagues, in 2021.It matched the offline R L methods of its time.
Later studies found stitching unreliable, as you saw.And in worlds with chance, it can copy moves that were merely lucky.

dt:15.t:
So that's the Decision Transformer. R L as sequence prediction.
Write each step as return to go, state and move, and learn to predict the move.At play time, ask for a high total, and subtract rewards as they come.
It stitches less reliably than value learning, and it can't use pieces the data never had.

grpo:0.t: R L for L L M Reasoning (G R P O). Let the model try, let a checker grade it, repeat.

grpo:1.t:
Bot is back, now helping Pip with sums, like four plus seven times three.
Sums like these can be checked by a program. Right scores one, wrong scores zero.
No people comparing answers, no reward model to fool. Just a cheap, exact check. A verifiable reward.

grpo:2.t:
A real language model writes its working word by word. Bot just picks one of four ways of answering.
Guess. Work left to right. Do times first. Or do times first, then check.
Watch the examples. Left to right goes wrong whenever times follows plus.

grpo:3.t:
How good is each way? Only the simulation knows.
Guessing is right less than a fifth of the time. Left to right, half.Times first, and check, almost always.
Overall, Bot starts out right about half the time.

grpo:4.t:
Take one question.Bot answers it eight times. That's a group.
Watch the cards. Green is right, rose is wrong.Two of eight are right. Both did times first.

grpo:5.t:
The group's average score is the yardstick. Here, one quarter.
An answer's advantage is its score, minus that average.G R P O also divides by the spread of the scores. That puts every question on the same scale.
If all eight scores are equal, the spread is zero, and every advantage is zero.

grpo:6.t:
P P O usually trains a critic, a second network, to be the yardstick.For a language model, the critic is about as big as the model.
G R P O uses the group's average instead.The price is several answers per question. The gain is one less big network.

grpo:7.t:
Now one update.Right answers push up their way's chance. Wrong ones push theirs down.
Watch times first grow, and left to right shrink.
A K L leash pulls gently back toward the original Bot, as in R L H F.

grpo:8.t:
Now a full run. Sixty four answers per update.
Watch accuracy climb, from about half, to point nine five.Guessing and left to right fade away.
Times first and check takes over. Even plain times first shrinks. Its slips lose to checked answers in the same group.

grpo:9.t:
If all eight answers are right, or all wrong, every advantage is zero. The group teaches nothing.
Watch the bars grow. Early on, few groups are silent.By the end, half of them are, because Bot is getting most sums right.
