Useful questions are the ones Bot gets right only sometimes.

grpo:10.t:
Your turn. Drag the group size. Every update still uses sixty four answers.
The curve shows how likely a group is to say something, for a question Bot gets right with chance p.
Tiny groups are often silent. Here, groups of sixteen do best.

grpo:11.t:
Now suppose Bot never checks. That chance starts at zero.
No group ever contains a check, so nothing can reward it.Watch the orange line. It ends lower, at point eight seven.
G R P O sharpens what Bot already does sometimes. It doesn't invent new ways.

grpo:12.t:
G R P O first appeared in DeepSeekMath, in 2024, training a model on maths problems.
In 2025, DeepSeek R1 used it with simple rule based rewards.Its answers grew longer, with more checking and rethinking, habits the model already showed now and then.

grpo:13.t:
So that's G R P O. When a program can check the answer, the checker gives the reward.
Sample a group of answers, and grade each against the group's average. No critic needed.
A K L leash keeps the model close, and groups that are all right or all wrong teach nothing.

saferl:0.t: Safe  and  Constrained R L. Win the game, but never cross the line.

saferl:1.t:
A new room for Pip. No rocks, no cat.Start at the bottom left. The cheese waits at the bottom right.
In the middle of the floor, four glass panels.Stepping on them changes nothing in Pip's reward. And that's exactly the problem.

saferl:2.t:
We care about that glass. Every step onto it risks breaking it.Watch Pip step on a panel.
So we count a second number, the cost. One for each step onto glass.Reward says how well Pip did. Cost says how much harm it risked. We keep them apart.

saferl:3.t:
There are two routes.The shortcut runs along the bottom. Five steps, two of them on glass.The detour goes up and around. Nine steps, no glass.
With discounting, the shortcut is worth point six six. The detour only point four three.Reward alone prefers the shortcut.

saferl:4.t:
First, Pip trains on reward alone.Watch it take the shortcut, straight across the glass.
That's about three glass steps per walk, counting the random moves.

saferl:5.t:
Why not just subtract a fixed penalty for each glass step?
Watch the shortcut's value fall as the penalty grows. The detour stays flat.Below the crossing point, Pip always takes the shortcut. Above it, always the detour.
Only a penalty exactly at the tie would mix the routes. A knife edge.

saferl:6.t:
Constrained R L says what we want directly.Maximise reward, subject to the average cost staying under a budget.
Our budget is one glass step per walk, on average.The shortcut costs two, the detour almost nothing. So Pip should take the shortcut only some of the time.

saferl:7.t:
The trick is a price on glass, called lambda.Pip maximises reward, minus lambda times cost.
After each walk, the price moves. Overspend, and it rises. Underspend, and it falls.In maths, lambda is a Lagrange multiplier. It turns a limit into a price.

saferl:8.t:
Pip keeps two numbers for every move. Reward to come, and glass steps to come.
Look at the yellow cell, where the routes split.Right promises more reward, but more glass. Up promises less of both.
Pip scores each move as reward minus the price times glass.

saferl:9.t:
Here's how to read the chart. It starts when the price is switched on.
Gold, on top, is the price.Rose, below, is glass steps per walk. The dashed line is the budget.
Watch the two lines push against each other.

saferl:10.t:
At first Pip overspends, and the price climbs, peaking at about point five three.
Then the detour wins. Glass drops under budget, and the price drifts back down, until the shortcut sometimes wins again.
By the end, Pip uses one glass step per walk. Right on budget.

saferl:11.t:
At the split cell, try different prices.Watch the bold arrow flip between right and up.
The two scores tie at a price of about point one three.The price settles right around there. Small swings mix the two routes.

saferl:12.t:
The budget holds on average, once the price settles.But while learning, Pip stepped on glass more than fourteen hundred times.
If even one break is a disaster, averages aren't enough.Safe exploration adds a shield, a rule that blocks known dangerous moves while Pip learns.

saferl:13.t:
Your turn. Pick a budget, and the whole run repeats.
Watch where the price settles, and how often Pip takes the shortcut.
A budget below even the detour's cost can't be met, so the price keeps climbing. A loose budget leaves it near zero.

saferl:14.t:
Eitan Altman's 1999 book set out constrained MDPs.In 2017, Constrained Policy Optimisation brought them to deep R L.
Then OpenAI's Safety Gym gave simulated robots goals to reach and hazards to avoid.

saferl:15.t:
Some limits to know.The constraint is about the average. Single walks can still go over, and learning itself breaks it.
And cost is written by people, just like reward. It can be mis-specified, and gamed.

saferl:16.t:
So that's safe R L. Keep harm in its own signal, the cost, separate from reward.
Maximise reward, while the average cost stays under a budget.A price on cost rises when you overspend and falls when you don't. It settles at the tipping point.

her:0.t: Goal-Conditioned R L  and  H E R. Missed the target? Pretend you were aiming there all along.

her:1.t:
The cheese and cat are gone. Now, each walk, a flag is planted somewhere random.That's Pip's goal.
Land close to the flag and Pip gets plus one, and the walk ends.Every other move pays nothing.

her:2.t:
A new flag every walk means no fixed set of Q-values can work.Up is great for a flag above Pip, and bad for one below.
So the goal becomes an input.The network reads Pip's spot, the flag's spot, and the gap between them.One network, for every goal. That's goal conditioned.

her:3.t:
At first, Pip's network knows nothing, so its moves are aimless.And the flag's circle is tiny.
Watch a few early walks. Missed. Missed again.Rewards this rare are called sparse.

her:4.t:
Look inside Pip's replay memory.Each box holds five cards. Gold means it holds a plus one.
Almost none are gold.So nearly every lesson copies one guess from another, with no real reward behind it.

her:5.t:
Here's how training goes, four runs.Every so often, Pip is tested on thirty fixed flags.
Watch the orange lines.One run breaks through late. The other three stay low.

her:6.t:
Here's one failed walk from training.Watch Pip wander, and get stopped well short of the flag.
Now ask a question, in hindsight.What if the flag had been right where Pip ended?Then the very same walk would have been a success.

her:7.t:
That's Hindsight Experience Replay, or H E R, from OpenAI in 2017.
Each failed walk is stored twice. Once with the real goal, and reward zero.And once with the goal moved to where Pip ended.
In the copy, the last move pays plus one. The earlier moves learn from it, just like T D.

her:8.t:
Isn't that cheating? No.
The copied cards tell the truth. From those spots, those moves really did reach that place.Watch the gold dots, where early walks ended. Many sit by the fence.
That still helps. The network reads the gap, so any goal teaches the same skill. Shrink the gap.

her:9.t:
Now look at the memory with H E R.Far more gold now.
Real successes are still rare at first.But plenty of lessons now end in plus one, teaching the network to steer toward a goal.

her:10.t:
Now the race.Teal is with H E R. Orange is without. Same seeds, same number of updates.
Watch the thick lines, the averages.Teal climbs well above orange.

her:11.t:
Here's the trained network, sent to six test flags it never practised on.
Watch it read the gap, and steer.Near a flag, it sometimes overshoots. One move is bigger than the flag's circle, so the last step has to land just right.

her:12.t:
Your turn. Tap the meadow to plant a flag.
Pip starts at the bottom left, and follows its network.Try flags far away, near the edges, and close by. The network was never told about your flag.

her:13.t:
The H E R paper trained a simulated robot arm.Push a block, slide a puck, pick and place an object, with reward only on success.
Without H E R, those tasks failed. With it, the arm learned all three.A pick and place policy even worked on a real arm.

her:14.t:
H E R has limits.
It needs goals that are reachable places, so wherever a walk ends can be written down as a goal.And it needs an off policy learner, like D Q N or D D P G, because the copies were made chasing a different goal.

her:15.t:
So that's H E R. A goal conditioned network gets the goal as an input.
With reward only at the goal, the memory fills with zeros.
H E R stores each miss again, as a success for the spot it reached. The lessons are true, and they teach Pip to steer.

rnd:0.t: R N D  and  Go-Explore. How agents finally cracked the hardest exploration game.

rnd:1.t:
Remember the meadow? Pip's position there is just two numbers, x and y.
Each move goes a fixed distance, plus a little random wobble.So Pip practically never stands on exactly the same spot twice.
Keep that in mind. It's about to break counting.

rnd:2.t:
Here's Pip's new meadow. Long and thin, with Pip starting at the left.
The cheese sits at the far right end.Each walk is cut off after forty moves, and even walking straight, the cheese takes twenty five.

rnd:3.t:
First, a Pip that moves completely at random.Watch thirty walks, each its own trail of dots.
The farthest it gets is about x equals one point one six. Not even halfway.Random steps cancel out. It never reaches the cheese.

rnd:4.t:
Those walks landed on twelve hundred spots. Only thirteen were exact repeats.
Look at the zoom. Two spots a hair apart each get counted once.So a count bonus would call almost everything new.
Counting only works when places repeat.

rnd:5.t:
What we want is familiarity that spreads to nearby spots.If Pip has been around here a lot, here should feel boring, even if this exact spot is new.
Networks do exactly this kind of spreading. A nudge at one spot moves the guesses nearby too.

rnd:6.t:
Here's the trick, from Burda and colleagues in 2018.Take a small network, fill it with random numbers, and never train it.
Feed it a spot, and out come four meaningless numbers.The map shows the first one across the meadow. Meaningless, but smooth, and fixed.

rnd:7.t:
Now a second network, the copier, tries to give the same four numbers.
But it only gets lessons at spots Pip actually visits.The gap between its numbers and the random network's is the copying error.

rnd:8.t:
Give the copier lessons at all the random walker's spots.
Watch the map change. On the left, where Pip walked, the error drops.Out at x equals three, where Pip never went, it stays high.
So copying error works as a novelty bonus. That's Random Network Distillation, or R N D.

rnd:9.t:
But look at the untaught copier.A pale band runs along the middle, where Pip has never been.
By pure chance, the copier already roughly matches there.
Spreading cuts both ways. Such accidents mislead Pip a little, until lessons fix them.

rnd:10.t:
Why a random network? It never changes, and it only looks at what Pip sees now.So it can be learned.Watch a fresh copier's error at one spot fall, lesson by lesson.
Predicting the next view would be fooled by a noisy TV. R N D is less fooled, though not immune.

rnd:11.t:
Now Pip peeks.Before each move, it checks the copying error at the four landing spots.It goes where the error is biggest.
This toy Pip only explores. Real R N D adds the bonus to the game reward.

rnd:12.t:
Here's the R N D explorer, with a fresh copier.
Watch the orange retreat as places grow familiar.Pip's peeks pull it into fresher grass, further and further right.
It first lands in the cheese in walk fourteen. The bonus knows nothing about cheese.

rnd:13.t:
To compare fairly, we run twenty different seeds.
Across is the walk number. Up is the farthest Pip has reached so far.The dashed line is the edge of the cheese.

rnd:14.t:
Gold is the random walker. It creeps along.Teal is the R N D explorer. It pushes all the way to the far end.
Hitting the small cheese circle is partly luck.R N D did it in eleven of twenty runs. The random walker, never.

rnd:15.t:
The famous hard case is an Atari game, Montezuma's Revenge.A pyramid of rooms, with keys, doors and deadly falls.
Points are rare, each one needing a long chain of exact moves.D Q N scored zero. R N D was the first to beat the average human without demonstrations.

rnd:16.t:
Even with a bonus, every walk starts over.
The explorer reached far once.Watch the next walk, from scratch. It falls short.
In games where a few wrong moves end the try, that frontier may never be reached again.Go Explore turns this around. First return, then explore.

rnd:17.t:
Go Explore lumps spots into coarse cells, and keeps an archive. One saved spot per cell.
Each round, it picks a cell, favouring rarely visited ones.It restores that spot, like loading a saved game, then takes random moves from there.

rnd:18.t:
Watch the archive grow outward, round by round.New cells light up orange as they join.
This run hits the cheese in round thirty one.Over twenty runs, Go Explore found the cheese every time. Remembering and returning do the work.

rnd:19.t:
Your turn. Tap the meadow to give the copier thirty lessons there.
Watch the orange fade at that spot, and a little around it.Tap a few spots in a row to paint a familiar trail. Tap below the meadow to start over.

rnd:20.t:
R N D, from OpenAI in 2018, first beat average human play on Montezuma's Revenge.
Go Explore scored far higher there, and did well on Pitfall, another very sparse game.It then trained a policy to follow its own best routes, even when the game behaves a little randomly.

rnd:21.t:
So that's R N D and Go Explore.
When places never repeat, counting fails. R N D measures novelty as a copier's error, which spreads to nearby spots.
Go Explore remembers reached places, returns, and explores from there. Reward novelty, and remember the frontier.

curriculum:0.t: Curriculum Learning. Nobody learns calculus before counting. Neither should agents.

curriculum:1.t:
A bigger maze. Two walls of rocks, no cat.The cheese is top right, and Pip starts bottom left.
The small numbers show how far each cell is from the cheese. Twelve steps from the start.A walk with no cheese after thirty steps is stopped, and pays nothing.

curriculum:2.t:
Pip learns with Q-learning, as in its reel.
Every number starts at zero.So until Pip first reaches the cheese, every nudge is zero toward zero.It learns nothing, and just wanders.

curriculum:3.t:
Here's walk one, from the real start.With every number at zero, each move is a random pick.
Thirty steps, no cheese. Stopped, and nothing learned.In its first fifty walks, Pip never reaches the cheese. The first time is walk fifty seven.

curriculum:4.t:
This strip shows Pip's first three hundred walks. Teal if it reached the cheese, pale if not.
Mostly pale.Each success pushes the good news back only about one move, so the next one is still mostly luck.
Only near the very end do Pip's numbers lead home.

curriculum:5.t:
A curriculum is a list of lessons, from easy to hard.
Lesson one starts Pip just three steps from the cheese. Then six, then nine.Then the real start, twelve away.
Only the starting cell changes. Everything else stays the same.

curriculum:6.t:
Lesson one, walk one. Just three steps from the cheese.Even at random, the cheese is close.
Pip finds it in nine steps, and the last move gets the first real number.Watch the gold trail grow back from the cheese, walk after walk.

curriculum:7.t:
Lesson two starts farther away.Pip still wanders, but it only has to stumble into the gold trail. Then the numbers lead it home.
Then lesson three, and then the real start.Watch the arrows line up, all the way back.

curriculum:8.t:
Here's the same strip, now with the curriculum.The black ticks mark the end of each lesson.
Teal from the very beginning. The reward is no longer rare.Two hundred eighty seven cheese walks, against twenty two without.

curriculum:9.t:
One seed could be luck, so here are fifty runs.Each line counts the runs whose numbers lead home from the real start.
Rose is no curriculum. Teal is the curriculum.After a hundred walks, every curriculum run passes. Without it, none do.

curriculum:10.t:
Why does it work? Learning needs rewards.On the hard task, rewards were so rare that most walks taught nothing.
Easy lessons pay off almost every time. And what Pip learns there is exactly the end of the route it needs later.Shaping changes the rewards. A curriculum changes the tasks.

curriculum:11.t:
Order matters.
Too big a jump, from three steps straight to the real start, is slower.Too slow, lingering on the easy lesson, wastes walks on a skill Pip already has.
The gradual curriculum, in teal, wins.

curriculum:12.t:
Your turn. Drag the number of walks per lesson. Zero means no curriculum.
All fifty runs are redone each time.Too few walks per lesson, and the trail isn't ready. Too many, and walks are wasted.

curriculum:13.t:
Writing lessons by hand takes knowledge, and trial and error.
Instead, a teacher program can pick the next lesson.For example, start cells where Pip succeeds about half the time. Not hopeless, not boring.
Self play is a curriculum too. The opponent gets harder exactly as fast as the learner.

curriculum:14.t:
In 2009, Yoshua Bengio and colleagues named curriculum learning, inspired by how people are taught.
In 2017, simulated robots were trained by starting near the goal, then moving the start away, just like here.And OpenAI's Rubik's cube hand made its simulation harder as its skill grew.

curriculum:15.t:
So that's curriculum learning.
When rewards are rare, start with easy versions of the task, and make them harder step by step.
Easy lessons pay often, and build the skills the hard task needs. Pace matters. And a teacher can pick the lessons.

metarl:0.t: Meta-R L: Learning to Learn. Train on many tasks so a new one takes minutes, not months.

metarl:1.t:
A new game. One room, five cups along the top, and the cheese under one of them.Pip can't see under a cup. It only finds out by stepping onto it.
Watch the cheese move. Each new maze, it hides under a different cup, and stays there for ten walks.

metarl:2.t:
First, plain Q-learning, treating every maze as brand new.Watch this walk. Pip wanders, and gets stopped after thirty steps.
The chart shows steps per walk, over three hundred new mazes.Even by walk ten, it still takes about twenty one steps. The shortest is about five.

metarl:3.t:
But these mazes are all alike. The cheese is always under a cup on the top row.
Meta R L trains on many related tasks, so a new one takes only a few tries.There are two loops. An inner one adapts to one maze. An outer one, across thousands of mazes, improves how the inner one adapts.

metarl:4.t:
Which cup hides the cheese is part of the state. And Pip can't see it.
That makes this a P O M D P, just like the fog reel.And the same fix applies. Memory, carried from one walk to the next.

metarl:5.t:
So give Pip a memory that survives between walks of one maze.
Watch the memory boxes fill. Empty cup. Another empty cup. Then the cheese.
It's wiped when a new maze begins. Pip is never told where the cheese is. It has to find out, and remember.

metarl:6.t:
The outer loop is ordinary Q-learning, on cell plus memory, across three thousand mazes.
Watch the mazes flick by.To collect the cheese fast in a new maze, the habit that pays is, search the cups, then remember.

metarl:7.t:
Now a new maze, with the cheese under cup five.
Watch walk one. Pip heads for the cups and looks under them, one by one. Ten steps.The memory now holds the spot.
Walk two. Straight there, six steps. The shortest.

metarl:8.t:
On new mazes, Pip's numbers are frozen. Yet it adapts.The fast learning lives in its memory. The slow outer loop learned a fast inner learner.
This is R L squared, from two groups in 2016.

metarl:9.t:
A second family of ideas is mammal. It keeps ordinary learning as the inner loop.
Instead, it learns good starting numbers, from which a few steps fit any maze.Our toy uses Reptile, a simpler cousin. Learn on one maze, move the start a little toward the result, and repeat thousands of times.

metarl:10.t:
Here's what the learned start knows.Watch the arrows. From any cell, they lead to the top row, and sweep along the cups.
It can't know which cup. That changes every maze. It only knows where the cups are.

metarl:11.t:
Now three learners, on the same new mazes.
Grey, from scratch, barely improves.Gold, the learned start, drops to under nine steps by walk three.Teal, with memory, takes nine steps on walk one, then under seven from then on.

metarl:12.t:
But meta learning only helps on tasks like its training ones.
New family. The cheese now hides on the left wall instead.By walk ten, the memory learner is the worst of the three.
Its memory only has slots for cups. It can't record this cheese.

metarl:13.t:
Your turn. Slide to change how many mazes the memory learner trained on.
Watch its line against the from scratch line.How much outer loop experience does it take before Pip has learned how to learn?

metarl:14.t:
Meta R L is studied for robots that must cope with a new load, a new floor, or a damaged leg, after just a few tries.
And for systems that must adapt quickly to a new user, or opponent.Most results so far are in simulation, on task families close together, like Pip's cups.

metarl:15.t:
So that's meta R L. Train on many related tasks, so a new one takes a few tries.
R L squared learns a fast learner that lives in memory. mammal learns a good starting point.
Both help only on tasks like those they trained on.
